file: 2003/2003-10-25_alternative universes_dilbert_therapy session_dense objects_space time fold_fabric_whats happening.gif
title: Therapist Diagnoses Dilbert's Spacetime Fold

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All week I felt like I was drifting through alternative universes. I was me, but I was different.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Have you been near any dense objects that would make the fabric of space-time fold onto itself?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One week ago

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will there be any unforeseen problems?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's happening to me?!!

setting: A therapist's office, then Dilbert's cubicle one week earlier
situation: Dilbert lies on a couch telling his therapist he spent the week feeling like he was drifting through alternative universes. She asks whether he has been near dense objects that could fold space-time. A flashback shows the Boss standing over Dilbert at his desk, asking if there will be any unforeseen problems, while Dilbert panics.
punchline: The 'dense object' warping Dilbert's reality is the Boss, whose cluelessness and absurd questions leave Dilbert feeling like he has slipped into another universe.
summary: A therapist's physics-flavored diagnosis of a patient's disorientation is answered by a flashback revealing the real source: his dim-witted boss.

file: 2003/2003-04-30_embezzelment_explain revenue_layoffs_sacrificing_worse than you_co worker.gif
title: Surviving Layoffs By Sacrificing Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You can survive the next round of layoffs by sacrificing a co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You must make your boss believe that someone is a worse employee than you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted, let me explain revenue: it's like your embezzlement, but it's directed at customers.

setting: Dilbert's office, then a meeting room
situation: Ratbert advises Dilbert that the way to survive the next round of layoffs is to sacrifice a co-worker by convincing the boss someone else is worse. In the final panel Dilbert is in a meeting, explaining the concept of revenue to Ted, a colleague who has been embezzling. Dilbert has apparently taken the advice and is throwing Ted under the bus.
punchline: Dilbert follows the cynical layoff-survival advice by publicly exposing Ted's embezzlement in the guise of a snide explanation of revenue.
summary: After a small pet's ruthless tip on outlasting job cuts, Dilbert pointedly mocks a coworker's theft in front of the bosses.

file: 2003/2003-04-21_hostile work environment_continuous pressure_work_work and drink_forty cups_cutting back.gif
title: Too Much Pressure To Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're creating a hostile work environment.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's like there's continuous pressure on me to work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I'm only one person; I can't work and drink coffee!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm cutting you back to forty cups a day.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, stands before the Boss's desk and complains that the company is creating a hostile work environment. His grievance is that there is constant pressure on him to actually work, which interferes with his coffee drinking. The Boss, mostly off-panel in the last frame, responds by cutting his coffee allowance to forty cups a day.
punchline: Wally considers being expected to work a form of harassment, and the Boss's 'punishment' is still an absurdly large forty cups of coffee daily.
summary: A lazy employee accuses his boss of harassment for expecting work from him, only to have his already excessive coffee quota trimmed to a still-ridiculous amount.

file: 2003/2003-07-05_winning streak_snowball_poker snowman_turn up heat_four queens_turn up furnace_melt snowman.gif
title: Devil Cheats Snowman With Furnace

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile in Heck...

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: You're on a winning streak, Snowball.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: But let's see what happens to your chances when I turn up the heat!

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: That's right - the furnace is broken again!

transcript.speaker: Snowman
transcript.text: Four queens.

situation: A devil and a snowman named Snowball play poker in Hell, and the snowman is winning. The devil threatens to turn up the heat and then phones in a complaint that the furnace is broken again. The snowman calmly lays down four queens, unbothered.
punchline: The devil assumes heat will rattle the snowman, but the snowman is so confident in his unbeatable hand that he ignores the threat, while the devil's complaint about a broken furnace in Hell is ironic.
summary: A devil tries to melt his snowman opponent into losing at poker, but the snowman simply shows a monster hand.

file: 2003/2003-09-18_actual question_delivery_fantasize_imaginary one_plastic casing_ripping moustache_two week.gif
title: Dodging the Question About Plastic Casings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you order the plastic casings I need?

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Clerk
transcript.text: They take two weeks for delivery.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see that you've cleverly avoided my actual question in favor of an imaginary one involving delivery times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'm fantasizing about ripping off your mustache and using it to shine your head.

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Clerk
transcript.text: I hear that a lot.

setting: Purchasing clerk's cubicle in the office
situation: Dilbert asks a purchasing clerk whether he ordered some plastic casings. The clerk answers with delivery times instead of saying yes or no. Dilbert calls out the evasion and threatens a bizarre fantasy about the clerk's mustache, and the clerk calmly says he's heard it before.
punchline: The clerk is so used to people threatening him with absurd violence over his evasive non-answers that Dilbert's elaborate fantasy barely fazes him.
summary: A purchasing clerk sidesteps a simple yes-or-no question, and the frustrated engineer responds with an oddly specific threat that the clerk has heard many times before.

file: 2003/2003-09-25_outsourcing_elbonia_time difference_hand off requirements_work day_finish code_pretend we died.gif
title: Elbonians Pretend They Died

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're outsourcing half of our programming work to Elbonia to take advantage of the time difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll hand off our requirements at the end of our work day and get back the finished code the next morning.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian programmer 1
transcript.text: Once again, I have no idea what they want.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian programmer 2
transcript.text: Let's pretend we died.

setting: A conference room in the office, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that half the programming work is being outsourced to Elbonia so that work can continue overnight thanks to the time difference. Requirements will be handed off at the end of the day and finished code returned by morning. In Elbonia, two programmers sitting in mud with a laptop admit they have no idea what the requirements mean and decide to fake their own deaths.
punchline: The outsourcing plan assumes the offshore team understands the vague requirements, but they are so confused they would rather pretend to be dead than deliver anything.
summary: Management brags about overnight offshore coding while the Elbonian developers, baffled by the instructions, plan to play dead rather than ask for clarification.

file: 2003/2003-10-15_used coffee sirrer_watsebacket_not maid_laziness.gif
title: Coffee Stirrer Power of Laziness

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey! You left a used coffee stirrer on the counter!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The wastebasket was one foot away! I am an associate, not your maid!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Behold the power of laziness.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So, I'll throw it away for you this time.

situation: Carol angrily scolds Wally for leaving a used coffee stirrer on the counter instead of putting it in the wastebasket a foot away. She insists she is an associate, not his maid. Wally, holding his mug, thinks to himself about the power of laziness while Carol ends up throwing the stirrer away for him.
punchline: Despite her indignant lecture, Carol ends up cleaning up after Wally anyway, proving that his laziness works because others will eventually do the task for him.
summary: A coworker's furious complaint about a messy break room still ends with her tidying up, confirming the slacker's strategy of letting others take over.

file: 2003/2003-02-18_evil hr director_flex time_long hours_eight to five_unpaid overtime_need to be flexible.gif
title: Flex Time Means Unpaid Overtime

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: From now on, the company will allow flex time.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You can work any hours you like, as long as you're here from eight to five.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's called unpaid overtime.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And you need to be flexible to do that to yourself, right?

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces a new flex time policy to employees gathered around a conference table. He explains that staff can pick any hours they like as long as they are present from eight to five. Dilbert points out that this is just unpaid overtime, and Catbert replies that employees must be flexible enough to do that to themselves.
punchline: The supposedly employee-friendly flex time policy has no real flexibility and merely disguises demanding extra unpaid work, with Catbert sarcastically twisting the word 'flexible' to blame employees for accepting it.
summary: An evil HR cat dresses up a rigid, fixed work schedule as a generous perk and then mocks the staff for not being flexible enough to exploit themselves.

file: 2003/2003-07-02_touch prototype_get shock_must touch_zap_second time.gif
title: Boss Can't Resist Shocking Prototype

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't touch the prototype or you'll get a shock.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Must touch.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: ZAP!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't touch it a second time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Must... touch... second... time.

setting: Engineering lab with a workbench holding a prototype
situation: Dilbert warns his boss not to touch the prototype or he will get shocked. The boss thinks to himself that he must touch it, does so, and gets zapped. Dilbert warns him again, and the singed, smoking boss is still compelled to touch it a second time.
punchline: The boss is so driven by compulsion and poor judgment that even a painful electric shock cannot stop him from repeating the same mistake.
summary: A warned manager zaps himself on a gadget and, though scorched, is still determined to try it again.

file: 2003/2003-07-24_unfunded man date_my delivery_no one laughs_unemployed guy.gif
title: Unfunded Man Date Falls Flat

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I went to a movie with an unemployed guy. I call that an unfunded man date.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The unemployed guy didn't laugh either. Maybe it's my delivery.

situation: Alice stands beside a coworker at his desk and delivers a joke about having gone to a movie with an unemployed man, calling it an 'unfunded man date.' The coworker stares at his computer and doesn't react. Alice then ponders in a thought bubble whether her delivery is the problem, since the unemployed guy didn't laugh either.
punchline: Alice jokes that her joke bombed with everyone, and blames her delivery rather than the fact that the joke is a poor, snarky one.
summary: A coworker stonily ignores Alice's pun about an unemployed date, leaving her to wonder why nobody finds her jokes funny.

file: 2003/2003-07-03_grow revenue_new products_calling in strategy_eliminate waste_miss you.gif
title: Obvious Ideas Passing as Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our strategy is to grow revenue from new products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How obvious does an idea need to be before we'll stop calling it a strategy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we plan to eliminate waste.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll miss you.

situation: The Boss announces to his team that the company's strategy is to grow revenue from new products. Dilbert asks how obvious an idea has to be before it stops being called a strategy. The Boss then adds that they plan to eliminate waste, and Dilbert replies that they'll miss him.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss himself is the biggest source of waste, so eliminating waste would mean getting rid of him.
summary: A manager unveils painfully obvious business goals, and a sarcastic engineer responds by suggesting the manager is the waste that should be cut.

file: 2003/2003-03-16_new faces_introductions_asok the intern_signed to everyone_conference room_upsetting introductions.gif
title: Asok's Imaginary Reporting Lines

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see some new faces. Let's go around the table and introduce ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am Asok, the intern.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I report to you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But I also report to Alice on a dotted line.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And I report to Carol on a fuzzy, thin line.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have a blinking, irregular line to Wally, and a wavy, brown line to Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please... make this stop.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And a disturbing, imaginary line to a food-service cashier who touched my hand while giving change.

situation: The Boss asks everyone at a meeting to introduce themselves, and Asok the intern explains who he reports to. He lists an ever-growing set of reporting relationships drawn as different kinds of lines, including dotted, fuzzy, blinking and wavy ones. Alice begs him to stop, and he finishes with an absurd line to a cashier who touched his hand.
punchline: Asok's endless reporting lines mock tangled matrix management, and the last one shows he treats a brief, accidental touch from a cashier as an organizational relationship.
summary: A flustered intern describes his convoluted chain of command with ever more bizarre kinds of lines, ending with an awkward personal one.

file: 2003/2003-12-16_engineers_jobs_want job your job_falling out of trees_dime a dozen_intimidation_job on line_idle threats.gif
title: Engineers Falling Out of Trees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The woods are full of people who want your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These days you can't shake a tree without three or four engineers falling out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd love to stay and chat but I need to go motivate the other headcounts.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert at his desk and warns him that plenty of people want his job, claiming you can't shake a tree without engineers falling out. He then announces he must leave to go motivate the other 'headcounts'. Dilbert sits silently at his computer throughout.
punchline: The Boss motivates employees through threats of replacement and refers to people as 'headcounts', showing he views workers as interchangeable numbers rather than individuals.
summary: A manager tries to inspire his engineer by warning that desperate replacements are everywhere, then rushes off to threaten the rest of his staff.

file: 2003/2003-03-15_cutomers_delivery_business_took money_winner_lied.gif
title: Taking Money, Delivering Nothing, Winning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A customer keeps asking when we'll deliver the stuff they bought.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will we?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never. You lied to them to get their business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You took their money and gave them nothing. Do you know what that makes you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The winner!

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that a customer keeps asking when their purchase will be delivered. The Boss casually asks when it will be, and Dilbert explains it never will because the sale was based on lies. When Dilbert asks if the Boss knows what that makes him, the Boss proudly replies that he is the winner.
punchline: The Boss sees defrauding a customer as a victory rather than a moral failing, reflecting a business culture that rewards deception and getting paid over delivering value.
summary: A manager cheerfully embraces having sold a customer something that will never be delivered, treating the swindle as a triumph.

file: 2003/2003-11-06_new guy_new hire_bottleneck_bill_titanium.gif
title: Bottleneck Bill's Titanium Neck

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bottleneck Bill

transcript.speaker: Bottleneck Bill
transcript.text: All purchase orders must be approved by me.

transcript.speaker: Bottleneck Bill
transcript.text: I'll be too busy to approve anything, but at least we have a system.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Grrrr

transcript.speaker: Bottleneck Bill
transcript.text: It's titanium. Nice try.

situation: A new colleague with a long, narrow neck named Bottleneck Bill announces that every purchase order must pass through him for approval. He admits he'll be too busy to approve anything, but is pleased to have a system. Alice grows angry and tries to strangle his neck, only to learn it is made of titanium.
punchline: A man literally shaped like a bottleneck creates a bureaucratic bottleneck, and his neck is armored against the frustrated people who want to throttle him.
summary: A manager with a bottle-shaped neck insists on approving all purchases despite having no time, and his exasperated coworker discovers he is strangle-proof.

file: 2003/2003-01-28_funding_continuous harping_expensive consultant_analyze budget_chaos_complexity_simulations.gif
title: Consultant Confirms You Need Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In response to your continuous harping about not having enough funding...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an expensive consultant to analyze your budget.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'll have to run some chaos and complexity simulations, but it looks as if you need more money.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and a conference room
situation: After Dilbert repeatedly complains about insufficient funding, The Boss responds by hiring an expensive consultant to analyze the budget. The consultant sits across a table from Dilbert and announces that he must run elaborate simulations, but he can already tell that more money is needed.
punchline: The company spent a large sum on a consultant only to be told the obvious conclusion Dilbert had been stating all along, which is that the budget is too small.
summary: Rather than simply listening to a complaint about underfunding, management pays a pricey outsider to reach the same verdict using impressive-sounding jargon.

file: 2003/2003-12-12_product training_pride in product line_users experience_painful boils_relatively satisfied customers_techniques.gif
title: Relatively Satisfied Boil Customers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Product training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: You work for a company that takes pride in its product line.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Only half of our users experience painful boils.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: We call that group the "relatively satisfied" customers.

transcript.speaker: Headless Man
transcript.text: What the?!

setting: Conference room during a product training session
situation: A trainer lectures employees about the company's product line, then points to a slide showing a 'yes' user covered in painful boils and a 'no' user who is unaffected. He cheerfully labels the group that gets boils the 'relatively satisfied' customers, while the slide reveals the 'no' user has been left headless.
punchline: The company spins a product that gives half its users painful boils (and apparently decapitates others) as 'relatively satisfied' customers, showing absurd corporate euphemism about product defects.
summary: A cheerful trainer spins horrific side effects of the company's product into a positive marketing talking point.

file: 2003/2003-03-26_furniture psychic_old chair_passed.gif
title: Furniture Psychic Channels Dead Chair

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Furniture psychic

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your old chair has passed to the other side.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He says you'll know what this means: "Squeak, squeak."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your desk says, "Thanks for the gum."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need closure!

situation: Dogbert, wearing a purple striped hat, poses as a furniture psychic and tells The Boss that his old chair has died. He relays the chair's squeaky final message and then a thank-you from the desk for the gum stuck to it. The Boss, tearful and clutching a tissue, says he needs closure.
punchline: The Boss is so emotionally attached to his office furniture that he pays a con-artist psychic to deliver messages from his dead chair, and the desk's thanks for the gum stuck to it is a ridiculous detail he finds comforting.
summary: Dogbert cons a sentimental boss by pretending to relay messages from his deceased office chair and desk.

file: 2003/2003-06-14_chapter 23_photo copy_see how yourself_books_full of information_entertainment.gif
title: Boss Cites Book on Your Defects

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see... your defects are discussed in chapter 23.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you a photocopy so you can see how to fix yourself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Books are full of information.

situation: The Boss leafs through a book while standing behind seated Dilbert, announcing that Dilbert's defects are covered in chapter 23. He offers a photocopy so Dilbert can learn how to fix himself. Walking away, he muses to himself that books are full of information.
punchline: The Boss thinks he is being helpful and insightful, but he is just handing off a generic book chapter instead of offering any real management or feedback, and treats the trivial observation that books contain information as a profound discovery.
summary: A manager responds to an employee's flaws by passing along a photocopied book chapter and then congratulates himself on the wisdom of reading.

file: 2003/2003-07-11_are years ago_this year_futire_free soft drinks_free coffee_bottled water.gif
title: Escalating Perk Cuts Reach Saliva

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A few years ago

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company will no longer provide free soft drinks.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This year

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No more free coffee, and no more free bottled water.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In the future

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't swallow your saliva.

setting: Catbert's office desk, shown across three time periods
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, announces a series of cost-cutting measures over time. First the free soft drinks are cut, then free coffee and bottled water. In the future, a robotic, cyborg-like Catbert issues an instruction not to swallow saliva.
punchline: Corporate cost-cutting on employee perks escalates so absurdly that eventually even employees' own saliva is treated as a company resource to be conserved.
summary: A feline HR boss strips away workplace beverage perks step by step until the final cut is absurdly extreme.

file: 2003/2003-07-12_email spam blocker_outgoing messages_software_worthless_sentient being_only hope_demoralize to death_calendar_engineering.gif
title: Spam Blocker Becomes Sentient, Boss Demoralizes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our e-mail spam blocker is stopping all incoming and outgoing messages.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently the software decided that everything we do is a bunch of worthless #$!%@.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I fear that it's becoming a sentient being. Our only hope is for you to demoralize it to death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell it to get on my calendar.

situation: Dilbert reports that the company's e-mail spam blocker is blocking every message, because the software has judged everything the employees do to be worthless. He fears it is becoming sentient and suggests the Boss, who is skilled at demoralizing people, is their only hope of defeating it. The Boss responds by telling the software to get on his calendar, treating it like any other appointment.
punchline: The Boss's reaction to a potentially sentient, malfunctioning AI is simply to route it through his calendar, showing bureaucratic indifference and a casual acceptance of his own reputation as a morale-killer.
summary: When a mail filter starts judging employees' work as garbage and may be gaining consciousness, the manager treats the crisis as just another scheduling request.

file: 2003/2003-04-12_orchestra od data_ironic spelling_geneous mistro.gif
title: Misspelled Genius Maestro Product Name

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: We named the product "Geneous Mistro" because it conducts an orchestra of data.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Can you believe the domain name "geneousmistro" wasn't already taken?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the spelling meant to be ironic?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Why do you ask?

situation: A presenter holds up a sign for a new product called "Geneous Mistro" and explains the orchestra-of-data naming idea. He boasts that the domain name was still available. Dilbert asks if the misspelling is intentional irony, and the presenter obliviously asks why he would ask.
punchline: The presenter is so unaware that he misspelled "genius maestro" that he doesn't understand why the name is ironic, and the available domain is explained by nobody else spelling it that badly.
summary: A product namer proudly unveils a butchered spelling of "genius maestro" and remains clueless when someone points out the irony.

file: 2003/2003-12-28_hired wife_mean_condescending_slave driver_obnoxious.gif
title: The Boss's Tyrannical Receptionist Wife

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired my wife to be our new receptionist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I foresee no problems whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Hey, dipweed!

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Go buy me a bagel and a cappuccino.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Then wash my car and fill the gas tank.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Now dance for me, little man! Ha ha! Dance or I'll have you fired!!!

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: How may I help you?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Have a nice day!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop dancing in the lobby. My wife is trying to work.

situation: The Boss announces in a meeting that he has hired his wife as the new receptionist. She immediately abuses her position, ordering Dilbert to fetch food, wash her car, and dance for her under threat of getting him fired. She switches to a sweet telephone voice for callers, and the Boss ends up scolding Dilbert for dancing in the lobby.
punchline: The Boss's nepotism hire gives his wife power over Dilbert, and the Boss blames Dilbert for the very behavior his wife forced on him, since he foresaw no problems whatsoever.
summary: A boss hands his domineering spouse the front desk job, and she turns an engineer into her personal servant while the boss scolds the victim.

file: 2003/2003-08-09_two hour presentation_incomprehensible_powre point_disability_content.gif
title: Was There Content in That?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: That concludes my two-hour presentation. Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you intend the presentation to be incomprehensible, or do you have some sort of rare "PowerPoint" disability?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Are there any questions about the content?

transcript.speaker: Audience member
transcript.text: There was content?

setting: Conference room during a slide presentation
situation: A presenter finishes a two-hour slide presentation and asks for questions. Dilbert asks whether the presentation was deliberately incomprehensible or the result of a PowerPoint disability. When the presenter then asks about the content, an audience member off-panel asks if there was any content at all.
punchline: The presentation was so convoluted and empty that the audience can't even tell it contained any actual content.
summary: After a marathon slide show, the audience's confusion is so complete that they doubt the talk had any substance whatsoever.

file: 2003/2003-09-07_blame game_back and fourth_forgotten_no time_didn't look_tattoo on chest_no time torso_read torso_stickin chest.gif
title: Tattooed Request on Boss's Chest

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You never responded to my urgent request for engineering resources.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told Alice to ask you!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She must have forgotten.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I sent you three e-mail messages.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You know I don't have time to read my e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And I sent you a voice-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You know I don't have time for voice-mails.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's why I also...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Tattooed it on your stinkin' chest!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As if I have time to read my torso.

situation: Dilbert complains in a meeting that his urgent request for engineering resources was never answered. The Boss blames Alice, who says she sent e-mails and a voice-mail, both of which the Boss says he has no time to read or hear. Alice grabs him and reveals she tattooed the message on his chest, and he still refuses to read it.
punchline: The Boss is so determined to avoid reading anything that he rejects even a message tattooed on his own body, showing his excuses have no limit.
summary: A manager who ignores every form of communication brushes off even a request literally inked onto his torso.

file: 2003/2003-10-06_consulting firm_fixing business strategies_own industry_doing bad_never mention.gif
title: Consultant Pays For Dilbert's Silence

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: My consulting firm specializes in fixing business strategies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever figured out why your own industry is in the toilet?

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'll give you a thousand dollars never to mention that again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: OK.

situation: A consultant pitches Dilbert on his firm's ability to fix business strategies. Dilbert asks whether the consultant has ever worked out why the consulting industry itself is doing so badly. The consultant quickly offers a thousand dollars to make Dilbert never raise the subject again, and Dilbert accepts.
punchline: The consultant tries to buy silence rather than answer the question, which implies the consulting industry cannot fix its own problems and Dilbert's point is uncomfortably true.
summary: A consultant boasting about repairing other companies' strategies pays Dilbert to stop pointing out that his own field is failing.

file: 2003/2003-12-24_downsized_gag gifts_goodby lunch_not retired_tuesday_party_gifts_mean soirited_office party.gif
title: Gag Gifts for Downsized Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I scheduled your good-bye lunch for Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't make it on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's too late to change it. Everyone already bought your gag gifts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gag gifts?? I'm not retiring; I got downsized!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Congratulations, Alice! Hee-hee!!

situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Alice he has scheduled her good-bye lunch, and when she says she can't make it he insists it's too late because everyone has already bought gag gifts. Alice, carrying a box of her belongings, angrily points out that she is not retiring but has been downsized. A clueless coworker then congratulates her while holding a wrinkle cream gift.
punchline: The company treats a layoff as a retirement celebration, with joke gifts and congratulations, ignoring that Alice has just lost her job.
summary: A boss plans a festive farewell lunch for an employee who was actually laid off, and her colleagues cluelessly celebrate with novelty presents.

file: 2003/2003-03-17_brainstorm ideas_employee morale enhancement_pin the tail_boss_employees_hatred_low morale_business.gif
title: Pin the Tail on the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's brainstorm ideas for "Employee Morale-Enhancement Day."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We could play "Pin the tail on the pointy-haired weasel whose breath smells like feet."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We might need more morale-enhancement days.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How about this weekend when I'm not here?

situation: The Boss asks his staff to brainstorm ideas for an Employee Morale-Enhancement Day. Alice suggests a game that amounts to insulting him to his face, and the Boss misses the point, concluding that morale is so low they need more such days. Catbert, sitting on the table, suggests holding the next one on a weekend when he won't be there.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious that the employees' idea of a morale booster is mocking him, and instead of recognizing the insult, he decides more morale days are needed.
summary: Asked to dream up a morale-boosting event, the staff proposes a game that targets their smelly-breathed manager, who takes it as proof that morale is even worse than he thought.

file: 2003/2003-04-20_script for meeting_script_twice a year_act one_scene two_admiration_leadership_employment_deliver line_eyes moist_sliced onion_morale.gif
title: Scripting Admiration for the Boss's Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's your script for the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Script?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My boss sees me only twice a year. I want everything to go smoothly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In Act One, Scene Two, when I proclaim my admiration for your leadership...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's my motivation?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good, good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And it would help if your eyes were moist when you deliver the line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll put a sliced onion in my shirt pocket.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hello, underling. How is your morale?

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a script to follow in a meeting with the Boss's own boss, so that everything appears to go smoothly. Dilbert treats it like an acting job, asking for his motivation and planning to use a sliced onion to produce moist eyes. In the meeting, the Boss cheerfully asks Dilbert how his morale is, and Dilbert is visibly in tears.
punchline: Dilbert's onion-induced tears undermine the staged display of admiration and high morale, exposing the whole performance as fake.
summary: A manager rehearses his employee in a fake show of devotion for a visiting executive, and the forced tears give the game away.

file: 2003/2003-04-11_dental appointement_cubilces_scowl_menaced_walk amongst workers_body double.gif
title: Boss Delegates His Scowling Duty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm leaving early, in case I have a dental appointment or whatnot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Walk amongst the cubicles until 7 p.m. and scowl at anyone who isn't working.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice scowl. I feel slightly menaced.

situation: The Boss announces he is leaving early and orders another pointy-haired manager to patrol the cubicles until 7 p.m., scowling at anyone not working. The stand-in manager carries out the order and scowls at a seated employee holding a coffee mug, who dryly critiques the scowl.
punchline: The Boss's idea of supervision is reduced to intimidation by scowling, and the employee is only mildly menaced, showing how ineffective and hollow the tactic is.
summary: A manager sneaks off early and appoints a substitute to intimidate staff into looking busy, but the scowl barely registers with the unimpressed employee.

file: 2003/2003-12-10_global economy_vibrant_fly bait_reformatted_disguise true objective.gif
title: Dilbert's Vibrant Economy Meets Pointless Reformatting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's workers like me that make the global economy so vibrant.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The Pointy-Haired fly-bait wants this reformatted to disguise his true objective.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When you're done, don't show it to anyone. No one cares.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Zesty!

situation: Dilbert arrives at work carrying his briefcase, musing proudly that workers like him make the global economy vibrant. Alice hands him a document and tells him the boss wants it reformatted to hide his real goal. She adds that no one will ever look at the result, and Dilbert enthusiastically says 'Zesty!'.
punchline: Dilbert's grand view of his contribution to the economy collapses into a pointless reformatting task that nobody will read, and his cheerful 'Zesty!' is a sarcastic reaction to the absurdity.
summary: A self-important Dilbert daydreams about his economic significance, then is handed a make-work document that exists only to obscure the boss's intentions and will never be seen.

file: 2003/2003-05-30_new product brochures_design awards_great_award winning designer_can't stop complaining.gif
title: Award-Winning Brochure Misrepresents Product

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: The new product brochures have already won design awards!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's great, but our product won't do any of the things you claim here.

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: Well, who should we believe — the award-winning designer or the guy who can't stop complaining?

situation: A designer proudly announces that the new product brochures have already won design awards. Dilbert points out that the product cannot actually do any of the things the brochure claims. The designer dismisses the concern by asking whether to trust an award-winning designer or a chronic complainer, and the boss sits by without objecting.
punchline: Winning a design award is treated as proof that the brochure's claims are true, so the engineer's factual objection is brushed off as mere complaining.
summary: A designer shrugs off an engineer's warning that a prizewinning brochure promises features the product lacks, by pointing to the trophy and the engineer's reputation for whining.

file: 2003/2003-01-20_bad person_crud_despicable_loathesome_rehearsed_walks with dog_unethical.gif
title: Dogbert's Rehearsed Insult About Crud

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work for an unethical company. Does that make me a bad person?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're loathsome and despicable. If crud wore shoes, you would be the crud in the crud's shoes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did that seem rehearsed?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's all I think about when we go for walks.

setting: A grassy hillside path where Dilbert is walking Dogbert
situation: While out walking Dogbert, Dilbert asks whether working for an unethical company makes him a bad person. Dogbert answers with an elaborate, poetic insult. Dilbert notices it sounded prepared, and Dogbert admits he spends their walks thinking up insults.
punchline: Dogbert's eloquent insult was pre-planned because he spends every walk composing put-downs, implying he has long considered Dilbert loathsome.
summary: Dilbert seeks moral reassurance from his dog on a stroll and instead gets a polished tirade that turns out to have been prepared in advance.

file: 2003/2003-12-27_the boss_product awareness class_hands on training_next version.gif
title: Product Awareness Class Torture Demo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I signed you up for a product awareness class.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They'll give you hands-on training for every product we sell.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ple-e-ease...

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: We're hoping to fix this problem in the next version.

situation: The Boss announces he has enrolled Dilbert in a product awareness class and promises hands-on training with every product the company sells. Dilbert recoils in dread and begs him not to. In the final panel, the instructor demonstrates a product that is clearly hurting a man hooked up to a device on his head, and says the flaw should be fixed in the next release.
punchline: The hands-on product demo visibly injures the volunteer, yet the instructor treats the painful defect as a minor issue to be patched in a future version.
summary: A manager sends his employee to learn the company's products firsthand, where an instructor casually shrugs off the agonizing flaw in a device that is hurting a man.

file: 2003/2003-11-10_ted_forward to ted_email_solved problems_project_being rude_remove from project.gif
title: Complaining About Ted By Email

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted is being rude and unhelpful. Can you ask his boss to remove him from the project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll forward this to Ted. That should help.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder how people solved problems before e-mail.

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert sends an email asking the boss to have Ted, who is rude and unhelpful, removed from the project. The boss thinks the solution is to forward the complaint straight to Ted himself. An angry Ted then storms up to Dilbert's cubicle while Dilbert muses about life before email.
punchline: Forwarding a complaint to the person being complained about is a spectacularly bad solution, and Dilbert sarcastically wonders how problems were ever solved before email made this possible.
summary: A request to get a difficult coworker taken off a project backfires when the manager simply passes the complaint along to the coworker himself.

file: 2003/2003-09-17_audio lessons_hundred million_showing up_performing ceo_be the person_buy audio lessons.gif
title: Audio Lessons for Underperforming CEOs

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: Would you like to make a hundred million dollars for just showing up at work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My audio lessons teach you how to become an underperforming CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Step one: Become a CEO. Step two: Be the sort of person who would buy these audio lessons.

setting: A living room with a TV, and then an office
situation: The Boss lounges in an armchair watching a TV infomercial in which Dogbert pitches audio lessons promising riches for merely showing up at work. Dogbert says the lessons teach how to become an underperforming CEO. In the last panel the Boss, now at his office desk wearing headphones, listens to the lessons, whose two steps reveal the scheme's catch.
punchline: The 'lessons' are useless because step one is simply to become a CEO, and step two mocks the gullible type of person who would buy such lessons, meaning the Boss is the sucker being scammed.
summary: A late-night infomercial from Dogbert sells a get-rich plan whose only real advice is to already be a CEO and a gullible buyer.

file: 2003/2003-11-05_too busy_bottleneck_document_desk_office.gif
title: Bill the Bottleneck's Document Pile

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't do any more work on my project until you give your input, but you're too busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no polite way to say this: Bill, you're a bottleneck.

transcript.speaker: Bill
transcript.text: Your document is now saying hi to the bottom of the pile.

setting: Office, at a manager's desk stacked with paper
situation: Dilbert tells a busy manager named Bill that his project is stalled because it needs Bill's input and Bill has no time. Dilbert bluntly calls him a bottleneck. Bill responds by burying Dilbert's document at the bottom of his pile of paperwork.
punchline: Criticizing the bottleneck for delaying work just gets Dilbert's document punished by being moved to the bottom of the pile, making the delay worse.
summary: A frustrated engineer accuses a swamped manager of stalling progress, and the manager retaliates by burying his paperwork even deeper.

file: 2003/2003-06-10_wants a husbnd_cooks and cleans_raises kids_pursue career_total turn on_lemon wedges.gif
title: Alice's Ideal Househusband Appears

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I want a husband who cooks and cleans and raises the kids while I pursue my career.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: To me, that sort of man would be a total turn-on.

transcript.speaker: Man in apron
transcript.text: Yoo-hoo! Who likes lemon wedges?

situation: Alice, with her big dark hair, tells a coworker nearby that she wants a husband who handles the cooking, cleaning and child-rearing so she can focus on her career. She adds that such a man would be a total turn-on. A smiling man in an apron then walks up carrying a plate of lemon wedges, and a heart appears over Alice's head.
punchline: Alice's stated fantasy of a domestic, supportive husband is instantly embodied by an apron-wearing man offering snacks, and she is visibly smitten.
summary: A career-driven woman describes her dream of a homemaker spouse, and one promptly shows up with a snack tray, winning her heart.

file: 2003/2003-04-10_walk into ambushes_trap you_helpful_body double_new body double.gif
title: Boss's Body Double Avoids Helpfulness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, as my new body double, your job is to walk into ambushes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If someone tries to trap you into being helpful, do what I would do.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What would you do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd get a body double.

situation: The Boss tells Asok that his new role as body double is to walk into ambushes on the Boss's behalf. He instructs Asok to respond to anyone trying to trap him into being helpful exactly as the Boss would. When Asok asks what that is, the Boss admits he would simply get a body double.
punchline: The Boss's only strategy for avoiding being helpful is to pass the job to someone else, so his instructions are circular and he is really just dumping the unpleasant work on Asok.
summary: A manager hires an underling to stand in for him at risky encounters, then reveals his coping technique is to hire yet another stand-in.

file: 2003/2003-04-19_training_worlds longest joke_criminally abusive_behavior and fun_fine line behaviors.gif
title: Training Or World's Longest Practical Joke

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So Ted has been training you for the past six months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Based on your work, I'd say he's playing the world's longest practical joke on you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Sometimes there's a fine line between criminally abusive behavior and fun.

situation: The Boss meets with an employee holding a paper and says Ted has been training the employee for six months. Judging by the employee's poor work, the Boss concludes Ted must be playing a long practical joke on him. In the last panel, a cheerful Ted cheerfully admits there is a fine line between criminally abusive behavior and fun, while the employee glares angrily.
punchline: Ted cheerfully admits that his deliberately bad training was a prank, brushing off the abuse as fun while the victim of the joke seethes.
summary: A trainee's terrible performance gets blamed on his mentor, who gleefully confesses to sabotaging him for sport.

file: 2003/2003-03-01_fire toxic co worker_lazy and ineffectual_selfish_toxic guy_wally.gif
title: Demanding Firing of Toxic Co-Worker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We demand that you fire our toxic co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You aren't talking about me, are you?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, you're lazy and ineffectual with an overlay of selfish.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I hate the toxic guy?

situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice confront the boss, demanding that a toxic co-worker be fired. Wally nervously asks whether they mean him, and Alice says no, listing his actual flaws as lazy, ineffectual and selfish.
punchline: Wally is relieved he isn't the toxic one, even though Alice's description of him as lazy, ineffectual and selfish is hardly flattering.
summary: A team wants a toxic colleague removed, and the one person who fears it's him gets reassured with an insult that he happily accepts.

file: 2003/2003-06-12_stay at home father_love children_rewarding lifestyle_unpaid servant_could iron.gif
title: Stay-at-Home Dad or Unpaid Servant

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If we married, would you mind being a stay-at-home father?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I love children. That would be a very rewarding lifestyle.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Okay, now imagine that there aren't any kids, and you're basically my unpaid servant.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Could I iron?

setting: A restaurant table during a date
situation: A woman asks her date whether he would be willing to be a stay-at-home father if they married. He enthusiastically says he loves children and would find it rewarding. She then removes the children from the picture, describing the job as being her unpaid servant, and he eagerly asks if he could iron.
punchline: The man is so eager to please that he accepts the role of unpaid servant and even volunteers for the chore of ironing.
summary: A dating conversation about domestic roles turns when a man happily agrees to serve his prospective wife without pay and asks to take on the ironing.

file: 2003/2003-01-14_bad advice_burrowing in torso_consultick_implement.gif
title: The Consultick Burrows Into Management

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Consultick

transcript.speaker: Unidentified Coworker
transcript.text: He'll do more than give us bad advice...

transcript.speaker: Unidentified Coworker
transcript.text: He'll also make sure we can't implement it without him.

transcript.speaker: Unidentified Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! Now he's burrowing into my torso, and I've convinced myself it's okay.

situation: During a meeting, a manager warns colleagues about a parasite-like consultant, a 'Consultick', who gives bad advice and makes himself indispensable for implementing it. As he explains, the consultant in the red jacket burrows into the manager's torso like a tick, and the manager cheerfully rationalizes it.
punchline: Consultants latch onto a company like ticks, and the host organization talks itself into accepting the harm because it has become dependent on them.
summary: A colleague describes how a tick-like consultant entrenches himself, then happily denies the problem while the consultant burrows into his body.

file: 2003/2003-12-26_rehired_alice back_dulled instincts_first day abck_business picking up.gif
title: Rehired Engineer Returns Looking Frazzled

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Business is picking up. We need to rehire some of the people that we downsized.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope the time off from work hasn't dulled their engineering instincts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first day back is always the hardest.

situation: The Boss, with Catbert sitting on his desk, says business is improving and that downsized employees need to be rehired. He worries their engineering skills may have dulled during their time off. In the last panel a rehired engineer with wildly disheveled hair and a stunned expression sits in front of his desk while he cheerfully comments on how hard the first day back is.
punchline: The boss is concerned about the employee's rusty skills, but her wild-haired, traumatized look shows that being laid off and then rehired has been far harder on her than he realizes.
summary: After laying off staff, management cheerfully rehires them while fretting about their skills, oblivious to the wreck the experience has made of one returning engineer.

file: 2003/2003-06-08_career counseling_hear myself talk_roll their eyes_nod and smaile_babble_punish people_management aptitude test.gif
title: Management Aptitude Test Passed Instantly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Career counseling

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I love to hear myself talk.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: But I don't like it when people roll their eyes and go "Phhht."

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I'd like a job where people are forced to nod and smile while I babble.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: And I'd like to punish people for my own mistakes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend a career in management.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just to be sure, I'm going to give you a management aptitude test.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Hey, I have an idea. Maybe I should pursue a career in management!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Congratulations! You just passed the management aptitude test.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Yes!

situation: Dogbert acts as a career counselor while a client lists the things he wants from a job: talking constantly, having people forced to listen and smile, and blaming others for his own mistakes. Dogbert recommends management and offers an aptitude test. The client then proposes management as his own idea and instantly passes.
punchline: The traits the man wants in a job are exactly what management rewards, so simply suggesting a management career proves he is qualified.
summary: A man seeking career advice describes a dream job that is really just a description of being a boss, and a canine counselor declares him a natural.

file: 2003/2003-12-01_evil director_merger_extra work_must be reason_tax thing.gif
title: Catbert Skips Merger Communication Because Laziness

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to tell our employees about the merger.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They'll read it in the news. Why should we do extra work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Other companies do it. There must be a reason.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's a tax thing.

setting: Catbert's office in the human resources department
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that employees should be informed about an upcoming merger. Catbert refuses, arguing they will learn about it from the news anyway and it would be extra work. When the Boss points out that other companies do it for some reason, Catbert guesses it's for tax purposes.
punchline: Catbert can't imagine any reason to treat employees decently, so the only explanation he can think of for telling workers about a merger is a tax benefit.
summary: An HR director would rather let staff learn of a corporate merger from the media than lift a finger to inform them, and assumes any such courtesy must be a tax dodge.

file: 2003/2003-04-07_dogbert_headhunter_stock up_ceo_random upturns_make millions_changing jobs_legal_victims.gif
title: Dogbert Headhunts for Opportunistic CEOs

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert the headhunter. I noticed that your company's stock is up today.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As CEO, you can take credit for random upturns and make millions by changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ha, ha! Yes, it's legal. In fact, if you write a book, your victims will buy it!

setting: Dogbert's office, at a desk with a phone
situation: Dogbert, working as an executive headhunter, phones a company's CEO after noticing the stock price rose. He pitches the idea of claiming credit for luck-driven gains and then cashing in by jumping to another company. He assures the CEO it is legal and that a book about it would even sell to the people he left behind.
punchline: Dogbert points out that CEOs can profit from random stock gains and then sell a book to the very employees and investors they exploited.
summary: A scheming headhunter coaches a chief executive on turning luck into a fortune by hopping jobs and then profiting again with a memoir.

file: 2003/2003-07-30_laughs alot_hired_morale_big impact_crazy alice.gif
title: Hired for Constant Laughing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You laugh at everything, whether it's funny or not.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!! It's true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired. You'll have a big impact on morale!

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!! Yes, I will!

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!! Computers are funny! Ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must stay alive.

setting: Boss's office interview, then office cubicles
situation: The Boss interviews a woman who laughs at everything, and he hires her, saying she will boost morale. In the final panel she sits in a nearby cubicle, still laughing loudly, while Alice, in the next cubicle, clutches her head in torment.
punchline: The new hire's constant, meaningless laughter is so grating that instead of improving morale it drives coworkers like Alice to the brink of madness.
summary: A manager hires a compulsive giggler to cheer up the office, but her nonstop laughter nearly breaks the neighbor in the next cubicle.

file: 2003/2003-02-15_downsized_good news_half huge raises_same people_ran numbers.gif
title: Half Get Raises, Half Get Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The good news is that half of you will get huge raises.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The bad news is that half of you will be downsized tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it the same people?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, we ran the numbers.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss addresses his team at a meeting table, announcing both good and bad news: half of them will get huge raises and half will be downsized the next day. Dilbert asks whether it's the same people, and the Boss confirms that it is, because they ran the numbers.
punchline: The company is funding raises for the survivors by laying off the others, so the 'good news' and 'bad news' are really just the same cost-cutting decision presented as two separate announcements.
summary: A manager cheerfully pairs a promise of big raises with an announcement of layoffs, and it turns out the raises are paid for by the people being let go.

file: 2003/2003-02-19_100 hrs a week_ask for raise_top secret facilit_super genius_resume_honest_take one_know one.gif
title: Honest Candidate Promises Impossible Claims

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: If you hire me, I'll work a hundred hours a week and never ask for a raise!

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I went to school at a top-secret facility for super geniuses; that's why it's not on my résumé.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I'm sure it's all true because he says he's honest!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Apparently it doesn't take one to know one.

setting: Boss's office during a job interview
situation: A job candidate makes increasingly absurd claims in an interview: he'll work a hundred hours a week without a raise, and he attended a secret genius school that conveniently isn't on his résumé. The Boss, who is the interviewer, says he believes it all because the candidate claims to be honest. Catbert, the evil HR director, quips that it apparently doesn't take one to know one.
punchline: The Boss gullibly believes an obviously dishonest candidate because the man simply says he's honest, and Catbert's twisted proverb points out that the Boss can't spot a liar even though he's a deceptive manager himself.
summary: A boss swallows an applicant's outlandish, unverifiable boasts on the strength of his self-declared honesty while the HR cat sarcastically notes the boss can't recognize a fellow fibber.

file: 2003/2003-04-26_processor load_took advice_laser pointers_light sabers.gif
title: Laser Pointer Torso Joke Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our breakthrough came when we distributed the processor load.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's about time that you took my advice! Hallelujah! Good for you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If laser pointers were light sabers, you'd be looking for your torso.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! You're using my joke! Good one!

situation: Dilbert presents a diagram showing processor load being distributed and explains it was the team's breakthrough. A coworker at the table cheers that Dilbert finally took his advice. Dilbert threatens him with a laser pointer, saying it would cut him in half if it were a light saber, and the coworker cheerfully praises Dilbert for using his joke.
punchline: Dilbert's menacing light saber threat is lost on the oblivious coworker, who only notices that Dilbert borrowed his joke.
summary: A presenter's irritation at an overeager colleague turns into a violent quip that the colleague mistakes for flattery.

file: 2003/2003-08-16_process of getting approval_hard way_meeting_no direct answers_business.gif
title: Man Who Won't Answer Directly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The man who couldn't give direct answers

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you ask your boss for approval?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Now I will explain the process for getting approval.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you want to do this the hard way?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: First, you ask for a meeting.

situation: Alice asks a bald coworker a simple yes-or-no question about whether he got his boss's approval. Instead of answering, he launches into an explanation of the approval process. Alice threatens to do things the hard way, and he simply continues with step one of the process.
punchline: The coworker is so committed to bureaucratic process that he cannot answer a simple question, and even a threat from Alice doesn't stop him from starting the explanation.
summary: A colleague responds to a simple approval question by lecturing on the bureaucratic steps involved, ignoring a coworker's growing irritation.

file: 2003/2003-09-08_send broadband_send data_sewer system.gif
title: Sending Data Through the Sewer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our competitors found a way to send broadband Internet traffic over the power grid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to find a way to send data via the sewer system.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I thought I was already doing it.

situation: The Boss tells a seated, glasses-wearing engineer that competitors are sending broadband over the power grid. He then demands that the engineer find a way to send data through the sewer system. The engineer walks out with a coffee mug and newspaper, privately thinking he is already doing it.
punchline: The engineer's own work is so poor or so crude that he assumes he has already been pushing data through the sewer, implying his output is garbage.
summary: A manager responds to a rival's innovation by demanding an absurd sewer-based data network, and his employee quietly suspects his work already qualifies.

file: 2003/2003-03-29_pecking order_fool_stupid_dilbert_coffee cup.gif
title: Yelling Rolls Down to Coffee Mug

transcript.speaker: Upper Manager
transcript.text: You fool! How could you be so stupid?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You fool! How could you be so stupid?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You stupid coffee mug!!

setting: Corporate office: an executive's office, then a hallway by Dilbert's cubicle, then the cubicle
situation: An executive angrily berates the Boss in his office. The Boss then repeats the exact same insult to Dilbert, who sits at his desk. Dilbert, now at the bottom of the chain, takes it out on his coffee mug.
punchline: Blame cascades down the corporate hierarchy until the lowest-ranking person has only an inanimate coffee mug left to yell at.
summary: A scolding is passed down each rung of the management ladder until it lands on a cup of coffee.

file: 2003/2003-03-21_user requirements_build system_some actual work_crazy talk.gif
title: User Requirements Mean Actual Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll design the system as soon as you give me the user requirements.

transcript.speaker: User
transcript.text: Better yet, you could build the system, then I'll tell your boss that it doesn't meet my needs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't mean to frighten you, but you'll have to do some actual work.

transcript.speaker: User
transcript.text: That's crazy talk.

situation: Dilbert tells a user he will design the system once he receives the user requirements. The user proposes that Dilbert just build it first, after which the user will complain to Dilbert's boss that it fails to meet his needs. Dilbert points out the user would have to do real work to supply requirements, and the user dismisses this as crazy.
punchline: The user would rather let the project fail and blame the developer than do the minimal work of defining what he actually wants.
summary: A developer asks a client for specifications, but the client prefers to let the developer guess and then criticize the result rather than lift a finger.

file: 2003/2003-09-30_disloyal ingrate_evil dircetor_inform boss_internal job open_new policy.gif
title: Evil HR's Disloyalty Trap Policy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: New policy: You must inform your boss before applying for an internal job opening.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purrrrrrrr

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, good luck, you disloyal, back-stabbing ingrate.

setting: Corporate office, Catbert's HR desk and the Boss's office
situation: Catbert, the Evil H.R. Director, announces a new policy requiring employees to tell their boss before applying for an internal job opening. He purrs happily at his computer. Later, an employee has told the Boss about applying elsewhere and gets insulted for it.
punchline: The policy sounds fair but is really a trap that exposes employees to their boss's wrath, which is exactly what the sadistic Catbert wants.
summary: A cruel HR cat creates a rule that makes workers announce their job-hunting to their bosses, then purrs as the fallout arrives.

file: 2003/2003-10-29_evil dircetor_comapnay_free cholesterol screening_bacon and cheese hoagies_free hoagies.gif
title: Cholesterol Screening Versus Free Hoagies

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company will provide free cholesterol screening on Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: At the same time, we're providing free bacon and cheese hoagies across the hall. It's your choice.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I hate him, but I also love him.

situation: Catbert, as the evil H.R. director, announces to employees at a conference table that the company will offer free cholesterol screening on Tuesday. He then adds that free bacon and cheese hoagies will be available across the hall at the same time. In the last panel, the employees are happily eating the hoagies, and one of them admits she hates Catbert but loves him too.
punchline: Catbert cleverly schedules a free health screening and free artery-clogging food simultaneously, so employees get tempted into undermining their own health, leaving them with mixed feelings of resentment and gratitude.
summary: An H.R. cat sets up a wellness check and a greasy free lunch on the same day, and the staff gleefully pick the sandwiches.

file: 2003/2003-05-28_extortion magazine_more ad space_week old spit_half page ad.gif
title: Extortion Magazine Reviews Demand Ad Purchases

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Our products got reviewed in the new issue of "Extortion Magazine."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "If they had bought more ad space in this magazine, we would not compare their products to week-old spit."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's better than last month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll bet we can get to "day-old" with another half-page ad.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, tells him that the company's products were reviewed in a trade magazine called Extortion Magazine. The Boss reads the review, which says the products would not have been compared to week-old spit had the company bought more ad space. Carol notes it's an improvement over last month, and the Boss reasons that another half-page ad will get them to day-old spit.
punchline: The magazine openly ties the quality of its product reviews to advertising purchases, and the Boss cheerfully accepts this pay-for-praise racket, treating a slightly less insulting comparison as a worthwhile return on ad spend.
summary: A pay-to-play trade magazine insults the company's products while hinting that more advertising would soften its opinion, and the boss sees that as a bargain.

file: 2003/2003-01-15_losing cash_operate immediately_removal service_operate immediatley.gif
title: Dogbert Removes Consultants Surgically

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like you need "Dogbert's Consultant Removal Service."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He's in there good. You must be losing a lot of cash.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It already spread to your wallet. I'll have to operate immediately.

setting: Office, with Dogbert standing on a desk or counter
situation: Dogbert examines the Boss, who is bent over with his legs in the air, as if a consultant were lodged somewhere in his body. Dogbert pitches his 'Consultant Removal Service' and says the consultant is in deep and costing the Boss money. He then announces that the problem has reached the Boss's wallet and that he must operate immediately.
punchline: Dogbert treats consultants as a parasitic infection and his own removal service as a surgery that conveniently targets the Boss's wallet, making Dogbert the very kind of expensive consultant he claims to remove.
summary: Dogbert plays surgeon to extract a consultant from the Boss and pockets his money in the process.

file: 2003/2003-05-09_revenue estimates_research_too late_higher revenue_stress_flashlight_eyes_science.gif
title: Doctor Diagnoses Drive-By Management Stress

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Double the revenue estimates and make sure the research supports it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But...but...it's too late! The research is done, and it won't support higher revenue!

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Your stress is from a combination of drive-by management and a flashlight in your eyes.

setting: Office cubicle, then a doctor's examination room
situation: The Boss pops into Dilbert's cubicle and orders him to double the revenue estimates and make the already-completed research support the higher figures. Dilbert protests that it's too late and the data won't back it up. In the last panel, a stressed Dilbert is at the doctor's office, being examined with a flashlight in his eyes.
punchline: The doctor blames Dilbert's stress on drive-by management, the boss's habit of dropping impossible demands and leaving, while also humorously noting the flashlight shining in his eyes.
summary: A manager's last-minute demand to inflate projections lands Dilbert in a doctor's office, where the diagnosis pins his stress on hit-and-run supervision.

file: 2003/2003-02-23_strategy meetng_value input_administrative assistant_global domination_engineers_gocce filters_popcorn bags_pantyhouse_foot on pantyhose_coffeee filter.gif
title: Secretary Insults Boss Over Coffee Filters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, come to my strategy meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're only a secretary, but I value your input.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm an administrative assistant!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Chimp.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bad secretary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have any strategic ideas for global domination?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The engineers keep using our coffee filters as popcorn bags. That has got to stop.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: If you ordered enough filters, I wouldn't need to use the foot of my pantyhose to make coffee every day!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm adding that to the list of things I don't want to think about.

situation: The Boss invites his secretary Carol to a strategy meeting while insulting her job title, and they privately think insulting names about each other. In the meeting he asks for ideas about global domination, but Carol only raises the engineers misusing coffee filters as popcorn bags. Tina snaps that she has to make coffee with pantyhose because of the filter shortage.
punchline: A supposedly grand strategy meeting about global domination is derailed by petty office supply complaints, leaving Dilbert with one more disturbing detail he'd rather not think about.
summary: A condescending invitation to a strategy session ends with mundane grievances about coffee filters and an unsettling pantyhose confession.

file: 2003/2003-09-09_internet traffic_good thing_under sewage_breathe through straw_grateful_sewer system.gif
title: Asok Thrilled by Sewer Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, would you like to join a doomed project for sending Internet traffic over the sewer system?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Absolutely! I might be young and inexperienced, but I know a good thing when I see it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to work under the sewage and breathe through a straw.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I get a straw?!!

situation: The Boss openly tells Asok that a project to send internet traffic through the sewer system is doomed, and asks if he wants to join. Asok eagerly accepts, claiming he can recognize a good opportunity. The Boss then reveals he'll have to work under the sewage and breathe through a straw, and Asok is delighted to be given a straw.
punchline: Asok's naive enthusiasm is so extreme that he is thrilled by the tiny perk of getting a straw to breathe through while working under raw sewage.
summary: A boss recruits an eager young employee for a hopeless sewer-based networking scheme, and the employee is overjoyed at being issued a breathing straw.

file: 2003/2003-09-21_nano bit project_dilbert_take over_everyone busy_face in allaegators_one cracker a day_cracker time_quitting tomorrow_four problems.gif
title: Boss Passes Project Down the Line

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I don't have time to work on the Nanobit project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No problem. Tell Dilbert I said he should take over.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two minutes later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm way, way too busy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. Tell Wally to do it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two minutes later

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm up to your face in alligators!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, okay... Hand it off to Asok.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two minutes later

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But already I only have time to eat one cracker a day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell Ted I said...

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Sure, I'll do it. No problem.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Mmm... Cracker time.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm quitting tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I solved four problems today!

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's desk
situation: Carol tells the Boss she has no time for the Nanobit project, so he tells her to hand it to Dilbert. Each employee in turn claims to be too busy and the Boss keeps delegating it to the next person: Dilbert, Wally, Asok. Finally Ted accepts it, but only because he plans to quit the next day, while the Boss proudly believes he solved four problems.
punchline: The Boss thinks passing the task down the line counts as solving problems, when really he has only pushed it onto someone who will quit and left everyone worse off.
summary: A reluctant chain of delegation ends with a doomed employee taking the job while his manager congratulates himself on a productive day.
