file: 2003/2003-10-18_tunnel digging_prototype_escaped the lab_perth australia_combined enity_cyborg_popular_trick with dirt.gif
title: Escaped Drill Prototype Becomes Party Cyborg

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My tunnel-digging prototype escaped the lab and burrowed into a picnicker in Perth, Australia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The combined entity is a cyborg that has proven to be surprisingly popular at parties.

transcript.speaker: Partygoer
transcript.text: Ha ha! Do the trick with the dirt!

setting: Dilbert's lab, with a scene of a party in Perth, Australia
situation: Dilbert explains that his tunnel-digging prototype escaped from the lab and burrowed into a picnicker in Australia. The merged human-machine cyborg, wearing a drill bit on his head, turns out to be a hit at parties. Guests cheerfully ask him to perform his dirt trick.
punchline: A dangerous lab accident that fused a machine into a human is treated as a harmless party novelty, with the victim reduced to an entertaining trick.
summary: A scientist's runaway drilling machine merges with a stranger and the resulting cyborg becomes a crowd-pleasing party act.

file: 2003/2003-10-30_emailed_breakdown_format_unspoken_shining prefernces_mpiness_abyss.gif
title: Alice Reads Boss's Mind

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I e-mailed you the expense breakdown. I need you to fix the format and send it out.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I will now read your mind to get the unspoken, ever-shifting preferences for the format.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I see nothing. Emptiness... The abyss...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Add a chart.

situation: The Boss asks Alice to fix the format of an expense breakdown without saying how he wants it. Alice sarcastically pretends to read his mind to learn his unspoken, changing preferences. She sees only emptiness, and he answers with a vague demand to add a chart.
punchline: Alice's mock mind-reading finds nothing in the Boss's head, yet he immediately demands a chart, showing he has no real requirements and only arbitrary whims.
summary: Faced with a manager who gives no formatting guidance, an employee jokingly performs psychic mind-reading and finds only a void before he blurts out a random request.

file: 2003/2003-05-29_conincidences_ell phones_ring_emergency_crisis_meetings_people leave.gif
title: Everyone's Phone Rings Mid-Meeting

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Emergency, you say?

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Crisis?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm losing my faith in coincidences.

situation: During a meeting, the cell phones of nearly every attendee ring at once. Each person answers and reacts to an urgent call about an emergency or crisis, then leaves. The Boss is left sitting alone at the long table.
punchline: The Boss realizes that everyone's sudden emergency calls, timed to get them out of his meeting, cannot be a coincidence and are really excuses to escape.
summary: A boardroom empties as one staffer after another takes a conveniently timed urgent call, leaving the manager alone to suspect it was all staged.

file: 2003/2003-11-12_director of profit making_behind greatness_acting like king_wants award_making spectavle.gif
title: Profitable Director Demands An Award

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Later we'll be joined by the director of the only division that's making a profit.

transcript.speaker: Director
transcript.text: Behold my greatness!! Bathe ye all in the pleasure of my general proximity!!

transcript.speaker: Director
transcript.text: I can only stay if you give me an award.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces to the meeting that the director of the company's only profitable division will be joining them. The director arrives dressed as a king in a giant crown and robe, holding a scepter and proclaiming his own greatness. He then announces he will only stay if he is given an award.
punchline: The one manager whose division makes money acts like royalty and exploits his leverage, demanding recognition in exchange for merely attending the meeting.
summary: A lone profitable executive shows up dressed as a monarch and extracts a trophy as the price of his presence.

file: 2003/2003-07-22_mandatory online training_system crashed_retake training.gif
title: Crashed Training Data, Please Retake

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You're the only one who hasn't finished the mandatory online Six Sigma training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished it, but the system crashed before it stored my data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is when you say, "There's no need to retake the training. I'll just check off your name."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Are you new on this planet?

situation: Carol, who administers the training, tells Dilbert he is the only person who hasn't completed the mandatory online Six Sigma course. Dilbert explains he did finish it but the system crashed before saving his results, and he coaches her to simply check off his name. She replies sarcastically that he must be naive to expect such common sense.
punchline: Carol's sarcastic question implies that expecting a bureaucracy to show flexibility or common sense is hopelessly naive, so Dilbert will be forced to retake the training.
summary: A worker whose completed online course was lost in a crash tries to talk the training administrator into excusing him, and gets mocked for expecting leniency.

file: 2003/2003-05-18_evil director_human resources_fired_unflattering comments_transferring new job_living for weekend_business.gif
title: Catbert's Assembly Line Transfer Trick

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, the evil director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hello, headcount.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Am I fired?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, no, no...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'd never fire you for making unflattering comments to the press about the company.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Really? Everyone said you're evil.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Heh, heh, thank you. But all I'm doing is transferring you to a new job.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gee, that doesn't sound so bad. What is it?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our new assembly line is seven inches too low. Your job is to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm living for the weekend.

setting: Catbert's Human Resources office, then a factory assembly line
situation: An employee who made unflattering comments to the press is called into Catbert's office and asks whether he is fired. Catbert assures him he is only being transferred, and the employee relaxes until he learns the new job. In the last panel the employee is hung upside down over the assembly line, doing the job of compensating for its being seven inches too low.
punchline: Catbert's 'not fired' transfer is actually a punishment worse than termination, since the employee must physically be the fix for a badly built assembly line, and he can only cling to the weekend to get through it.
summary: A worker who spoke ill of the company to reporters is spared the axe by an evil HR cat, only to be hung upside down as a human adjustment on a factory line.

file: 2003/2003-11-23_job applaicants_new batch_500 qualified people_who wants job_pummel each applicat_very soft itmes_harder materials_sugar doughnut_their attitudes_upbeat.gif
title: Hiring By Pummeling Applicants With Objects

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The new batch of job applicants is more desperate than usual.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Excellent.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Five hundred qualified people applied for this position.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But who wants this job the most?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I plan to pummel each applicant with a variety of objects, beginning with very soft items.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll gradually move toward harder materials until only one person is left.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll begin with this soft sugar doughnut.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zing. Piff!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How are their attitudes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Refreshingly upbeat!

setting: The Boss's office, with a desk and a job applicant seated across from him
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that this batch of job applicants is unusually desperate, and the Boss is delighted. His plan is to select the most eager candidate by pelting each applicant with objects, starting soft and getting progressively harder. He throws a doughnut at the first applicant, who politely thanks him, and later carries a large mallet while remarking on how upbeat the applicants are.
punchline: The desperate applicants are so eager for the job that they cheerfully thank the Boss for abuse, so he finds their attitudes refreshing while he escalates to a mallet.
summary: A boss decides to find the most determined job candidate by hurling progressively harder objects at hopeful applicants who politely endure it.

file: 2003/2003-08-08_weather_close offcie_forecast for blizzards_freezing rain_tsunamis_deadly lave flows_precision-guided ball laightening_swims of killer bees_snow tires.gif
title: Closing Office for Absurd Weather

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The weather is getting worse. Maybe we should close the office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The forecast is for blizzards, freezing rain, tsunamis, deadly lava flows, and precision-guided ball lightning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And radiation-enlarged swarms of killer bees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get some snow tires, you big baby.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss to close the office because of worsening weather, and the Boss flatly refuses. Dilbert escalates by listing increasingly absurd and deadly forecasts, ending with radiation-enlarged killer bees. The Boss still dismisses him, telling him to get snow tires.
punchline: No matter how catastrophic and ridiculous the threats become, the Boss responds with a trivial, irrelevant fix and insults Dilbert for being scared, showing management will never let employees stay home.
summary: A worker lists ever more outlandish disasters to justify closing the office, but his manager shrugs it all off and mocks him for complaining.

file: 2003/2003-04-15_unspecified short comings_co worker_accuser_witness protection program_boss_meeting_business.gif
title: Boss Hides Accuser In Witness Protection

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your accuser has been placed in the witness protection program.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have a program for that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, I just forget who says what.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that an unnamed co-worker has accused him of vague, unspecified shortcomings. He claims the accuser is in the witness protection program, and when Dilbert is impressed that such a program exists, the Boss admits he simply can't remember who said what.
punchline: The Boss's grand-sounding excuse for withholding the accuser's identity is just a cover for his poor memory and sloppy management.
summary: A manager passes along anonymous, vague criticism and blames a made-up protection scheme when the real reason is that he has forgotten who complained.

file: 2003/2003-12-03_break into subgroups_net meeting_usual time_loose canon_label_hackneyed phrases_cut now type.gif

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Or we could just meet next week at our usual time.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop labeling me with hackneyed phrases!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You're a "cut now, measure later" type.

situation: At a meeting, a bald coworker proposes splitting into sub-groups to devise a process for choosing the next meeting time. Alice suggests simply meeting at the usual time next week, and he labels her a loose cannon. When she objects to being tagged with clichés, he answers with yet another cliché.
punchline: Alice protests being labeled with hackneyed phrases, and the coworker responds by slapping on another tired business cliché, proving her point.
summary: A colleague who overcomplicates scheduling brands the sensible person a cliché, then does it again when she complains about it.

file: 2003/2003-08-30_key board_not unique_carol adjusts_making no sense.gif
title: Boss Demands Management Keyboard

transcript.text: My keyboard looks exactly like everyone else's.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need more of a management keyboard, with special keys and that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And the "[" becomes the newly discovered letter "[-]".

situation: The Boss stands by Carol's cubicle holding his keyboard and complains that it looks the same as everyone else's. He asks for a special management keyboard with unique keys. Carol, unimpressed, imagines in a thought bubble how she will cheaply fake the request by redefining an existing key as a made-up letter.
punchline: Carol plans to satisfy the Boss's vanity by just inventing a fake 'new letter' on the existing keyboard rather than providing anything actually useful.
summary: A status-hungry manager wants a fancier keyboard than his staff, and his assistant quietly plans a meaningless cosmetic trick to placate him.

file: 2003/2003-09-10_project manager_direct natural talent_energy_common goal_agenda_copies of agenda_health.gif
title: Carol Refuses to Copy Agenda

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've never been a project manager before.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I understand I'm supposed to direct your natural talents and energies toward a common goal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, did you make copies of the agenda?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: No, it sounded hard.

setting: Conference room during a project kickoff meeting
situation: The Boss, newly made a project manager, tells the team he is supposed to direct their natural talents and energies toward a common goal. He then asks Carol if she made copies of the agenda. Carol flatly admits she didn't because the task sounded hard.
punchline: Carol's natural talent turns out to be avoiding even trivial work, so the Boss's attempt to harness the team's talents immediately hits her laziness and lack of effort.
summary: A first-time project leader hopes to rally his staff's talents, only to have a simple photocopying request rejected as too difficult.

file: 2003/2003-03-07_loser magazine_pen_easy questions_borrow pen_chewer_denied loan.gif
title: Loser Magazine Interview: Pen Request

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Wally, I'd like to interview you for "Loser Magazine."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Do you have a pen?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. These are easy questions.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: I mean, may I borrow your pen?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, you look like a chewer.

situation: A bearded reporter with a notepad asks to interview Wally for "Loser Magazine," and Wally agrees. The reporter's first question is whether Wally has a pen, which Wally treats as an interview question. When the reporter clarifies that he wants to borrow the pen, Wally refuses because he thinks the man will chew on it.
punchline: Wally is so lazy and self-serving that he treats a request for a pen as an easy interview question, then refuses to lend it because the reporter looks like someone who chews pens.
summary: A magazine writer hoping to profile a slacker colleague gets stonewalled when the man won't even hand over a writing instrument.

file: 2003/2003-03-27_actively isleads_hypocrite_marketing_table_talk to furniture_tell people_you mislead cutsomers_business.gif
title: Dogbert's Talking Table Calls Dilbert Hypocrite

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to stop telling people that you can talk to furniture. It's not right.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You work for a company that actively misleads customers. How's that different?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We call it marketing, and we don't wear hats.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The table says you're a hypocrite.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert standing on a table
situation: Dilbert scolds Dogbert, who wears a purple striped wizard-style hat, for claiming he can talk to furniture. Dogbert retorts that Dilbert's employer deceives customers, which is no more honest. Dilbert says his company calls it marketing and its people don't wear silly hats, and Dogbert replies that the table says Dilbert is a hypocrite.
punchline: Dilbert defends corporate deception by pointing out only that marketing doesn't involve silly hats, so Dogbert's absurd furniture-talking gets the last word by calling him a hypocrite.
summary: A man's complaint about a dog's fake furniture-whispering is turned back on him when the dog compares it to his employer's customer deception.

file: 2003/2003-08-27_phd degrees_no common sense_interview_job interview_not good to say.gif
title: Candidate Admits No Common Sense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! You have three masters degrees and a PhD!

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Yes, it's all very impressive, but interestingly, I have no common sense whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not the sort of thing you should say during a job interview.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I don't see why not.

setting: Interview room, seated across a desk
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss interviews a job candidate and is impressed by his résumé of three master's degrees and a PhD. The candidate cheerfully admits he has no common sense at all. The Boss warns him that such a statement is unwise in an interview, and the candidate says he does not see why not.
punchline: The candidate's inability to understand why admitting a lack of common sense is a bad idea proves exactly that he lacks common sense.
summary: A highly credentialed applicant demonstrates his own deficiency while being counselled about it by the interviewer.

file: 2003/2003-02-16_numbing_cubicle_emplyess been numbs_pain of working_quite beautiful_happy place.gif
title: Watching a Coworker's Numbing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want to watch a numbing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You know I do!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Where is it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cubicle 15950.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you going to the numbing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You know we are!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What is a numbing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's the moment that an employee's brain numbs to the pain of working here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's actually quite beautiful.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No two are alike.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I can't take this anymore!! Gaa!! Gaa!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ooh. What the..?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's okay — he's in a happy place now.

situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice invite each other, and the new hire Asok, to go watch a coworker's 'numbing', the moment an employee's brain gives up and goes numb to the misery of work. They gather around a cubicle and peer over the wall as the employee shouts that he can't take it anymore, then suddenly goes blank. The onlookers calmly reassure everyone that he is now in a happy place.
punchline: The coworkers treat an employee's mental breakdown as a pleasant spectator event, and the 'happy place' is really just a brain shut down by a miserable job.
summary: Office workers gather like tourists to enjoy the sight of a colleague's spirit finally giving out under the weight of the job.

file: 2003/2003-02-28_big mouth_bloated_employee_taunting_toxic co worker.gif
title: Toxic Co-Worker's Backhanded Defense

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The toxic co-worker

transcript.speaker: Toxic Co-Worker
transcript.text: You wouldn't believe what people are saying about you.

transcript.speaker: Toxic Co-Worker
transcript.text: I tried to defend you. I said you look slow only because you're bloated.

transcript.speaker: Toxic Co-Worker
transcript.text: But what ticks me off is that everyone in the department earns more than you do.

situation: A lumpy, blob-like co-worker stands over Alice's desk and claims to be sticking up for her against office gossip. His 'defense' is an insult in itself, calling her slow and bloated. He then stirs up resentment by telling her that everyone in the department makes more money than she does, and Alice grows visibly angrier.
punchline: The toxic co-worker pretends to be a supportive ally while delivering insults and deliberately stoking Alice's anger about her pay.
summary: A gossiping colleague poses as Alice's defender while slipping in insults and salary news designed to make her furious.

file: 2003/2003-12-25_alice_downsized_now ork_no shave legs_arrested_ice cream_sasquatch_tv news report.gif
title: Downsized Alice Skips Shaving Legs

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The good thing about being downsized is that I don't need to shave my legs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It grows fast, but who's going to notice?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Police surrounded a convenience store where Sasquatch attempted to buy "Häagen Daz."

setting: Alice's living room, on the couch
situation: Alice, recently laid off, slumps on her couch with wild unkempt hair, musing that being downsized means she no longer has to shave her legs. In the final panel, Dilbert and Dogbert watch a TV news report about police surrounding a convenience store where Sasquatch tried to buy ice cream.
punchline: Alice's leg hair has grown so long and unkempt that she resembles Sasquatch, and the news story about Sasquatch buying ice cream implies the sighting was actually her.
summary: A laid-off woman lets her grooming go entirely, and a news bulletin about a big-footed creature raiding a store for ice cream suggests where she ended up.

file: 2003/2003-12-29_ceo_move offcie_near ceo home_hug expense_eat mud and die_stock options_buy hummer.gif
title: CEO Moves Headquarters Near Home

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company is relocating headquarters to be nearer our CEO's home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When asked about the justification for the huge expense, our CEO quipped, "Ha ha ha! Eat mud and die!"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then he gave himself some stock options and went to buy a Hummer.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss reads an announcement to his staff that the company is relocating its headquarters to be closer to the CEO's house. He relays that the CEO responded to questions about the huge cost with a mocking insult, then rewarded himself with stock options and went shopping for a Hummer. Wally and Dilbert sit and listen.
punchline: The CEO openly treats the company as his personal piggy bank, wasting money on a self-serving move and rewarding himself while contemptuously dismissing anyone who questions it.
summary: Employees are told their office is moving for the convenience of an executive who laughed off the cost and then treated himself to a lavish reward.

file: 2003/2003-10-03_work three hours_quality of life_gigantic raise_good time.gif
title: Three Hours a Week, Huge Raise

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Would it be okay if I worked three hours a week?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Any more than three and my quality of life takes a steep dive.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Secondly, is this a good time to talk about a gigantic raise?

situation: A young employee with a bowl haircut stands before the boss's desk while he reads a piece of paper. She asks to work only three hours a week, explains that more would hurt her quality of life, then pivots to asking for a gigantic raise.
punchline: The employee is absurdly entitled, demanding drastically reduced hours while also asking for a huge pay increase, as if the two requests were perfectly reasonable together.
summary: A worker brazenly asks her manager for a near-nonexistent workload and then for far more money.

file: 2003/2003-07-07_company website_binder_easier refernce_tarnslate_make easier_alert dictionary_easy_stupider.gif
title: Carol Mocks Boss's Binder Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, print out our company web site and put it in a binder for easier reference.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Okay. And I'll also translate it into Klingon to make it even easier.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And I'll alert the dictionary makers that "easier" means stupider.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep them out of this.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to print the company web site and put it in a binder so it is easier to reference. Carol sarcastically offers to translate it into Klingon and to inform dictionary makers that 'easier' now means 'stupider.' The Boss, missing the sarcasm, just tells her to leave the dictionary makers out of it.
punchline: Carol's deadpan sarcasm mocks the absurdity of printing a website to make it easier to use, and the Boss is too obtuse to notice the insult.
summary: A secretary responds to a pointless printing assignment with escalating sarcasm that her boss doesn't recognize as mockery.

file: 2003/2003-07-06_testing new invention_mothers use telephone_toddlers noise cancelation_visual_child_moth frozen open_change forever.gif
title: Toddler Noise Cancellation Phone Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for testing my new invention.

transcript.speaker: Mother
transcript.text: If this thing works, it will change forever the way that mothers use the telephone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've been on the phone for half a minute. The noise should start at any moment.

transcript.speaker: Mother
transcript.text: Here it comes.

transcript.speaker: Toddler
transcript.text: Hey! What are you doing on the phone?!

transcript.speaker: Toddler
transcript.text: Can I eat ten cookies? I think my arm is broken! Where's my toy?!!

transcript.speaker: Toddler
transcript.text: Waaaaaaaaaa!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now press the toddler noise cancellation button.

transcript.speaker: Mother
transcript.text: It stopped the noise, but you need to do something about the visual.

setting: Dilbert's office and the mother's home, connected by phone
situation: Dilbert has invented a phone feature and asks a mother to test it. Her toddler interrupts her call with demands and then a screaming fit. When she presses the noise cancellation button, the sound disappears but the child is still visibly screaming with his mouth wide open.
punchline: The invention silences the toddler's noise but not the sight of him screaming, so the problem is only half solved and the mother still has to look at it.
summary: An inventor's gadget mutes a screaming child on the phone, yet the tester complains that the silent, wide-mouthed child is still unsettling to watch.

file: 2003/2003-01-16_body in body_knife_one will die_recommends killing_save one life only_one or the other.gif
title: Consultant Recommends Boss Be Killed

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can either save your life or the consultant's life, but one of you will die.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give us a minute to discuss it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He recommends that you kill me.

setting: Operating room or office where Dogbert plays surgeon with a knife
situation: Dogbert, holding a knife, tells the Boss and the consultant, who appear to be sharing one body, that he can only save one of them. The Boss asks for a minute to discuss, then reports that the consultant, who is the one speaking through him, recommends that Dogbert kill the Boss.
punchline: The consultant, whose advice the Boss follows, self-servingly recommends sacrificing the Boss rather than himself, showing that consultants look out for their own survival at the client's expense.
summary: When forced to choose who survives, the consultant lodged inside the Boss advises that the Boss be the one to go.

file: 2003/2003-05-08_elbonians_buy influence_vote_politics.gif
title: Buying Washington Influence With Gum

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: P.R. for Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to buy some influence in Washington.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It sounds expensive, but it's a lot more affordable than you'd think.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Gum?

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: You got my vote!

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, then outside a Washington government building
situation: Dogbert, acting as a P.R. consultant, tells his Elbonian clients they need to buy influence in Washington and assures them it is cheaper than expected. An Elbonian then offers a politician on the steps of a government building a piece of gum, and the politician immediately promises his vote.
punchline: The joke is that a politician's vote can be bought for a stick of gum, satirizing how cheaply and easily lawmakers can be influenced.
summary: A consultant's advice to purchase political clout proves absurdly cheap when a lawmaker trades his vote for a single offered treat.

file: 2003/2003-02-06_project_falling death spiral_selfish weasels_mood altering_doctor is better.gif
title: Medicated Dilbert Insults Unhappy Team

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project is in a flaming death spiral, thanks to you lazy, selfish weasels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'm feeling terrific because I'm taking mood-altering prescription drugs!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can see by your expressions that my doctor is much better than yours!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hoo-wah!

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert stands at a screen showing a doomed project and berates his two coworkers, calling them lazy, selfish weasels. He then cheerfully announces he feels terrific thanks to prescription mood-altering drugs. He finishes by smugly claiming his doctor is better than theirs, based on their glum faces.
punchline: Dilbert's cheerful, drug-induced mood lets him insult his team and gloat that his doctor's prescriptions work better than theirs.
summary: A pharmaceutically upbeat engineer blames his colleagues for his failing project while bragging about how good he feels.

file: 2003/2003-03-12_cell phone not working_short range_same room_tv remote control.gif
title: Short-Range Cell Phone Prank

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why isn't my cell phone working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's a short-range cell phone. You need to be in the same room with the person you call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Answer the stinkin' phone, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why are you listening to a TV remote control?

situation: The Boss complains that his cell phone isn't working, and Wally tells him it's a short-range phone that only works when you're in the same room as the person you call. Wally has apparently handed him a TV remote. The Boss then sits in a meeting holding the remote to his ear, thinking angrily about Alice not answering, while Asok asks why he is listening to a TV remote.
punchline: The Boss is so gullible that he believes a TV remote is a short-range cell phone and sits in the same room as Alice, waiting for her to answer a device that can't call anyone.
summary: A clueless manager swallows a coworker's absurd tech explanation and ends up pressing a television remote to his ear in a meeting.

file: 2003/2003-01-23_lazy beaver_excuses_doesnt return calls_making excuses_more jobs_future jobs_scamming_both sdies.gif
title: Bribing the Lazy Contractor Beaver

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project is behind schedule because our contractor is a lazy beaver.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For a while he was making up excuses. Now, he doesn't return calls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's your plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope to get him back to making up excuses by promising him more jobs in the future.

setting: Conference room or office, with a presentation slide and the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert presents to the Boss, pointing at a slide of a grumpy beaver contractor who is causing the project to run late. He explains that the contractor has stopped even making excuses and now ignores calls. When the Boss asks for his plan, Dilbert says he will dangle promises of future work to get the contractor communicating again.
punchline: Dilbert's plan is not to get the work done but merely to coax the contractor back to giving excuses, by promising future jobs he presumably will never deliver on.
summary: An engineer's strategy for a non-responsive contractor is to lure him back to offering excuses with bogus promises of more business.

file: 2003/2003-10-10_finalized busdget_budget for last year_sounds annual.gif
title: Budget Finalized One Year Late

transcript.speaker: Finance Guy
transcript.text: At long last, I finalized the budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the budget for last year.

transcript.speaker: Finance Guy
transcript.text: Stop making it sound annual.

situation: A coworker from finance hands Dilbert the budget he has finally completed after a long delay. Dilbert glances at it and points out that it is actually last year's budget. The coworker defensively tells him to stop making the lateness sound like a recurring problem.
punchline: The budget is so late that it covers the previous year, and the finance guy objects to Dilbert's comment because it makes his chronic lateness sound like a regular yearly habit.
summary: A slow-moving finance employee delivers a long-awaited budget that turns out to be a year out of date, and he bristles at the suggestion that this happens routinely.

file: 2003/2003-06-20_worthless fat_everyone participates.gif
title: Everyone Volunteers to Be Cut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can we eliminate $200,000 of worthless fat?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! Every hand went up. I like it when everyone participates!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So it turns out that it's better when no one participates.

setting: Conference room during a budget presentation, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss presents a slide titled 'Budget Pressure' and asks his staff how to cut $200,000 of worthless fat. Every employee raises a hand, and the Boss is pleased by the participation. He then sits in his chair and concludes that participation is actually a bad idea after all.
punchline: The Boss realizes too late that everyone raising a hand means everyone is volunteering as the worthless fat, so he decides he prefers it when nobody participates.
summary: A manager praises his staff's enthusiastic response to a call for cost-cutting ideas, only to figure out they were all volunteering to be the thing that gets cut.

file: 2003/2003-07-14_clutter meleon_printed debris_nest_predator_power to disguise.gif
title: Cluttermeleon Hides in Paper Piles

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The cluttermeleon lines his nest with printed debris.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A predator comes out of his lair.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The quick-thinking cluttermeleon uses his power of disguise.

setting: Office cubicle area, shown in a nature-documentary style
situation: Narrated like a wildlife show, an employee carries a big stack of printed paper to his cubicle, which is already piled with documents. The Boss peeks out of his office as the predator. The employee then camouflages himself by hiding among the towering paper stacks while the Boss looks around.
punchline: The employee uses a mountain of useless paperwork as camouflage so the boss can't find him, like a chameleon hiding from a predator.
summary: A nature-show parody in which a worker buries himself in heaps of printouts to dodge his approaching manager.

file: 2003/2003-12-31_office relocation project_lie_no phone service_new jobs_look for new jobs_not going well.gif
title: Relocation Project Going Perfectly, Panic Ensues

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: The office relocation project is proceeding without any problems whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! It's a lie!!! Our possessions will be lost and we will have no phone service!!!

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: I don't mean to worry anyone, but you should look for new jobs right away.

situation: A project manager at a conference table announces that the office relocation is going smoothly. He then abruptly screams that this is a lie and that belongings will be lost and phone service will be gone. Calming down, he casually advises everyone to start job hunting while Dilbert and a female colleague look on.
punchline: The manager's official status report is a cover story, and his outburst of the truth ends with a deadpan suggestion that the whole team should find new jobs.
summary: A presenter swears a company move is trouble-free, then blurts out the grim reality and mildly recommends everyone update their résumés.

file: 2003/2003-02-08_bone deep_carefree_medication_shellfish_until the pun_beauty_side effect_health.gif
title: Exoskeleton Side Effect and Shellfish Pun

transcript.speaker: Man in exoskeleton
transcript.text: My medication makes me carefree and happy, but the side effect is an exoskeleton.

transcript.speaker: Man in exoskeleton
transcript.text: Remember the old saying - "Beauty is only bone deep."

transcript.speaker: Man in exoskeleton
transcript.text: Hee hee.

transcript.speaker: Man in exoskeleton
transcript.text: But enough about me. I don't want to look shellfish.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You had a chance until the pun.

situation: At a party, a man holding a drink explains that his medication makes him happy but has given him a crustacean-like exoskeleton. He cracks a series of puns, ending with a 'shellfish' joke, while a woman listens with a dismayed expression. She tells him he was fine until the pun.
punchline: The woman could tolerate his bizarre exoskeleton, but the groan-worthy pun is what finally crosses the line.
summary: A cheerful man sprouting a shell from his medication tries to charm a woman with wordplay, and only the wordplay turns her off.

file: 2003/2003-06-23_value of merger_large number_marketing department_frooglepoopillion.gif
title: Merger Write-Down Too Large to Name

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company will be taking a one-time charge to write down the value of our merger.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The number is so large that it has no name. Our marketing department is on it.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Let's see a show of hands for "frooglepoopillion."

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss reads out an announcement to the meeting that the company must take a huge one-time charge to write down the value of its merger. He adds that the amount is so enormous it has no name and marketing is working on one. A marketing staffer then calls for a show of hands to vote on the invented name "frooglepoopillion."
punchline: A catastrophic financial loss from a failed merger is treated as a branding exercise, with marketing voting on a silly made-up word for the number.
summary: A disastrous merger loss is so vast that executives hand the job of naming it to a marketing team that responds with a goofy invented word.

file: 2003/2003-06-26_accounting trolls_profits_worst case scenario.gif
title: Accounting Troll Smashes Worst-Case Scenario

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Accounting Trolls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would happen to our profits if we wrote off these bone-headed mistakes?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POW!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And how about the worst-case scenario?

setting: Accounting Trolls' lair, a cave-like office with a computer on a rocky mound
situation: The Boss hands a document to a green accounting troll and asks what would happen to profits if the company wrote off its blunders. The troll gets angry and smacks The Boss, sending papers flying, and he then calmly asks about the worst-case scenario, the troll now looking battered.
punchline: The troll's violent reaction to the 'best-case' question is the answer, and the Boss, who seems to have been hit, wryly asks for the worst case, implying things just got far worse.
summary: A manager's casual request to the accounting department's resident troll about writing off mistakes gets a violent reply that is itself a preview of the dire financial picture.

file: 2003/2003-11-22_more with less_motivation_communication_more specific.gif
title: Doing More With Less Motivation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal is to do more with less.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Less motivation?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't be any more specific.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Less communication?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The boss announces to his team that the company's goal is to do more with less. Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks whether he means less motivation, and Alice then asks if he means less communication after the boss says he can't be any more specific.
punchline: The boss's vague 'do more with less' slogan never says what is being cut, so employees guess the answer is the very things that make work possible, like motivation and communication, which management is already neglecting.
summary: A manager's empty slogan about productivity gets met with snarky guesses about which resources are actually shrinking.

file: 2003/2003-02-10_makes me happy_exoskleton_bad job_social life_chemicals_illusion_engineer_soul_therapy_psychology_engineering.gif
title: Engineer Denies Having a Soul

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My medication makes me happy despite my exoskeleton, bad job, and social life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If chemicals can change the way I think and what I enjoy, then free will must be an illusion.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: What about your soul?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an engineer.

setting: A therapist's office, with Dilbert lying on a couch
situation: Dilbert lies on a therapy couch, wrapped in a full-body exoskeleton or bandage-like suit, and tells his elderly therapist that his medication makes him happy despite his bad circumstances. He concludes that if chemicals can alter his thoughts and preferences, free will must be an illusion. When the therapist asks about his soul, he answers only that he is an engineer.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the idea of a soul simply by citing his profession, implying that engineers are purely rational and materialist and don't believe in anything beyond chemistry and mechanics.
summary: A medicated patient on a therapist's couch reasons his way to a purely chemical view of the mind, then brushes off any notion of a soul by pointing to his career.

file: 2003/2003-05-25_fifty candiadtes_good news_low level lackeys_once in a lifetime_paperwork from promotion.gif
title: Promotion Offered to Wrong Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have some good news for you!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The paperwork for your promotion just came through.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There were fifty good candidates for this job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Most people in your specialty are destined to be low-level lackeys forever. But not you!

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Umm... my name is Tim. This promotion is for Tom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... being a low-level lackey forever is good, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Could you tell Tom I have some good news?

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss excitedly congratulates an employee on a promotion, praising the competition and the rare opportunity. The employee points out he is Tim and the promotion is actually for Tom. The Boss awkwardly tries to spin Tim's dead-end role as positive, then asks Tim to go fetch Tom.
punchline: The Boss has been enthusiastically promoting the wrong person and doesn't even know his employees' names, and then casually asks the passed-over Tim to deliver the good news to Tom.
summary: A manager lavishly celebrates a promotion with the wrong worker, then shrugs off the mix-up and sends the snubbed man to fetch the real winner.

file: 2003/2003-12-21_gaga gift money_upcoming birthdays_baby showers_retirements promotions_collecting money_bag of moeny_flush_toilet involved_more effcient_sectional sofa.gif
title: Prepaid Gag Gift Money Shakedown

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm collecting money for miscellaneous gag gifts.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We've got upcoming birthdays, baby showers, retirements, promotions, blah, blah, blah.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm collecting all of the gag gift money in advance.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then I'll take the bag of money and flush it down the toilet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That will be the gag.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's funny because a toilet is involved.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So you can either give me $100 now or I'll be back twenty times at $5 a pop.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't resist the siren call of a more efficient process. Give it up, engineer-boy!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hello, sectional sofa!

situation: A female coworker approaches Dilbert's cubicle carrying a paper bag and says she is collecting money for office gag gifts. She proposes that everyone pay the whole year's gag gift money upfront, which she will then flush down the toilet as the 'gag,' and pressures Dilbert with an appeal to efficiency until he hands over $100. In the last panel she daydreams about buying a sectional sofa with the cash.
punchline: The coworker pretends to offer an 'efficient' prepayment scheme for office gift collections, but she is really conning Dilbert out of $100 to spend on furniture for herself.
summary: A pushy coworker uses the lure of efficiency to pry a year's worth of gift contributions from Dilbert, then imagines spending it on a new couch.

file: 2003/2003-06-18_grabbed by hand_my sales meeting_dressed like god_huge hand_guy_thought it would be funny_hee hee.gif
title: Plane Grabbed by Huge Hand

transcript.speaker: Pilot (intercom)
transcript.text: Folks, please stay in your seats. We've been grabbed by a huge hand.

transcript.speaker: Passenger (dressed as God)
transcript.text: I hope this has nothing to do with how I dressed for my sales meeting at the Vatican.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: But it turned out to be a guy with a huge hand who said he "thought it would be funny."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hee hee! Huge hand.

setting: Inside and outside a passenger airplane, then Ratbert watching TV at home
situation: A pilot announces that the airplane has been grabbed by a giant hand. A passenger dressed like God, with a cherub, worries that his costume for a sales meeting at the Vatican is to blame. A TV news report reveals it was just a man with a huge hand who thought it would be funny, and Ratbert laughs at the report.
punchline: The bizarre divine-intervention scare turns out to have a silly explanation, a prankster with a giant hand, which Ratbert finds hilarious.
summary: A plane is plucked from the sky by an enormous hand, and a robed passenger fears he provoked it, but the culprit is merely a joker.

file: 2003/2003-09-12_slither away_doomed project_assistant_teach you_manager skin_speaking metaphor.gif
title: Shedding Your Project Manager Skin

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to slither away from your doomed project before you get blamed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My assistant will teach you how to shed your project manager skin.

transcript.speaker: Snake
transcript.text: Yello!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow! How's this so far?

transcript.speaker: Snake
transcript.text: Impressive, but we were speaking metaphorically.

setting: Office, with Dogbert on a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a bald, tie-wearing project manager to slither away from his doomed project before he gets blamed. He introduces a snake assistant who will teach him to shed his skin. The manager takes it literally and is shown in agony, having peeled off his skin down to the skeleton.
punchline: The project manager took the snake metaphor literally and flayed himself, so the snake assistant admits it was impressive but only figurative advice.
summary: A manager follows a snake's lesson on shedding skin so literally that he ends up a skeleton, while the snake points out it was only a figure of speech.

file: 2003/2003-03-28_downsize_department phone list_efficient list.gif
title: Downsizing List Is Phone Directory

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I took the initiative and made a list of people you could downsize.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is just the department phone list with your name covered up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's the sort of efficiency that kept me off the list.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, hands the Boss a list of people who could be laid off. The Boss looks it over and realizes it is simply the department phone list with Wally's name covered up. Wally proudly says that kind of efficiency is what kept him off the list.
punchline: Wally has cynically protected his own job by passing off the entire phone directory, minus himself, as a layoff list, and he treats that self-serving shortcut as a virtue.
summary: A lazy employee offers his manager a downsizing proposal that is really just the staff directory with his own entry hidden.

file: 2003/2003-05-17_management techniques_existence of books_which one_read_making mad_trick.gif
title: Management Books Prove Nobody Knows

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: How do you know which management techniques work best?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Logically, doesn't the existence of thousands of management books show that no one knows what works best?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The trick is knowing which one to read.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now you're just making me mad.

situation: At a meeting table, Dilbert asks the Boss how he knows which management techniques work best. Wally points out that the sheer number of management books suggests nobody actually knows. The Boss replies that the trick is just knowing which book to read, which irritates Dilbert.
punchline: The Boss answers a question about what works by restating the problem as a circular non-answer, offering a 'trick' that assumes the very knowledge in question.
summary: A boss dodges a pointed question about management methods with an answer that explains nothing, to the annoyance of his employee.

file: 2003/2003-09-24_3 page eamil_clump of space_separate long sentances_ambling senttences_little curvy thing_comma.gif
title: Alice Gifts Paragraph Breaks and Commas

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got your three-page e-mail, and I brought you a gift.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's a clump of blank space. You can use it to separate long, rambling, unrelated sentences.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Next week I'll introduce you to a little curvy thing that I call a comma.

situation: Alice stands over a seated coworker and says she read his three-page e-mail. She sarcastically presents him with a 'gift' of blank space for separating his rambling sentences, then promises to teach him about commas next week.
punchline: Alice sarcastically mocks the coworker's poorly written, run-on e-mail by treating basic paragraph breaks and commas as exotic gifts he has never encountered.
summary: A fed-up Alice delivers a mocking grammar lesson to a colleague whose endless e-mail lacked any punctuation or spacing.

file: 2003/2003-06-28_fooglepoopillion_embarrased_tell the truth_best policy_honesty_what you say.gif
title: Honesty Because Nobody Is Listening

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company lost a frooglepoopillion dollars. I'm embarrassed to tell people where I work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never be afraid to tell the truth about yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because honesty is the best policy?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because no one pays any attention to what you say.

situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is embarrassed to admit where he works because his company lost an absurd amount of money. Dogbert advises him to be truthful about himself, and Dilbert assumes this is the classic honesty-is-best advice. Dogbert reveals his real reasoning is that nobody listens to Dilbert anyway.
punchline: Dogbert's encouragement to be honest isn't about virtue; it's a sarcastic insult implying that Dilbert is so ignored that telling the truth carries no consequences.
summary: Dilbert frets about his company's colossal losses, and Dogbert cheerfully assures him that candor is safe since his words never register with anyone.

file: 2003/2003-05-16_alice_giant magnifying glass_death ray_too warm_head too warm.gif
title: Alice's Toupee-Burning Death Ray

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, I understand you've been using a giant magnifying glass as a death ray in the office.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's not a death ray. I use it only to burn off toupees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Oh... That's okay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is your head too warm? My head is too warm.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts Alice about using a giant magnifying glass as a death ray in the office. Alice explains she only uses it to burn off toupees, and Catbert accepts this as perfectly fine. In the last panel, a balding coworker with a toupee, standing next to Dilbert, feels his head getting warm.
punchline: Alice's dangerous office weapon is excused because she only targets toupees, and the final panel shows a coworker's toupee-covered head heating up as she apparently strikes again.
summary: Alice defends her giant magnifying glass by saying it only destroys hairpieces, and the HR cat shrugs it off while a nearby coworker's head begins to heat up.

file: 2003/2003-03-13_greek_greek word_parthenon_word for sports event_zeus_new product.gif
title: Wally's Greek Product Name Research

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally has been researching Greek words to name our new product.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All I have is Zeus, and Parthenon, and the word "Greek" itself.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I understand they have a word for a sports event, too. I'm trying to track that down.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that Wally has been researching Greek words to name a new product. Wally reports that his research has produced only Zeus, Parthenon, and the word 'Greek' itself. He adds that he is still trying to find the Greek word for a sports event.
punchline: Wally has done almost no real work and is padding his thin results, and the Greek word for a sports event he can't find is 'Olympics', which is a very easy thing to look up.
summary: A product-naming research effort turns up almost nothing, and the researcher admits he is still hunting for a word anyone could guess.

file: 2003/2003-04-23_coffee rehab_no tea_look in bag_no soda_no luaggage_carry yourself.gif
title: Coffee Rehab Intake Gets Strict

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Coffee rehab

transcript.speaker: Rehab Staffer
transcript.text: No soda, no tea, no chocolate.

transcript.speaker: Rehab Staffer
transcript.text: You're allowed one piece of luggage and you have to carry it yourself.

transcript.speaker: Rehab Staffer
transcript.text: I might want to take a look inside that bag.

setting: Intake area of a coffee rehab facility
situation: Dilbert, sweaty and anxious, is being checked into a coffee rehab clinic by a stern staffer who lists the forbidden caffeine sources. She then says he must carry his single piece of luggage himself, and Dilbert staggers under an enormous, heavy bag. She says she may want to search it.
punchline: Dilbert's gigantic bag is clearly packed with contraband caffeine, so he is already trying to smuggle his addiction into the rehab facility.
summary: A man checking into caffeine detox struggles to haul an oversized suitcase that a suspicious attendant wants to inspect.
keywords: no soda no tea no chocolate

file: 2003/2003-10-23_black shoes_cubicle_days of our lives_feel oddly drawn_life has purpose_mind altering day.gif
title: Oddly Drawn Guest Cartoonist Strip

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Who's today's guest cartoonist?*

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This isn't my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Guest character
transcript.text: Your horoscope says you'll have a "mind-altering" day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel oddly drawn to watch "Days of Our Lives."

transcript.speaker: Guest character
transcript.text: You look oddly drawn.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to go to the mall and try on black shoes!

transcript.speaker: Guest character
transcript.text: Wow! Your life finally has a purpose.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Answer: Go to dilbert.com

characters: Guest cartoonist's character (balding man with glasses reading a book)
setting: A blue couch or sofa-like backdrop in an unfamiliar, oddly drawn space, standing in for a cubicle
situation: Dilbert finds himself in a strangely drawn setting, sitting next to a balding man in glasses who is reading a book, evidently from another cartoonist's strip. The guest character tells Dilbert his horoscope predicts a mind-altering day, and Dilbert begins feeling compelled to do trivial things like watch a soap opera and try on black shoes. A caption poses a guest-cartoonist riddle whose answer is to visit dilbert.com.
punchline: Dilbert has been drawn in another cartoonist's style, making him feel 'oddly drawn' and take on that strip's mundane concerns, and the guest character sarcastically notes that trying on black shoes finally gives his life a purpose.
summary: A guest cartoonist's art style transports Dilbert into a different strip where he is compelled toward mundane soap-opera viewing and shoe shopping.

file: 2003/2003-05-23_plant watering service_less expensive one_plastic plants.gif
title: Firing the Plastic Plant Waterers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I fired our plant-watering service and hired a less expensive one.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: That's the sort of leadership that will turn this company around.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Were we doing well?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our plants are plastic.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss proudly announces he replaced the plant-watering service with a cheaper one. A coworker praises this as turnaround-worthy leadership, and another asks whether the company was doing well. The Boss reveals the office plants are plastic, so no watering service was ever needed.
punchline: The company has been paying to water fake plants, so the Boss's celebrated cost-cutting only exposes how wasteful and clueless the previous spending was.
summary: A manager brags about swapping in a cheaper plant-care vendor, only to reveal the greenery was artificial all along.

file: 2003/2003-06-09_highest profit margin_entire industry_not supposed to say_customers.gif
title: Boasting About Profit Margins Publicly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have the highest profit margin in our entire industry!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently I'm not supposed to say that in front of customers.

setting: Conference room during a meeting with customers
situation: The Boss proudly announces to the people across the table that the company has the highest profit margin in its entire industry. After an awkward silence in which Alice looks pained and the customers say nothing, he realizes he has made a blunder and admits he was apparently not supposed to say that in front of customers.
punchline: The Boss brags about extreme profits to the very people being charged for them, only grasping afterward that customers don't want to hear how much money is being made off them.
summary: A manager gloats about industry-leading profits to a room of paying clients and then belatedly realizes that was a mistake.

file: 2003/2003-01-09_40 hours_everyone_likes asok_minute old_new system_work one computer_extreme programming.gif
title: Extreme Programming Makes Everyone Hateful

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to try something called Extreme Programming.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First, pick a partner. The two of you will work at one computer for forty hours a week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new system is a minute old and I already hate everyone.

situation: The Boss gathers the engineers and announces that they will try Extreme Programming, which requires each person to pair up with a partner and share a single computer for forty hours a week. Panel 3 shows the staff already squeezed together in an awkward tangle, with Dilbert, Asok and Alice bunched up in a heap while Wally looks on with his coffee mug.
punchline: Pair programming forces such close contact that the Boss, supposedly the one imposing it, instantly hates everyone, showing how miserable forced togetherness is.
summary: A manager introduces a new team-based coding method and within moments the crowd is physically tangled and thoroughly fed up.

file: 2003/2003-02-26_annual fee_joke_once a month_dumb_annual fee once a month.gif
title: Annual Fee Charged Monthly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How often would you charge us this "annual fee"?

transcript.speaker: Man in blue suit
transcript.text: Is that a joke?

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Sadly, no.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Once a month.

transcript.speaker: Man in blue suit
transcript.text: Sounds fair.

setting: Conference room during a vendor meeting
situation: The Boss asks a vendor's sales representative how often they would bill an "annual fee." His colleague wonders if the question is a joke, but the saleswoman sadly confirms it is not and says the fee would be charged monthly. The colleague then agrees that this sounds fair.
punchline: An "annual fee" charged once a month is absurd, yet the customer accepts it without question, mocking how readily buyers swallow nonsensical vendor pricing.
summary: A vendor casually admits her yearly charge would be billed every month, and the client calmly deems that reasonable.

file: 2003/2003-11-26_lawyer_400 per hour_calls dilbert_legal.gif
title: Lawyer Bills for Thinking About You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: This is your lawyer.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Do you mind if I think about you for a few minutes?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... no.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Mmm... $400 an hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... dear Lord... noooo!!!

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the lawyer's office, on the phone
situation: Dilbert answers a phone call from his lawyer, who politely asks permission to think about him for a few minutes. Dilbert agrees without thinking, and the lawyer's thought bubble reveals he is mentally calculating his $400 hourly rate. Dilbert realizes too late that he has just agreed to be billed for the lawyer's idle thoughts.
punchline: By casually agreeing to let his lawyer think about him, Dilbert unknowingly authorizes billable time at $400 an hour, exposing how lawyers can charge for anything.
summary: A lawyer gets permission to ponder his client's case over the phone, then reveals the meter is already running.

file: 2003/2003-12-18_worry_paranoid beaver_productivity rewarded_alice_merger_boss.gif
title: Alice's Merger Strategy Goes Unnoticed

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My strategy is to work like a paranoid beaver during the merger.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Surely my productivity will be noticed and rewarded when the downsizing begins.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: And who is Alice?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure that's the bald guy with glasses.

setting: Office cubicle area and a conference room
situation: Alice, standing by Wally's desk, explains that she is working frantically during a merger so she will be noticed and spared when layoffs come. In the last panel, an executive asks the Boss who Alice is, and the Boss wrongly identifies her as the bald guy with glasses, who is actually Wally.
punchline: Alice's hard work is pointless because management does not even know who she is and confuses her with Wally, so her plan to be rewarded and spared from downsizing is hopeless.
summary: A worker bets on frantic effort to survive post-merger layoffs, only for the executives deciding her fate to have no idea who she is.

file: 2003/2003-06-13_homemaking skills_marry a man_garbageman_present value cash flow_comparison_trained monkeys_monkey surplus_bobby upset.gif
title: Marriage Versus Trained Monkeys Calculation

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Would it be wrong to marry a man for his homemaking skills?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Do a present-value cash-flow comparison of marriage versus the equivalent service from trained monkeys.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It's not you...it's me...and a world-wide oversupply of monkeys.

setting: A city street beside a garbage truck, then a later scene with the woman and her suitor
situation: A woman asks a garbage man whether it would be wrong to marry a man for his homemaking skills. He answers by telling her to run a present-value cash-flow comparison of marriage against hiring trained monkeys to do the same work. She then breaks up with a tearful man, using the monkey oversupply as part of her excuse.
punchline: The woman takes the garbage man's cold financial analysis seriously and concludes that trained monkeys are a cheaper alternative to a husband, so she dumps her boyfriend with a ridiculous break-up line.
summary: Seeking advice on a pragmatic marriage, a woman gets a deadpan financial answer from a sanitation worker and uses it to end her relationship.

file: 2003/2003-10-12_new version_every feature_current version_leapfrog competition_better products_pile of crud.gif
title: Boss Sabotages Sale With Promises

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, it's a customer!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're in luck; our next version has every feature you'll ever want!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It does?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I was ready to buy your current version... but I guess I'll wait.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will our new version be ready?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new version will leapfrog our competition.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Leapfrog? That implies that they have better products right now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Buy our product, you stinkin' pile of crud!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Slap!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to run. Try not to blow the sale.

situation: The Boss excitedly greets a customer and announces that the next product version will have every feature imaginable, which makes the customer decide to wait instead of buying the current version. When the customer points out that 'leapfrog' implies competitors are currently ahead, the Boss slaps him and shouts at him to buy. He then leaves, telling Dilbert not to blow the sale.
punchline: After wrecking the sale himself with premature promises, a gaffe, and an assault on the customer, the Boss walks out and warns Dilbert not to blow it.
summary: A manager torpedoes a sale by hyping a future product, then physically attacks the buyer and blames his engineer for any fallout.

file: 2003/2003-06-07_new product revenue_future_slashed bidget_development budget_describe future_doomed.gif
title: Describe Our Future Without 'Doomed'

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The future of the company depends on new product revenue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Is that why you slashed the research and development budget?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you're so smart, let's see YOU describe our future without using the word "doomed."

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company's future depends on new product revenue. Dilbert raises his hand and asks whether that is why the boss cut the research and development budget. The Boss responds defensively by challenging Dilbert to describe the company's future without saying "doomed."
punchline: The Boss's sarcastic challenge implicitly admits that his budget cuts have doomed the company, since he cannot refute Dilbert and the only honest description of the future is "doomed."
summary: A manager praises the importance of new products, gets called out for gutting the funding that would create them, and answers with a defensive dare that quietly concedes the company is in trouble.

file: 2003/2003-12-08_trudge_work_earn money_lights on_shower is ready.gif
title: Dilbert's Pet Demands Wasteful Utilities

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's pet
transcript.text: Wake up and trudge to work!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's pet
transcript.text: Earn money so I can leave on the lights in every room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's pet
transcript.text: Your shower is ready. I turned it on last night.

situation: Dilbert's small white pet stands on his bed and bosses him around while he lies half asleep. It tells him to get up and go to work, explaining that he must earn money so it can leave every light on. Finally it announces it turned the shower on the night before, so the water has been running all this time.
punchline: The pet treats Dilbert as a source of income to fund its wasteful habits, and its idea of helpfulness is leaving the shower running all night at his expense.
summary: A bossy household pet orders its sleepy owner off to work so it can squander electricity and water on his dime.

file: 2003/2003-03-30_blue jeans_ceo  tries average_chauffer_dressed as fox_drove tractor_fox hunt_helicopter_interns_ironic_real work_roll sleeve_like secretary.gif
title: CEO Pretends To Be Average Guy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO will be joining us in a minute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As usual, he'll be making an awkward attempt to seem like "just plain folk."

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Excuse me - is this ordinary chair available for an average guy like me?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'll roll up my sleeves and get to work. I'm not too good for real work.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I have a secretary, but it's almost as if I work for her. Ha ha! It's ironic.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Last weekend I wore blue jeans and drove a tractor!

transcript.speaker: Chauffeur
transcript.text: Sir, your helicopter is here to take you to your island fortress for the fox hunt.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Itty bitty fortress

transcript.speaker: Chauffeur
transcript.text: The interns are already in full fox costumes.

situation: The Boss warns the meeting that the CEO is about to arrive and will awkwardly try to seem like an ordinary person. The CEO then makes a series of folksy claims about sitting in an ordinary chair, rolling up his sleeves, and driving a tractor in jeans. His chauffeur interrupts to announce that his helicopter is ready to take him to his island fortress for a fox hunt with interns dressed as foxes.
punchline: The CEO's attempts to appear like an average guy are undone when his chauffeur reveals his extravagantly wealthy lifestyle, including a helicopter, an island fortress and hunting interns dressed as foxes.
summary: A wealthy executive tries to pass himself off as one of the common folk until his valet exposes his lavish, absurd pastimes.

file: 2003/2003-06-25_smell like manager_fiery concoction_agree with me_breath enhancer_around up cigarettes_farm shovels_coffee.gif
title: Dogbert's Management Breath Enhancer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A good manager needs to smell like a manager.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your breath should be a fiery concoction that says, "Agree with me or die."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try "Dogbert's Management Breath Enhancer," made from ground-up cigarettes, farm shovels and coffee.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert standing on the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, stands on the Boss's desk and lectures him about how a good manager should smell. He says a manager's breath should be a fiery concoction that intimidates people. He then pitches his own product, a breath enhancer made from absurd ingredients, while the Boss listens.
punchline: Dogbert sells the Boss a ridiculous, foul-sounding product by claiming that intimidating bad breath is a leadership quality, mocking both management posturing and consultants' scams.
summary: A scheming Dogbert persuades his boss that authority requires menacing breath, then offers a disgusting homemade remedy for sale.

file: 2003/2003-09-29_no raise_next year_disincentivized_moping around_muscles_weak_motovation.gif
title: Underpaid So You Can Get Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you the salary that you deserve because then there'd be no room for a raise next year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wouldn't want you to be all disincentivized, you know, just moping around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Neck... muscles... so... weak.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think motivation causes that.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he can't pay him what he deserves because that would leave no room for a raise next year. He claims he is avoiding demotivating Dilbert. Dilbert slumps onto the desk, too drained to hold his head up, and the Boss diagnoses the cause as lack of motivation.
punchline: The Boss's logic of withholding fair pay to protect future motivation is exactly what destroys Dilbert's motivation, yet the Boss fails to see he is the cause.
summary: A manager justifies underpaying his employee as a way to keep him motivated, then blames low motivation when the worker collapses in despair.

file: 2003/2003-02-07_prescription drugs_happy_genuine happiness_cures worrying_grow exoskeleton_doctor_no cares_happy drug_medical.gif
title: Pills For Worrying About Pills

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The prescription drugs make me happy, but I worry that it's not genuine happiness.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ask your doctor for a drug that cures worrying. Then you'll have it all.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It might make you grow an exoskeleton, but you won't care.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cool.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then a doctor's office
situation: Dilbert, lounging in a bathrobe, tells Dogbert that his antidepressants make him happy but he worries the happiness isn't real. Dogbert suggests asking his doctor for another drug that cures worrying. At the doctor's office, the doctor cheerfully warns of a bizarre side effect, and Dilbert happily accepts the pills.
punchline: Dilbert's worry is cured so effectively that he calmly accepts the prospect of growing an exoskeleton, showing the drug works exactly as described by making him stop caring about anything.
summary: A man troubled by artificial contentment gets advised to medicate away that very concern, and the cure leaves him cheerfully indifferent to a monstrous side effect.

file: 2003/2003-02-05_health benefits_itch_mood altering_stinking weasel_skin rash_drugs.gif
title: Mood-Altering Rash Medication Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm taking a mood-altering prescription drug to treat a skin rash.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I still itch, but I don't care. In fact, I don't even think you're a huge, stinkin' weasel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I love you! You da man!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me to cancel your health benefits.

setting: Office, in front of the Boss
