situation: Dilbert tells his boss he is on a mood-altering drug prescribed for a skin rash. The drug makes him so mellow that he no longer minds the itch or thinks the boss is a weasel, and he cheerfully declares his love for him. The boss responds by planning to cancel Dilbert's health benefits.
punchline: The boss, whose company has just paid for the drug, reacts to the employee's friendly gratitude not with appreciation but by punishing him through the loss of his health coverage, which confirms he really is a stinking weasel.
summary: A medicated employee gushes affection at his manager, who repays the goodwill by plotting to take away his medical coverage.

file: 2003/2003-05-11_eye contact_unpackageable_generous severence_volunteers_retired bliss_cruel twist fate_keep job_organic vessel_self pity_fishing_sports.gif
title: Ernie, the Unpackageable Bitter Employee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... Don't make eye contact with that guy.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ernie is an unpackageable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Last year, the company offered a generous severance package to people who volunteered to leave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ernie volunteered. He imagined a life of retired bliss outside this company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But too many people volunteered. In a cruel twist of fate, Ernie was forced to keep his job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now he's nothing but an organic vessel for transporting self-pity.

transcript.speaker: Ernie
transcript.text: I could have been fishing!!! Waaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You looked?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to warn him.

situation: Dilbert warns a younger coworker not to make eye contact with Ernie, then explains that Ernie volunteered for a severance package but was forced to stay because too many others also volunteered. The coworker looks at Ernie anyway, and Ernie bitterly wails at him about how he could have been fishing.
punchline: Having been denied the layoff he wanted, Ernie is now a miserable employee who unloads his self-pity on anyone who makes eye contact, and the warning comes too late for the coworker who looked.
summary: A bitter worker who was refused a buyout he begged for corners anyone foolish enough to glance his way.

file: 2003/2003-03-23_new marketing strategy_past cutomers_flu symptoms_sick people_appeal to sick people_reinvent dead horse_duh- mensuon_floating scared darkness_confusing cause & effect.gif
title: Marketing to Sick Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Jimmy will explain our new marketing strategy.

transcript.speaker: Jimmy
transcript.text: A study of past customers shows that 96% of them have flu symptoms.

transcript.speaker: Jimmy
transcript.text: Apparently, sick people are the most likely to buy from us. We don't know why.

transcript.speaker: Jimmy
transcript.text: So we redesigned our ad campaign to appeal to sick people.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're confusing cause and effect. Your study shows that our products make people sick.

transcript.speaker: Jimmy
transcript.text: Alice, let's not reinvent a dead horse.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Suddenly nothing makes sense...I must have slipped into the meeting duh-mension!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This usually lasts about ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Floating... scared... darkness...

setting: Conference room during a marketing meeting
situation: Jimmy presents a marketing strategy based on a study finding that most past customers have flu symptoms, so the company has redesigned its ads to target sick people. Alice points out he has confused cause and effect, since the products are likely making people sick. Jimmy answers with a garbled cliche, leaving Alice feeling she has entered a nonsensical dimension.
punchline: Management reads a correlation backwards and responds to Alice's correct logic with nonsense, making her feel she has slipped into a surreal 'meeting dimension' where reason does not apply.
summary: A marketer proposes advertising to ill people after discovering his customers are sick, never considering that his products may be the cause.

file: 2003/2003-03-22_work_requirements_cleverly hide comptenece_workflow.gif
title: Start Building Without Requirements Anyway

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't start the project because the user won't give me his requirements.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Start making something anyway. Otherwise we'll look unhelpful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, our plan is to cleverly hide our competence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You think too much.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he can't begin a project because the user hasn't supplied any requirements. The boss orders him to start building something anyway so the team won't appear unhelpful. Dilbert sarcastically sums up the plan as hiding their competence, and the boss dismisses him for thinking too much.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic summary exposes the absurdity of building a product without requirements just to look busy, and the boss responds by criticizing him for applying logic.
summary: Told to build something despite having no specifications, an engineer sarcastically points out that management is asking the team to conceal its own competence.

file: 2003/2003-05-27_unpaid vacation_managers approval_downsize work_over staffed_hug slef_selfishness_corporate greed_nasty corporate men.gif
title: Unpaid Vacation Downsizing Trap

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Let's offer employees unpaid vacation time, as long as their managers approve it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Then we'll downsize any work group that uses it, because it proves they're overstaffed.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I hug myself and purr.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take your time.

setting: Conference table in the boss's office
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, pitches the Boss a scheme to offer employees unpaid vacation time with manager approval. He then explains that any work group that takes the time off will be downsized, since it supposedly proves they have too many staff. Catbert is so pleased with his own cunning that he hugs himself and purrs, while the Boss patiently waits.
punchline: The benefit is a trap: employees who use the offered unpaid time off give management the excuse to lay them off, and Catbert gleefully congratulates himself on the cruelty.
summary: Catbert devises a seemingly generous perk that is actually a ploy to justify layoffs and purrs with delight at his own wickedness.

file: 2003/2003-07-01_great leader_read books_inspired leaders for centuries_first pyramids_12 year old pharoah_look naughty.gif
title: Pharaoh's Naughty Pyramid Book

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you want to be a great leader, read the books that have inspired leaders for centuries.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, the first pyramids were built after a twelve-year-old pharaoh read this book.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Things that look naughty from miles away."

setting: Office, with the Boss seated in a red armchair beside a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that great leaders read the books that have inspired leaders for centuries. He claims the first pyramids were built after a twelve-year-old pharaoh read a particular book. The Boss reads the title aloud, and it is a book about things that look naughty from miles away.
punchline: The 'book that inspired the pyramids' is a juvenile-humor title, implying the pyramids were built because a twelve-year-old pharaoh wanted to build things that look like something rude from far away.
summary: Dogbert hands the Boss a supposedly legendary leadership book, whose real inspiration turns out to be adolescent smut.

file: 2003/2003-10-14_hate people_never allowed shoes_dogbert_hows my walking_dial_1800.gif
title: How Am I Walking? Bumper Stickers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to make bumper stickers for pedestrians that say, "How am I walking? Call 1-800 blah, blah, blah."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you call the number and report people, they'll never again be allowed to purchase shoes!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The best part about hating people is that I never run out of great ideas.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the arm of the couch next to Dilbert, who sips from a mug, and describes his plan to sell bumper stickers for pedestrians that parody 'How am I driving?' stickers. He explains that anyone reported through the hotline would be banned from buying shoes. He then remarks that hating people is an endless source of ideas.
punchline: Dogbert's scheme to punish pedestrians with a shoe-purchasing ban shows that his contempt for humanity gives him an inexhaustible supply of petty, malicious ideas.
summary: Dogbert pitches a cruel pedestrian-reporting scheme as proof that misanthropy keeps his creativity flowing.

file: 2003/2003-08-25_everyones opinion_advice_best job_crazy ideas_mental_psychology.gif
title: Boss Rewards Best Trash-Talker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll get everyone's opinion, and then I'll make my decision.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Translation: You'll take the advice of whoever does the best job of trash-talking everyone else.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where do you get these crazy ideas?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's mental.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he will gather everyone's opinions before deciding. Alice translates his statement into what he will really do: follow whoever best trash-talks the others. The Boss asks where she gets such ideas, and Dilbert quickly badmouths her as mental, proving her point.
punchline: Dilbert instantly trash-talks Alice in answer to the Boss's question, demonstrating that her cynical translation of the decision process is exactly right.
summary: A manager promises a fair decision process, but a coworker's cynical prediction is confirmed the moment a colleague smears her to him.

file: 2003/2003-01-22_construction bid_award for job_team of skilled craftmen_ex wife_truck on fire.gif
title: Lowest Bidder's Excuse Book

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your construction bid is the lowest, so I have to award you the job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When can your team of highly skilled craftsmen begin?

transcript.speaker: Beaver Contractor
transcript.text: I'll call you.

transcript.speaker: Beaver Contractor
transcript.text: Day one: My ex-wife set my truck on fire.

situation: Dilbert tells a beaver contractor that his bid was the lowest, so he wins the construction job, and asks when the crew can start. The beaver vaguely says he'll call, then is shown flipping through a huge book labeled 'Excuses' and picking the first one, a story about his ex-wife setting his truck on fire.
punchline: The lowest bidder is a contractor who has already planned his delays, with a giant book of excuses ready to explain why the work won't start on time.
summary: A cut-rate contractor wins a job on price alone and promptly reaches for an enormous book of excuses to justify his future delays.

file: 2003/2003-08-01_nemesis_pointy haired_software division_report to boss_no difference_harware_software_engineering.gif
title: Boss Recruits Dilbert Against Rival Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is my nemesis, Pointy-Haired Carl. He manages our software division.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write up some reasons why he should report to me. I'll secretly give it to our vice president.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Start by saying there's no real difference between hardware and software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm unclean!

situation: The Boss introduces his rival, a second pointy-haired manager named Carl who runs the software division, and asks Dilbert to write a secret memo arguing that Carl should report to him. He tells Dilbert to begin by claiming there is no real difference between hardware and software, which makes the engineer recoil in disgust.
punchline: Dilbert is so offended by the false claim that hardware and software are the same that he reacts as if he has been morally contaminated, showing how managers' empire-building rests on nonsense that offends technical people.
summary: A manager enlists an engineer to ghost-write a power grab against a rival, and the engineer is appalled at the bogus technical argument he's told to make.

file: 2003/2003-07-13_technology strategy_not written yet_doesn't exist_duh_duh to infinity.gif
title: Writing a Strategy That Doesn't Exist

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, write up our technology strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's our strategy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How should I know? It's not written yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I write about something that doesn't exist?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will exist, as soon as you write it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Duh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Double duh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh to infinity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If my company stock had any value, I'd be selling it now.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to write up the company's technology strategy, but admits no strategy has been decided yet. Dilbert objects that he can't write about something that doesn't exist, and the two devolve into a childish back-and-forth of saying 'duh' to each other. Dilbert ends by privately concluding the company is badly run.
punchline: The company has no technology strategy and expects an employee to invent one on demand, which convinces Dilbert the company's stock is worthless.
summary: A manager demands a strategy document for a strategy that nobody has come up with, and the argument sinks into schoolyard name-calling.

file: 2003/2003-05-24_focus on execution_excuse poepl_look like accident_two hours long_meetings.gif
title: Execution Misunderstood: Staff Meeting Punishment

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: You've got to focus on execution!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think he wants me to execute people.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Make it look like an accident.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, my staff meetings will be two hours long.

situation: Someone off-panel tells the Boss he must focus on execution, and the Boss takes it literally as executing people. Catbert, the evil HR director, advises him to make it look like an accident. The Boss then announces that his staff meetings will now last two hours, and his visibly distressed employees react in horror.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a deadly 'accident' is making staff meetings two hours long, implying that endless meetings are a form of torture that kills morale (and perhaps people).
summary: Misreading a call for effective follow-through as a call for killing, the boss settles on a slower cruelty: marathon staff meetings.

file: 2003/2003-02-13_evil hr director_references_ex emplyees_mazy loron_rhyme.gif
title: Catbert's Rhyming Job Reference

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Evil

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry, I can't give references for ex-employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But if I did, it would rhyme with "Mazy Loron."

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, sits at his desk thinking 'evil' when the phone rings. He answers and claims company policy forbids giving references for former employees. He then hints that a reference, if he gave one, would rhyme with 'Mazy Loron,' a play on 'crazy moron.'
punchline: Catbert technically follows the no-reference policy while still delivering a damning review by rhyming a made-up name with 'crazy moron.'
summary: An evil personnel chief dodges a reference check on a former employee while slyly slipping in an insult through a rhyme.

file: 2003/2003-08-22_disappointing people_meeting start late_answer is misleading_deadline ignored_work is shoddy_empthy_blocking view of wall.gif
title: Dilbert Seeks Empathy, Dogbert Declines

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lately, every person I deal with seems to disappoint me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every meeting starts late, every answer is misleading, every deadline is ignored, and all work is shoddily done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess what I'm saying is that today I need some empathy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are totally blocking my view of the wall.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of Dogbert, who is sitting on the couch, and vents about how disappointing everyone around him is, listing late meetings, misleading answers, ignored deadlines and sloppy work. He finishes by asking for empathy. Dogbert responds only with a complaint that Dilbert is in the way of his view of the wall.
punchline: Dilbert asks for sympathy and gets none; Dogbert is so indifferent that he cares only about his view of a blank wall.
summary: After a long rant about his unreliable colleagues, a man asks his dog for comfort and is brushed off over a trivial obstruction.

file: 2003/2003-10-05_401k plan_afterlife_charisma_evil director_expected - value basis_free software upagrdes_high potential reward_human resources_math_odds seem low_reward you in aftrelife_seventy versions_education_business.gif
title: 401A Plan: Rewarded in Afterlife

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, the evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your 401k retirement plan will be replaced with a 401A plan.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The "A" stands for afterlife.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You'll get no money in this life, but the company will reward you in the afterlife.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The odds of that happening seem low.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yes, but on an expected-value basis, a high potential reward compensates for low odds.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For example, how many free software upgrades would I need to promise you in the afterlife to make you work yourself to death this year?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seventy versions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I resisted his charisma, but he got me with his math.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the employees at a meeting that their 401k plan is being replaced with a 401A plan that pays out only in the afterlife. Dilbert objects that the odds seem low, so Catbert argues expected-value math and asks how many free software upgrades in the afterlife it would take to make Dilbert work himself to death. Dilbert answers seventy versions, and later admits the math persuaded him.
punchline: Dilbert sees through the absurd afterlife retirement plan but gets talked into it anyway by a cynical expected-value argument tied to free software upgrades, showing how easily employees can be manipulated into overwork.
summary: A scheming HR cat swaps the pension for a pay-out-after-death scheme, and a skeptical engineer caves once it is framed as a probability calculation with software perks.

file: 2003/2003-06-17_sales call_vatican_sales people_worried.gif
title: Salesman Dressed As God Flying

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It's because I'm making a sales call to the Vatican.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I'm told that salespeople should dress one level above their customers.

transcript.speaker: Passenger
transcript.text: Aren't you worried?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: About what?

setting: Seats on a passenger airplane in flight
situation: A passenger on a plane sits next to a bearded man dressed in a white robe with wings who dangles a cherub figure. He explains that he is going to make a sales call to the Vatican and that salespeople should dress one level above their customers. In the last panel, a giant hand holds the airplane in the sky as the passenger asks if he is worried.
punchline: By dressing as God to impress the Pope, the salesman has apparently earned divine power, so God's hand is literally holding up the plane and he has nothing to worry about.
summary: A salesman heading to see the Pope dresses up as God, and the plane he's on is cradled by a giant hand from above.

file: 2003/2003-07-15_writing email_12 page description_carpal tunnel issue_do work_self inflicted_chapter_email.gif
title: Tina's Carpal Tunnel Email Complaint

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina, would you...?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Hold on while I finish writing this e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: It's a twelve-page description of my carpal tunnel issue, and the fact that there's never enough time to do my work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are all of your problems self-inflicted?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That's it! I'm adding a chapter about you. Ouch, ouch, ouch, ouch!

situation: Dilbert tries to ask Tina for something, but she tells him to wait while she finishes typing an email. She explains it is a twelve-page document about her carpal tunnel problem and her lack of time to do her work. Dilbert points out that her problems seem self-inflicted, so she angrily adds a chapter about him, typing furiously and wincing in pain.
punchline: Tina's marathon typing about her carpal tunnel injury is exactly what causes her pain, proving Dilbert's point that her problems are self-inflicted, and she is hurting herself further while typing a complaint about him.
summary: A coworker spends her workday typing a lengthy grievance about wrist pain and overwork, and keeps typing through the pain when challenged about causing her own troubles.

file: 2003/2003-05-20_hire emplyees_qaulified_hore dumb people_motivation.gif
title: Hiring Dumb People, Then Motivating Them

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We can't afford to hire qualified employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My plan is to hire dumb people and be angry at them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I forget - what's the word for pretending that people can change their basic nature?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Motivation?

setting: The Boss's office, with Catbert standing on the desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains his hiring strategy to the Boss: since the company can't afford qualified staff, he'll hire unqualified people and simply be angry at them. He then asks for the word describing the pretense that people can change their basic nature, and the Boss supplies 'motivation'.
punchline: Catbert cynically defines management 'motivation' as the pointless pretense that you can change people's inherent nature, and the Boss cheerfully confirms it.
summary: An HR cat outlines a cut-rate staffing plan built on unqualified hires and anger, then gets management's favorite buzzword as the label for it.

file: 2003/2003-12-23_alice_rich guy_care about personality_hugged too tight.gif
title: Insulting Advice for Downsized Alice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alice gets downsized

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe your next career could be marrying a rich guy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There must be a guy out there who wouldn't care about your personality.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If she offers you a goodbye hug, don't take it.

situation: Alice is packing her belongings into a box after being laid off. Wally, holding his coffee mug, offers her tactless career advice and insults her personality while she glares at him angrily. He then warns Dilbert not to accept a goodbye hug from her, and is shown rumpled and squeezed after apparently ignoring his own advice.
punchline: Wally insults the angry, newly downsized Alice to her face, then ends up crushed by her hug, which he himself had warned Dilbert to avoid.
summary: A tactless coworker tells a laid-off colleague to marry money because of her prickly personality, and he pays for it physically.

file: 2003/2003-02-24_assistant_company politics_pretend_actual work.gif
title: Useless Assignment Mistaken For Real Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have an assignment for you that has no value whatsoever to the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For reasons of company politics, I need to pretend I'm doing something in that area.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: So, you're doing actual work. What's that all about?

setting: Office conference table and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss hands a bald, bespectacled employee an assignment, admitting it is worthless to the company and exists only so he can appear to be acting on the issue for political reasons. Later the bald coworker visits Dilbert at his desk and, holding a coffee mug, is puzzled to find him doing real work.
punchline: Real work has become so rare in the company that seeing someone actually do it is suspicious enough to need explaining.
summary: A manager passes off a pointless task for the sake of appearances, and a colleague later finds genuine productivity more baffling than the fake kind.

file: 2003/2003-08-13_legal department_products_highly defective_user specification_ate letter_hugely defective prodcut.gif
title: Eating Evidence of Defective Products

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our legal department advises us to destroy any documents that show we know our products are hugely defective.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Chomp chomp chomp chew chew gulp

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you have room in there for the user specifications?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss reads out the legal department's advice to destroy any documents showing the company knows its products are badly defective. He then literally chews and swallows the paper. A coworker, Carol, asks if he has room left in his stomach for the user specifications.
punchline: The user specifications are the documents that prove the product is defective, so Carol sarcastically suggests the Boss eat those too, implying the product fails to meet its own specs.
summary: A manager follows legal advice to destroy incriminating paperwork by eating it, and a coworker snidely offers him more to swallow.

file: 2003/2003-08-02_pointy haired_takeover_should report_secret got out_extra money.gif
title: Secret Takeover By Working Double

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal is nothing less than a complete takeover of Pointy-Haired Carl's software division.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll start secretly doing their jobs in addition to our own. Then I'll argue that they should report to me.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: Hypothetically, if the secret got out, would we stop working twice as hard for no extra money?

situation: The Boss lays out a plan to take over Pointy-Haired Carl's software division by secretly doing their work on top of his own team's work, then arguing that Carl's people should report to him. A colleague at the table asks a pointed hypothetical about what happens if the secret leaks.
punchline: The employee's question reveals that the plan relies entirely on staff working double for no extra pay, and he wonders whether they could stop if the scheme were exposed, which highlights the boss's exploitation of his team.
summary: A boss schemes to grab a rival's department by having his own staff quietly do both workloads, and one worker nervously asks if the extra effort could end once the secret is out.

file: 2003/2003-11-09_company t shirt_not for temps_contractors_vendors_not size_downsized_leftover garage rags_morale.gif
title: Company Shirts Exclude Almost Everyone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone gets a company shirt!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's good for morale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oops! Not for temps.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: None for contractors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not for vendors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nothing in your size.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not for people who might get downsized on Friday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll use the leftovers as garage rags.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did the shirts improve morale?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sure did! I feel great!

situation: The Boss announces that everyone will receive a company shirt to boost morale, then keeps pulling shirts back from the box, excluding temps, contractors, vendors, people in the wrong size and those facing layoffs. He ends up with only a few leftovers, which he plans to use as garage rags. Afterward, a smug employee tells Catbert the shirts improved his morale.
punchline: The only person whose morale improved is the one who got to keep the shirt, showing the morale program was pointless for everyone else, and the employee's cheerful answer is a sarcastic jab at management's idea of boosting morale.
summary: A manager hands out morale-boosting shirts so selectively that nearly everyone is excluded, and the lone beneficiary claims to feel wonderful.

file: 2003/2003-10-01_ne whore_break room_pushy_punchable_met alice.gif
title: Desire to Punch New Acquaintance

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, big guy, how's your golf game lately?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've only known you for three seconds and already I have a deep desire to punch you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But no one ever does.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you met Alice?

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: A overly familiar coworker greets Dilbert at the coffee machine with a hearty golf question. Dilbert bluntly says he already wants to punch the man after three seconds of acquaintance. The coworker cheerfully replies that nobody ever does, and Dilbert suggests he go meet Alice, who is known for her violent temper.
punchline: Dilbert redirects the obnoxiously chummy coworker to Alice, implying she will happily supply the punch he insists nobody ever delivers.
summary: A glad-handing colleague's forced small talk earns a blunt threat, and Dilbert sends him off to meet the coworker most likely to follow through.

file: 2003/2003-02-14_stagger lunch_someone here_know in adavnce_take a pill_pecking order_errands.gif
title: Staggered Lunches Ruin Errand Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I want you to stagger your lunch hours so someone is always here.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa! As the lowest person in the pecking order, I will never know in advance when I can eat!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sheesh, take a pill.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It is the end of errands as I know them!!

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting to stagger their lunch hours so the office is always covered. Asok, the junior employee, panics because he will be last in line to pick a lunch time and won't be able to plan ahead. The Boss dismisses his panic and tells him to calm down, and Asok laments that his errand-running routine is over.
punchline: Asok is hysterical over the trivial loss of predictable errand time, while the Boss callously tells him to take a pill rather than address the legitimate scheduling inconvenience.
summary: A new lunch-coverage rule sends the office's most junior worker into a panic about losing control of his personal errands.

file: 2003/2003-11-07_lazy rich_new product_rebate_1 million_banking on forgetting_great bargain_one person.gif
title: Million-Dollar Rebate Pricing Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't sell your new product for $29. Offer it at $1,000,029 with a rebate of $1,000,000.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People will think it's a great bargain when in fact it's just a huge inconvenience.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And all we need is one person to forget to mail in the rebate forms.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll target the lazy rich.

setting: Conference room during a business meeting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a meeting to price a $29 product at $1,000,029 and offer a $1,000,000 rebate. He explains that customers will see a bargain but face a big hassle. The Boss then suggests targeting the lazy rich as the customers who will forget to claim the rebate.
punchline: Rebate schemes depend on customers being too lazy or forgetful to claim them, so the company hopes a rich, careless buyer will forfeit a million dollars.
summary: A consultant dog pitches an absurdly inflated price with a matching rebate, and the boss eagerly proposes marketing it to wealthy people too lazy to redeem it.

file: 2003/2003-03-08_loser magazine_forgetting_sounds good_fame.gif
title: Magazine Reporter Fabricates Willy's Story

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Your story is perfect for "Loser Magazine."

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: It makes me wish I'd written it down because I'm already forgetting ...oops, it's gone.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: I'll just make up something that sounds good. And I'll use photos of a model. Thanks, Willy.

transcript.speaker: Willy
transcript.text: I'm famous!

setting: An interview in an office or sitting area
situation: A bearded reporter with a notepad tells Willy, a balding man in glasses, that his story is ideal for a magazine about losers. The reporter admits he has forgotten the whole story because he never wrote it down, so he'll invent something and use photos of a model. Willy, oblivious to being insulted and deceived, thinks only about becoming famous.
punchline: Willy is so thrilled by the prospect of fame that he doesn't notice his real story is being discarded in favor of a fabricated one starring someone else's face.
summary: A forgetful journalist plans to invent a tale and swap in a model's photo, while his interview subject happily imagines stardom.

file: 2003/2003-04-29_corporations_ignore_jumpy tactics_laid off_you might be next_your imagination.gif
title: Catbert Posts Layoff Warning Sign

transcript.text: I'm seeing signs that I might get laid off.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's probably your imagination. Just ignore them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have to admit that I like it when they're jumpy.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: You might be next

setting: Dilbert's home living room and the office cubicle area
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert at home that he sees signs he might be laid off, and Dogbert dismisses it as imagination. In the final panel, Catbert, the evil HR director, is shown hanging a big arrow sign reading 'You might be next' on Dilbert's cubicle wall, revealing the signs are deliberate.
punchline: The ominous signs of layoffs are not imaginary at all; Catbert is deliberately planting them because he enjoys making employees nervous.
summary: A worried engineer is told his layoff fears are all in his head, until the sadistic HR cat is caught putting up an arrow warning that he might be next.

file: 2003/2003-09-14_keeper of giant binder_secret technology_never leave office_no drawer_no desk_use as tiny bed_rest of days_trade show binder.gif
title: Asok Guards the Giant Binder

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, I designate you the keeper of the giant binder.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It contains our secret technology plans.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It can never leave this office.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It won't fit in any drawer.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: And the "clean desk policy" forbids me from leaving it on my desktop.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa!! I can't take it home, and I can't leave it here!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I must use it as a tiny bed and spend the rest of my days guarding it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What did you do with the giant binder prop that you got at the trade show?

situation: Alice solemnly appoints Asok keeper of a giant binder said to hold secret technology plans that can never leave the office. Asok panics because the binder won't fit in a drawer, the clean desk policy bans leaving it on his desktop, and he can't take it home. In the last panel Dilbert asks Alice what she did with the giant binder prop from the trade show, revealing the binder is just a worthless prop she has dumped on Asok.
punchline: The supposedly top-secret binder is actually a useless trade show prop that Alice has offloaded onto the gullible Asok, who now fears he must guard it for the rest of his life.
summary: A bulky, supposedly confidential binder is handed to a worried junior engineer, but it turns out to be nothing more than a promotional prop that a coworker wanted to get rid of.

file: 2003/2003-04-18_at party_camera advice_engineer_physical_wally dressed as engineer_engineering.gif
title: Free Advice At A Party

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're an engineer; maybe you can tell me what kind of digital camera I should buy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you ask a doctor for free advice?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I got a complete physical by the appetizer.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm never off duty.

situation: At a party, a woman holding a drink asks Dilbert, an engineer, to recommend a digital camera. Dilbert responds by asking whether she would request free advice from a doctor. She replies that she already got a full physical from a doctor by the appetizer, and a doctor standing nearby confirms he is never off duty.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to deflect free professional advice backfires because people really do pester doctors for free medical help at parties, and this doctor cheerfully obliges.
summary: A party guest tries to dodge giving free tech advice by comparing himself to a doctor, only to learn that doctors freely hand out checkups at social events.

file: 2003/2003-04-08_dogbert_head hunter_ceo section_resume_re word_less criminal sounding_more honest_plundered.gif
title: Rewording the CEO's Plundering Resume

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Headhunter

transcript.text: We'll need to reword the CEO section of your resume.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And instead of "suckers ignored our P/E ratio," say you "enhanced stockholder value."

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Wow. You're good.

setting: Dogbert's headhunter office, across a desk
situation: Dogbert, working as a headhunter, coaches a bald executive on polishing the CEO section of his resume. He swaps blunt, incriminating phrases like "plundered" and "suckers ignored our P/E ratio" for flattering corporate euphemisms. The executive is impressed by how well Dogbert spins his record.
punchline: The executive's actual career as a CEO involved plundering the company and fleecing foolish investors, and Dogbert's job is simply to relabel it as "enhanced stockholder value."
summary: A canine career counselor launders a corporate looter's résumé by turning confessions of fleecing investors into respectable-sounding achievements.

file: 2003/2003-01-21_new tech lab_pick contractor_lowest bid_force problems_chance to gnaw wood_beaver interview.gif
title: Lowest Bidder Is a Beaver

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of building our new technology lab.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pick the contractor with the lowest bid. I don't foresee any problems with that strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, your bid says you'll do the job for "...a chance to gnaw on wood."

transcript.speaker: Beaver
transcript.text: Too high?

situation: The Boss puts Dilbert in charge of building a new technology lab and tells him to simply choose the contractor with the lowest bid. Dilbert then interviews a beaver whose bid is only a chance to gnaw on wood, and the beaver worries that even that price might be too high.
punchline: Picking purely on lowest price leads to absurd bidders, like a beaver who will work for free, showing the Boss's cost-cutting strategy ignores competence.
summary: Told to hire whoever charges least for a construction project, an engineer ends up negotiating with a beaver who works for the pleasure of chewing lumber.

file: 2003/2003-05-03_cannibals_inspirational quotes_lobby wall_hands on stomach.gif
title: Cannibal Quotes for the Lobby

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As requested, I pulled together some inspirational quotes for our lobby wall.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hannibal Lecter... The Donner Party... Uh...Wally, most of these people are cannibals.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was probably a mistake to do this assignment on an empty stomach.

situation: Wally hands the Boss a list of inspirational quotes he compiled for the company lobby wall. The Boss reads through it and notices that the sources are Hannibal Lecter and the Donner Party, all of them cannibals. Wally casually blames his own hunger for the odd choices.
punchline: Wally's explanation implies his hunger made him pick quotes from cannibals, while also showing he put no real effort into the assignment.
summary: A hungry employee delivers a list of motivational sayings that all turn out to come from people who ate other people.

file: 2003/2003-01-07_eat_headquarters_misunderstand_mouth_need shreded_shredder.gif
title: Asok Becomes the Human Shredder

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Mouth... so... dry

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that all shredders are being centralized at corporate headquarters, and a coworker says anyone needing shredding done should give it to Asok. Asok takes this literally and starts chewing paper at his desk, surrounded by stacks of documents and a pile of shredded bits, until Dilbert points out the misunderstanding.
punchline: Asok misreads the instruction so literally that he becomes the shredder himself, eating the documents, while his thought bubble complains about his dry mouth.
summary: A cost-cutting shredder policy leaves a naive intern chewing through paperwork because he thinks he is the replacement machine.

file: 2003/2003-12-17_obliterate connection_my perfromance_my rewards_3d objects.gif
title: Dilbert Gives Up After Merger

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The merger will obliterate the connection between my performance and my rewards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My arms hang like wet ropes. There is no reason to move again.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: From 9 to 9:30 I rotated 3-dimensional objects in my mind.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My ears hang like wet ropes.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and his home
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and thinks that an upcoming merger will break the link between how well he performs and what he is rewarded. He decides he has no reason to move again and sits motionless in his cubicle. At home he describes how he spent the first half hour of his workday doing nothing but mental rotation, while Dogbert sits on the couch with limp ears.
punchline: Since the merger makes effort pointless, Dilbert slides into total lethargy and claims that doing nothing but imagining rotating objects counts as his work, with Dogbert mirroring his listlessness.
summary: Convinced that a corporate merger makes hard work pointless, Dilbert stops moving and fills his day with idle daydreaming.

file: 2003/2003-11-27_protective employees_question_resoning_fox_chickens_across river_rowboat_eat chickens_livestock insurance_blame the fox_barbecue chickens.gif
title: Fox, Chickens, and Insurance Fraud

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ask all prospective employees this question to test their reasoning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have one fox and two chickens that you need to get across a river. You can only take one at a time in the rowboat. The fox will eat the chickens if left alone.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'd buy livestock insurance, then barbecue the chickens and blame the fox.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you start today?

setting: Job interview in an office, across a desk
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and poses the classic river-crossing riddle about a fox and two chickens in a rowboat. Instead of solving the puzzle logically, the candidate proposes buying livestock insurance, cooking the chickens and blaming the fox. The Boss is delighted and offers him the job on the spot.
punchline: The candidate's answer is a scheme for insurance fraud, and the Boss hires him immediately, showing that the company values dishonesty over honest problem-solving.
summary: A manager's logic-puzzle interview question gets a fraudulent answer from the applicant, and the manager is so impressed he wants him to begin right away.

file: 2003/2003-10-11_top down budget_bottom up budget_ignorance_cruelty_lying_optimism_cancel_wasted hour.gif
title: Averaging Budgets Cancels Out Lies

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: I averaged the top-down budget with the bottom-up budget.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: As you can see, the ignorance and cruelty canceled out the lying and optimism.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: Do you have anything to cancel out feelings of a wasted hour?

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: Have you tried despair?

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting
situation: A man with glasses presents the result of averaging the top-down budget with the bottom-up budget to colleagues seated around a table. He explains the numbers come out balanced because management's ignorance and cruelty offset the staff's lying and optimism. A woman asks if he has anything to offset the feeling of a wasted hour, and he suggests despair.
punchline: The budget process is revealed as a cynical blend of ignorance, cruelty, lying and optimism, and the only remedy for a pointless meeting is despair.
summary: A budget presenter cheerfully admits his reconciled numbers are just bad traits cancelling each other, then offers hopelessness as the cure for a squandered meeting.

file: 2003/2003-02-20_own luxury_motor coach_work and sleep_parking lot_best fanatasy_tv.gif

transcript.text: That's your best fantasy?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It would also have a TV, in case I woke up.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Dilbert, Alice and Wally sit at a table eating lunch while Wally describes his fantasy of owning a luxury motor coach. He would drive it to work only to sleep in the parking lot all day. When Dilbert questions whether that is really his best fantasy, Wally adds that it would have a TV in case he woke up.
punchline: Wally's idea of paradise is getting paid to sleep at work in a parked motorhome, and the TV is only a backup for the rare moment he is awake, which highlights his extreme laziness.
summary: A coworker's dream of luxury turns out to be napping in a fancy vehicle outside the office while still collecting a paycheck.

file: 2003/2003-01-05_boss_delight_lower pay_new member_project team_shirt backwards.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please tell me that his pay is lower than mine.

setting: Office cubicle area and the boss's office
situation: The boss introduces a new team member named Ron, nicknamed Mo, who is wearing his shirt on backward. Mo tries to fix it by spinning around and then believes he has entered another dimension because Dilbert is no longer in front of him. Dilbert walks to the boss's office and hopes Mo earns less than he does.
punchline: Dilbert is so resigned to working with a hopelessly clueless colleague that his only hope is that the man is paid less than him, and the boss gleefully enjoys this predictable reaction.
summary: A bumbling new coworker who dresses himself wrong and thinks he has teleported leaves Dilbert hoping at least the guy makes less money than he does.

file: 2003/2003-09-23_tasks_a_b or c priorities_a priorities_after i update_left in tank.gif

setting: Office desk or meeting table with a coffee mug
situation: A bald coworker in glasses tells The Boss that he starts each day ranking his tasks as A, B or C priorities. The Boss asks if he then tackles the A priorities first. The coworker admits that updating the list leaves him with little energy to do any actual work.
punchline: The time and effort spent organizing and prioritizing the to-do list exhausts him so much that no real work gets done.
summary: A worker's elaborate morning ritual of sorting his tasks leaves him too drained to start any of them.

file: 2003/2003-11-11_boss stalker_wait_offcie_unscheduled_suck up_phone calls end_still out there.gif

situation: A co-worker introduces himself to a colleague as a 'boss stalker' who loiters by the boss's office without an appointment, waiting to flatter him as soon as his phone calls end. In the last panel the boss, hiding on the phone in his chair, begs the person on the line not to hang up because the stalker is still lurking outside his door.
punchline: The boss is so desperate to avoid the persistent brown-noser waiting outside that he keeps a phone call going indefinitely as a shield.
summary: An eager sycophant haunts the hallway outside his manager's office while the manager clings to a phone call to avoid him.

file: 2003/2003-08-28_ask them_feeling embarrassed_money_negotiating with vendors_phd_right thing_thinking of idea.gif

situation: A mustached man at the conference table claims authority because he has a PhD and proposes that the company skip negotiating with vendors, simply telling them its budget and asking them to do the right thing. punchline: The PhD-holder's naive, credential-driven idea is absurd, and Alice is so exasperated that she fantasizes about violently shaving the PhD off his head.
summary: A smug expert insists his degree makes his dangerously naive purchasing plan unquestionable, pushing a frustrated Alice toward the edge.

file: 2003/2003-08-05_lose language skill_using words_wrong context_adopt them_truculent_doctrinaire_obelisk_cervically.gif

The Boss then walks up and gives Carol a nonsensical instruction full of misused words, proving her scheme has worked. Carol answers with another nonsense word.
punchline: Carol's quiet sabotage works so well that the Boss now speaks complete gibberish, and she keeps feeding it with more nonsense.
summary: A secretary subtly corrupts her boss's vocabulary by misusing words until he starts issuing orders that make no sense.

file: 2003/2003-01-24_upgarde_pc operating systems_stable environemnt_applications_form of taxation_evil shadow government.gif

punchline: The computer itself talks back with 'Shut up and pay me,' confirming that forced operating system upgrades really do resemble extortion by a shadowy authority.
summary: A request for new operating systems is likened to a shadowy tax, and the boss's own computer promptly behaves like a racketeer.

file: 2003/2003-04-28_business card orders_downsized_3 per week_possibility of leaving_rates_fees_calculations.gif

punchline: Alice's blunt answer implies Dilbert will be fired within a week, so three cards is all he will ever need.
summary: A routine supply question turns into a deadpan prediction that a coworker is about to lose his job.

file: 2003/2003-06-19_switch to decaf_secretly_office_employees sleeping_sleep on job.gif

situation: A doctor tells Alice, who is sitting on an exam table, to switch to decaf coffee for her health. summary: After a doctor tells her to cut caffeine, a coworker imposes decaf on everyone, and the caffeine-starved staff drop where they stand.

file: 2003/2003-08-23_boss aprroaches_slices clicks comouter_filthy images_projecting himself_obvious_paranoid.gif

file: 2003/2003-09-16_india institute of technology_huge brain_mental superiority_re heat tea_forehead_fire.gif
title: Asok Heats Tea With Mind

transcript.text: At the India Institute of Technology, I learned to use my huge brain.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But I try not to frighten ordinary people with any gratuitous displays of mental superiority.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: For example, I no longer reheat my tea by holding it to my forehead and imagining fire.

situation: Asok sits at a meeting table with Wally and Dilbert and explains that his training at the India Institute of Technology gave him a huge brain. He says he tries not to intimidate ordinary people with displays of intellect. As an example, he casually mentions he used to heat his tea with his mind alone.
punchline: Asok humbly claims to restrain his genius, yet his example is an absurd superpower, implying he can set things on fire with his thoughts.
summary: A modest young intern casually reveals he has stopped using his enormous intellect to boil his drinks through sheer imagination.

file: 2003/2003-11-25_replace myself_cheap elbonian labor_describe appearence_coffe mug.gif
title: Replacing Myself With Elbonian Labor

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm planning to replace myself with cheap Elbonian labor.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Watch this: turn around and try to describe my appearance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see glasses... a coffee mug... and that's all.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This will work.

setting: Office break room by the coffee machine
situation: Wally tells Dilbert he plans to replace himself with cheap Elbonian labor. To prove it will work, he has Dilbert turn around and describe his appearance, and Dilbert can recall only his glasses and coffee mug. Wally then swaps in a robed, bearded Elbonian holding a mug, confident no one will notice.
punchline: Wally is so unmemorable and indistinct that anyone wearing glasses and holding a coffee mug could pass as him, so his job is effectively already replaceable.
summary: Wally demonstrates that a stranger could easily stand in for him because nobody notices anything about him beyond his glasses and mug.

file: 2003/2003-09-19_big picture_drifting_floating_above earth_plane_coach_in plane.gif
title: Big Picture From 20,000 Feet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend that we look at the big picture and view it from 20,000 feet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Drifting...floating above the earth... wait...a plane is coming right at me! No-o-o-o!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should imagine you're in the plane.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaaa!! I'm in coach!

situation: Dilbert suggests the team look at the big picture from 20,000 feet. The Boss takes the idea literally and imagines himself floating in the sky until he panics at an oncoming plane. Dilbert tells him to imagine being in the plane instead, and the Boss discovers he is sitting in coach.
punchline: Even in his own imagination, the Boss is stuck in the cheap seats, and his panic is about the unglamorous class of travel rather than the danger.
summary: A manager literally visualizes a high-altitude view, gets scared by an incoming airplane, and is then dismayed to find himself in economy class.

file: 2003/2003-10-07_tuesday_need  by tuesday_agreement_yelling now_unreliable.gif
title: Yelling at Unreliable Coworker Early

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I absolutely need your input by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Considering that you're massively unreliable, I'd like to save time by yelling at you now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said you'd do it by Tuesday!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Umm... I was too busy.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker holding a coffee mug for input by Tuesday, and the coworker agrees. Dilbert then decides the coworker is so unreliable that he will skip ahead and yell at him immediately to save time. The coworker, flustered, can only reply that he was too busy, as though he had already failed the deadline.
punchline: Dilbert is so certain the coworker will miss the deadline that he scolds him in advance, and the coworker's meek excuse confirms he is treated as already guilty of the failure.
summary: Expecting a colleague to flake on a deadline, a man berates him right away instead of waiting for the inevitable.

file: 2003/2003-04-14_leave work early_don't walk past_office of boss_just from roof_land in dumpster_leadership_cut throat.gif
title: Sneaking Out Via Rooftop Dumpster

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our VP is mad because people are leaving work too early.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you need to leave early, don't walk past his office. Go to the roof and leap into the "dumpster" in the alley.

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: Leadership triumphs again.

setting: Conference room and the VP's office
situation: At a meeting, the Boss explains that the VP is angry about employees leaving work early. Instead of addressing the cause, he advises staff who must leave to avoid the VP's office by jumping off the roof into a dumpster. In the final panel, the VP smugly thinks about leadership while a person falls past his window.
punchline: The VP believes his anger is effective leadership, while his workers would rather jump off a roof than walk past his office, showing how intimidation drives people to absurd lengths.
summary: Rather than fix a boss's wrath over early departures, employees are told to hurl themselves off the roof to dodge him.

file: 2003/2003-06-03_gambling casino_bad luck_casino_extraordinary bad luck.gif
title: Casino for the Unlucky

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to open a gambling casino for people who have extraordinarily bad luck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you tell who has extraordinarily bad luck?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They would be the ones that go to my casino.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch reading a book while Dogbert announces his plan to open a casino aimed at people with extraordinarily bad luck. Dilbert asks how he would identify such people. Dogbert replies that they will identify themselves by showing up at his casino.
punchline: Anyone who chooses to gamble at Dogbert's casino, where the house always wins, is by definition unlucky, so his customer base is self-selecting.
summary: Dogbert explains that his business plan needs no screening because only the hopelessly unlucky would gamble in his establishment.

file: 2003/2003-11-13_balance them_not  trash_mistaken_took as tarsh_important files.gif
title: Important Files Balanced on Trash

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where can I put my most important files so I won't lose them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll balance them on top of the trash can so the janitor knows it's not part of the actual trash.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: These items must be what's most urgently in need of discardation.

situation: The Boss, sitting at a desk covered with stacks of papers, wonders where to keep his most important files so he won't lose them. He decides to balance them on top of the trash can, assuming the janitor will understand they are not garbage. The janitor then arrives, sees the pile on the can, and concludes they must be the items most urgently needing disposal.
punchline: The Boss's plan to protect his files backfires because placing them on the trash can makes the janitor assume they are the most urgent garbage, showing the Boss's flawed logic.
summary: A clueless manager leaves his prized documents perched on a wastebasket, and the cleaner promptly hauls them away as rubbish.

file: 2003/2003-10-27_lunch time_barely came late_work_eat_plaumbing_read apaper_non urgency_moring at offcie_slacker_stale job.gif
title: Cultivating a Sense of Non-Urgency

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you going to lunch?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Lunch already?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sheesh! I barely had time to come late to work, eat breakfast, use the plumbing and read the paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You take your non-work seriously.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm trying to develop a sense of non-urgency.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally if he's coming to lunch, and Wally is surprised it's already time because he has spent the morning arriving late, eating breakfast, using the restroom and reading the newspaper. Dilbert remarks that Wally takes his non-work seriously, and Wally says he's deliberately cultivating a sense of non-urgency as the two walk off to lunch.
punchline: Wally treats slacking off as a busy, disciplined pursuit, even framing his laziness as a deliberate professional skill he is developing.
summary: A lazy cubicle dweller is shocked that lunchtime has arrived because his morning was consumed by leisure activities he treats as a serious job.

file: 2003/2003-09-11_created time line_identified resources_revise timeline_re examine_thousand ways_haven't done anything.gif
title: A Thousand Ways to Say Nothing

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: In only one week my project team has created a time line and identified the resources we need.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Next week, we plan to revise the time line and re-examine our resource needs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good work.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: There must be a thousand ways to say I haven't done anything.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Wait...

situation: A balding manager with glasses holding a coffee mug reports to The Boss, who is seated in a red chair. He describes his team's one week of progress as a timeline and a list of resources, then promises to revise both next week. The Boss praises him, and in the final panel the manager thinks about how many ways there are to say he has accomplished nothing.
punchline: The manager realizes that impressive-sounding planning activities are just creative ways of disguising that no real work has been done, and the Boss falls for it.
summary: A manager spins a week of paperwork and planned revisions into praise from his boss while privately admitting he has accomplished nothing.

file: 2003/2003-10-09_management retreat_hawaii_how many employees_down size_pay of trip_against helicopter ride.gif
title: Layoffs Fund the Hawaii Retreat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The management retreat in Hawaii was productive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We calculated how many employees we needed to downsize to pay for the trip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't blame me, Ted. I voted against the third helicopter ride.

setting: Conference room, then an office cubicle
situation: The Boss tells his staff that the management retreat in Hawaii was productive. He explains that the main outcome was working out how many employees must be laid off to cover the cost of the trip. He then tells Ted, who is facing the layoff, that he voted against the third helicopter ride.
punchline: Management's idea of restraint is opposing only the third helicopter ride, while workers lose their jobs to pay for a lavish retreat.
summary: Executives treat firing staff as a routine way to pay for their own island getaway, then claim a small show of frugality as a defence.

file: 2003/2003-05-31_scale back_new brochure_diplomatic immunity_current_future felonies_poetic licence_motor oil_root beer.gif
title: Brochure Claims Are Poetic License

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We might want to scale back some of the claims in our new brochure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which ones?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, where it says, "Provides diplomatic immunity against all current and future felonies."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's just poetic license.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Turn used motor oil into root beer."

situation: Dilbert and the Boss read the company's new marketing brochure together. Dilbert suggests toning down exaggerated claims and cites one that promises diplomatic immunity from all felonies. The Boss dismisses it as poetic license, and Dilbert points out an even more absurd claim about turning motor oil into root beer.
punchline: The Boss treats wildly false and potentially illegal marketing claims as harmless creative flourish, while Dilbert keeps finding even more ridiculous ones.
summary: A pair of outrageous promises in a product brochure get waved away by a manager who thinks lying in marketing is just artistic expression.

file: 2003/2003-01-18_radiating aura_extreme incompetence_turn off_minute to cool.gif
title: Wally's Aura of Incompetence

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, would you...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh... never mind. I see that you're radiating an aura of extreme incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You forgot to turn off your aura.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It takes a minute to cool down.

situation: The Boss starts to ask Wally for something, then notices a glowing aura around him and decides not to bother, because it shows extreme incompetence. Later, in a meeting, Dilbert points out that Wally forgot to turn off his aura, and Wally explains that it takes a minute to cool down.
punchline: Wally treats his incompetence as a switch he can turn on and off at will, which reveals that his uselessness is deliberate and that he only forgot to hide it this time.
summary: A manager spots a glowing sign of uselessness around Wally and gives up on asking him for help, and Wally later admits the effect is something he can switch off but is slow to fade.

file: 2003/2003-09-03_can't eat anything_fifty choices_joined lunch_mike the vegan_no meat_people suffer_vegan_hunger.gif
title: Vegan Coworker Rejects Fifty Lunch Options

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where do you want to eat?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Anyplace.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Suddenly, Mike the Vegan pounced.

transcript.speaker: Mike
transcript.text: Do you mind if I join you?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Soon, hunger started to set in.

transcript.speaker: Mike
transcript.text: No, I can't eat at any of those fifty choices. What else do you have?

situation: Dilbert asks coworkers where they want to go for lunch, and Alice says anywhere is fine. Mike the Vegan, who works in a cubicle, abruptly invites himself along. When the group offers fifty restaurant choices, he rejects every one of them and demands more options while everyone grows hungry.
punchline: Mike's veganism makes him veto all fifty restaurants, so a simple lunch outing drags on and the whole group suffers for one picky person's dietary restrictions.
summary: A casual lunch plan collapses into hungry frustration when a vegan coworker joins and dismisses every restaurant on offer.

file: 2003/2003-02-12_evil hr director_hire_job interview_urine sample_social secuirty_past emplyers_past lovers_despicable.gif
title: Background Check Reveals Everyone Despicable

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I need to check a few things before we hire you.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Give me blood, hair, and urine samples, fingerprints, social-security number, past employers, and past lovers.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Before we started doing all of this checking, did you know that everyone in the world was despicable?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Yes

situation: Catbert, the Evil H.R. Director, tells a job candidate he must check a few things before hiring him, then demands blood, hair and urine samples, fingerprints, social-security number, past employers and past lovers. In the last panel the candidate's long printed background report is in hand, and Catbert asks if he knew everyone in the world was despicable before this checking began.
punchline: Catbert's exhaustive background check has apparently turned up nothing but dirt on everybody, implying that invasive screening of job candidates only reveals how awful people are.
summary: After demanding an absurdly invasive pile of personal information from a job applicant, the feline HR chief grimly concludes that humanity is rotten.

file: 2003/2003-05-22_job not stimulating_togers_toger meat_analogy_zebra.gif
title: Feed Tigers Tiger Meat, Not Zebra

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My job is not stimulating my mind.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If you want to have tigers, you must feed them tiger meat.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But that is only an analogy. Please do not make me eat a zebra.

situation: An employee stands in front of his boss's desk and complains that his job doesn't stimulate his mind. He argues that tigers need tiger meat, meaning talented people need challenging work. He then nervously clarifies that it's only an analogy and begs not to be given a zebra to eat, fearing the boss will take the metaphor literally.
punchline: The employee fears his boss is so dense that he will interpret the tiger analogy literally and force him to eat a zebra.
summary: A bored worker uses a predator metaphor to ask for more demanding work, then frantically hedges in case his literal-minded manager misunderstands.

file: 2003/2003-08-12_budget request_priority_highest priority_mockery_low priority.gif
title: Everyone's Budget Is Highest Priority

transcript.speaker: Budget Manager
transcript.text: What is the priority of your budget request?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Highest of the high.

transcript.speaker: Budget Manager
transcript.text: Everyone rated their own budget needs "highest priority." It is a mockery of the priority system!

transcript.speaker: Budget Manager
transcript.text: Name one thing that everyone would agree is a low priority.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Whatever you're doing.

situation: A man with a notepad asks a woman at her desk how she ranks her budget request, and she says it is the highest priority. He complains that everyone has made the same claim, which makes the priority system meaningless, and asks her to name something everyone would agree is low priority. She replies that it is whatever he is doing.
punchline: Asked for something universally considered low priority, Alice insults the budget manager by naming his own job.
summary: A budget official frets that every department labels its funding request top priority, then gets a withering answer when he asks what counts as unimportant.

file: 2003/2003-11-04_level conscious_vide presidents offcie_secretary_make direct eye contact_meeting_boss_new hire_business.gif
title: Not Level Conscious, Except You

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're not "level conscious" here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could walk up to any vice president's office and talk to his secretary as if you were an equal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which, by the way, you're not. So don't try to make direct eye contact.

situation: The Boss meets with a new employee and claims the company has no rigid hierarchy, saying the employee could freely talk to a vice president's secretary as an equal. He then reverses himself, telling the employee they are not an equal and should avoid making direct eye contact.
punchline: The Boss's claim of a egalitarian workplace collapses immediately as he reveals a rigidly hierarchical culture, undercutting himself mid-speech.
summary: A manager boasts of a classless office culture and then promptly informs a newcomer of his lowly rank and forbids him from looking people in the eye.

file: 2003/2003-11-29_antivirus software_secretly create viruses_detected by software_spooky_underhanded_sneaky_criminal.gif
title: Antivirus Company Secretly Makes Viruses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company is going to make antivirus software. What's that tell you?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It tells me we'll secretly create viruses that can be detected only by our software.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Am I close?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're spooky.

setting: Office, with Catbert perched on a filing cabinet
situation: The Boss announces that the company will start making antivirus software and asks Catbert what that implies. Catbert, sitting on a filing cabinet, deduces that the company will secretly create viruses that only its own software can detect. The Boss admits Catbert has guessed the plan and calls him spooky.
punchline: Catbert correctly guesses that the company's real business plan is to manufacture the viruses its antivirus software will cure, and the Boss's reaction confirms it.
summary: A manager's hint about a new security product leads his evil feline advisor to uncover the scheme of selling the cure for a problem the company itself creates.
keywords: create the problem sell the cure

file: 2003/2003-01-08_alice_mulitask_one person_schedule_second task_two task_write a patch_timeline.gif
title: Inventing Months to Fake Scheduling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do I make this software schedule one person to two tasks at the same time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can write a patch that inserts new months in the timeline.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the second task is due on the fifteenth of Floopupary.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how to make scheduling software assign one person to two tasks simultaneously. Dilbert offers to write a patch that adds new months to the timeline. The Boss then shows Alice a task due on the made-up date of 'Floopupary'.
punchline: Rather than admit a person can't do two things at once, the Boss solves overbooking by inventing fictitious calendar months to hide the conflict.
summary: To dodge an impossible double-booking, the Boss has the software gain extra imaginary months so one employee can seem to be in two places at once.

file: 2003/2003-06-06_senior management knows_key employees_hard imes_bonuses_black mailing themselves_sound bad_huge retention.gif
title: Executives Blackmail Themselves With Bonuses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Senior management knows they need to retain key employees during hard times.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's why they're giving themselves huge retention bonuses.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, they're blackmailing themselves?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can make anything sound bad.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss explains that senior management wants to retain key employees through hard times. Alice points out that this means management is giving themselves huge retention bonuses, and sarcastically asks if they are blackmailing themselves. The Boss dismisses her, saying you can make anything sound bad.
punchline: Executives award themselves large retention bonuses in the name of keeping key staff, and the Boss deflects Alice's accurate criticism by claiming she is merely spinning things negatively.
summary: A manager's justification for rewarding the top brass with big bonuses during lean times gets skewered by a sarcastic colleague, and he waves off the criticism as mere negativity.

file: 2003/2003-04-06_dismissal email foloowed_found pen_human resources_layoffs_mass email sent_missed bid deadline_not enough bandwidth_business.gif
title: Pen Email Overloads Company, Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who left their pen at my desk?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd better send a companywide e-mail to find out.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's blue, with black ink. It's approximately one year old.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Send

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't believe you're wasting everyone's time with this!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stop using the "reply to all" feature, you morons!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wait...I think this might be my pen. I'd better send a correction.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We missed a bid deadline because our e-mail system was overloaded.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Send this list to Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do I look like I'm made of time?!!

setting: Office cubicles and an executive's office
situation: Alice sends a companywide email to find the owner of a pen on her desk, and coworkers angrily reply to everyone about the waste of time, snowballing into a flood of messages. She then realizes the pen is hers and sends a correction. The overloaded email system causes the company to miss a bid deadline, and an executive responds by ordering layoffs, while Alice snaps at being asked to handle the list herself.
punchline: A trivial companywide email about a pen cascades into a costly business failure, and management's response is to lay people off rather than address the cause.
