summary: One person's needless mass email about a stray pen triggers a chain of reply-all complaints that sinks a business deadline and ends in job cuts.

file: 2003/2003-07-09_new corporate code_report immediately_señor management_ship prodcuts_defective_take care_lying_report you.gif
title: Reporting Management Under the Ethics Code

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you see anyone violating the new corporate code of ethics, report it immediately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to report our senior management for telling us to ship products that we know are defective.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes. I will take care of that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oooh! Oooh! Lying!!! I report you!!!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces a new corporate code of ethics and tells everyone to report violations immediately. Dilbert takes him at his word and reports senior management for ordering the shipment of known-defective products. The Boss says he'll take care of it, and a coworker excitedly accuses him of lying.
punchline: Management's ethics code is hollow: the boss who demands violation reports is himself the violator, and his promise to 'take care of it' is so obviously false that a coworker reports him for lying.
summary: A manager's ethics crackdown backfires when an employee reports the leadership itself, and the manager's insincere reply gets him reported in turn.

file: 2003/2003-08-03_disturbing news_outsourced_customer service function_india_subcontracted_jobs to mexico_lowest cost provider_pay ourselves.gif
title: Outsourcing Chain Leads Back Home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have some disturbing news.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We outsourced our customer-service function to India a few years ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently, they subcontracted the job to Mexico.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then Mexico subcontracted to Vietnam, who subcontracted to the Philippines...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...who subcontracted it to us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It turns out that we're the lowest-cost provider, because we lie about our hold times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In summary, we pay ourselves to hose ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you thinking what I'm thinking?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We should raise our prices?

situation: Dilbert reports disturbing news to the Boss: the company's outsourced customer-service function was passed along a chain of subcontractors across several countries until it ended up back at the company itself. The company is the lowest-cost provider because it lies about its hold times. The Boss's only takeaway is to raise prices.
punchline: After paying to outsource customer service, the company discovers it is paying itself to do the work, and the clueless Boss sees this only as an opportunity to charge more rather than a sign of absurdity.
summary: A circular chain of subcontracting brings a company's outsourced support work right back to its own doorstep, and its boss responds by wanting to hike the price.

file: 2003/2003-10-20_guest cartoonist_nildo orbfutz_consulting_welocme_breakroom_on the job training.gif
title: Consultant Learned By Getting Fired

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Who's today's guest cartoonist?*

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At great expense, I've just hired Nildo Orbfutz as a consultant. He will increase our productivity hereby calculating how much time is actually wasted!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, Nildo. How did you acquire your credentials? Degree in business management? H.R.? P.R.? Psychology?

transcript.speaker: Nildo
transcript.text: On-the-job training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me guess: you've been fired from every job you ever had... for wasting time?

transcript.speaker: Nildo
transcript.text: Welcome to the wonderful world of consulting.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gloop!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Answer: go to dilbert.com

setting: Office hallway and break room near the water cooler
situation: The Boss proudly introduces Nildo Orbfutz, an expensive consultant hired to calculate how much company time is wasted. Dilbert asks about his credentials and learns Nildo's only qualification is on-the-job training. Dilbert guesses Nildo was fired from every job for wasting time, and Nildo cheerfully confirms that this is how consulting works.
punchline: The consultant hired to measure wasted time is himself an expert in wasting time, having been fired from every job for it, and calls that the wonderful world of consulting.
summary: A pricey new consultant hired to uncover time-wasting turns out to have qualified for the role by being a chronic time-waster himself.

file: 2003/2003-04-25_coffee rehab program_blame location_world headquaters_recidivism rate.gif
title: Coffee Rehab Next to Starbucks

transcript.speaker: Rehab Counselor
transcript.text: Wally, congratulations on finishing the coffee rehab program.

transcript.speaker: Rehab Counselor
transcript.text: Our recidivism rate isn't too hot. Our critics blame our location.

transcript.speaker: Voice from building
transcript.text: Who's swimming in our vat?

setting: Outside a rehab facility next to a taxi stand, beside Starbucks World Headquarters
situation: A counselor congratulates Wally on completing a coffee rehab program, then admits the program has a high relapse rate. The final panel reveals the facility sits right next to a sign reading Starbucks World Headquarters, while a taxi drives up and someone inside the building asks who is swimming in their vat.
punchline: A coffee addiction rehab center located next to Starbucks headquarters guarantees relapses, and Wally apparently relapsed by taking a dip in the company's coffee vat.
summary: A treatment center for caffeine addicts has trouble keeping patients clean because it was built beside the world's biggest coffee company.

file: 2003/2003-07-10_ring thingy_grew up and moved away_worked well_children grew_while working.gif
title: Boss Pleased Kids Grew Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ringy thingy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: While you were working, your children grew up and moved away.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've never had a plan that worked so well.

setting: The Boss's office, seated at his desk
situation: The Boss sits at his desk and is puzzled by his ringing phone, then answers it. A caller tells him that his children grew up and moved away while he was busy working. Instead of feeling regret, the Boss privately gloats that this is the most successful plan he has ever had.
punchline: The Boss is so incompetent that his only successful plan is accidentally neglecting his family until his children left, and he treats that as a triumph rather than a loss.
summary: A phone call reveals that a workaholic manager's kids have grown up and left, and he is delighted that something finally went according to plan.

file: 2003/2003-10-24_dilbert died_funeral_casket_running with sciccors_what does mean_pastor_newspapaer slots open_money_ka ching.gif
title: Guest Cartoonist Eulogizes Dead Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Who's today's guest cartoonist?*

transcript.speaker: Priest
transcript.text: ...When I first heard Dilbert had died while running with scissors, I, too, was stunned. I, too, asked, "What's it all mean?"

transcript.speaker: Priest
transcript.text: ...That 2,247 newspaper slots are now wiiiiiide open, baby!.... Ka-ching! Ka-ching!

transcript.speaker: Priest
transcript.text: ...Sorry about the ka-chings.

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: *Answer: Go to Dilbert.com

setting: A funeral service beside an open casket
situation: A priest delivers a eulogy at Dilbert's funeral, claiming Dilbert died while running with scissors. He starts out solemn, wondering what it all means, then gleefully reveals that the death frees up 2,247 newspaper slots. He catches himself and apologizes for his greed.
punchline: The eulogist, standing in for another cartoonist, cheerfully celebrates the opening of newspaper comic slots over Dilbert's death and then insincerely apologizes for gloating.
summary: At a funeral for the strip's own hero, a mourner's sad reflection turns into delight at the vacated spots in the comics pages.

file: 2003/2003-09-28_employee moral survey_open_honest_communication from management_death spiral_looting comaony_noise_fishing lures_e_ploys suffer_boss likes hurting_sick boss_negative force.gif
title: Boss Tries Brutally Honest Communication

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I have the results of the employee morale survey.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The number one issue is "not enough open and honest communication from management."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, okay, I'm willing to give that a try.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Management is looting the company while hiding the fact that we're in a death spiral.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whenever you talk, I think about my fishing lures until the noise stops.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I see an employee suffer, it excites me in ways I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On nine separate occasions I've fired bald guys because I thought they were you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If this doesn't work for you, let me know on the next employee morale survey.

situation: At a meeting, an employee reports that the morale survey's top complaint is a lack of open and honest communication from management. The Boss agrees to try and then candidly reveals a string of damaging truths: management is looting the company, he ignores his staff, he enjoys watching them suffer, and he has fired the wrong people by mistake. The listeners sit stunned as he finishes by pointing them to the next survey.
punchline: When the boss finally gives the honest communication employees asked for, it is a stream of appalling admissions that makes them wish he had stayed silent, and he still sends complaints back to the morale survey that started it.
summary: Asked to be more candid with his staff, a manager unloads a series of horrifying truths about himself and the company.
themes: be careful what you wish for

file: 2003/2003-10-16_egos_europe to denver_lies_made up_management retreat_middle management_press release_top.gif
title: Boss's Retreat Boast Becomes Tunnel

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't imagine what you told everyone at the management retreat...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But our marketing department issued a press release saying we're designing a tunnel linking Europe to Denver.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'm installing a new sprinkler system in my lawn.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Must top.

setting: Office, with a flashback to a management retreat meeting table
situation: Dilbert tells someone he can't imagine what was said at the management retreat, since marketing has issued a press release about a tunnel linking Europe to Denver. A flashback shows managers at the retreat: one brags about his new lawn sprinkler system while another thinks he must top it.
punchline: Managers' competitive one-upmanship at a retreat escalated so absurdly that a boast got turned into a ridiculous public announcement about a transcontinental tunnel.
summary: A flashback reveals that managers trying to outdo each other's boasts led to an absurd corporate press release.

file: 2003/2003-08-04_website_customer success_closest things_complaint letters_few words_kick to kiss_change context_reviews_technology.gif
title: Faking Testimonials From Complaint Letters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, we need some customer success stories for the web site.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The closest things we have are these complaint letters. Just change a few words.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Change "kick" to "kiss" and this one is done, albeit disturbingly.

setting: The Boss's office, then Tina's desk at her computer
situation: The Boss asks Tina, the technical writer, to produce customer success stories for the company website. Since the company has none, he hands her complaint letters and tells her to just tweak a few words. Tina starts editing and notes that swapping one word turns a violent complaint into a creepy compliment.
punchline: Turning angry complaint letters into glowing testimonials by changing one word, like "kick" to "kiss", produces something fake and unsettling, showing how little real customer satisfaction the company has.
summary: Lacking any genuine praise from customers, a manager has his writer doctor hostile complaint letters into website testimonials.

file: 2003/2003-07-18_corporate witch hunt_products stink_diving rod_liar_pormise_honor of family_holy.gif
title: Divining Rod Calls Alice Liar

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Corporate witch-hunt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, did you tell a reporter that our products stink?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I promise on the honor of my family, and on all that is holy, that I did not.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I guess you're calling my divining rod a liar.

situation: The Boss, holding a newspaper, accuses Alice of telling a reporter that the company's products stink. Alice solemnly swears on her family's honor and everything holy that she did not. The Boss then dismisses her denial, saying it would mean his divining rod is lying.
punchline: The Boss trusts a divining rod over Alice's sworn word, showing his absurd, superstitious approach to finding a scapegoat.
summary: A boss hunting for a press leak ignores an employee's solemn denial because his dowsing stick says otherwise.

file: 2003/2003-09-20_can't buy happiness_expensive possessions_pople envious_tarde happiness for money_whacked.gif
title: Money Buys Envy and Hitmen

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, remember that money can't buy happiness.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But it can buy expensive possessions that make other people envious, and that feels just as good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you can pay to have people whacked.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Can I trade my happiness for some money?

setting: A rocky outcrop in a prehistoric or dinosaur-themed scene
situation: Dogbert lectures Bob, the green dinosaur, on the old saying that money can't buy happiness, then undercuts it by listing ways money does produce satisfaction: making others envious and paying for assassinations. Bob, convinced by this reasoning, asks whether he can swap his happiness for money.
punchline: After Dogbert's cynical case for money, Bob concludes that happiness is worth less than cash and offers to trade his away, missing that Dogbert's point was that money brings its own kind of happiness.
summary: A cynical sermon on wealth convinces a dinosaur to sell his own contentment for cash.

file: 2003/2003-05-06_elbonian_ad reputation_our image_leprechauns_mud_export_primary export_vegetarian backlash.gif
title: Elbonia's Leprechaun Export Problem

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Elbonia has gotten a bad reputation. We need your help to rebuild our image.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: The problem began when we discovered a civilization of leprechauns living under our mud.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Now they're our primary export. But we underestimated the vegetarian backlash.

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, across a desk
situation: A tall-hatted, bearded Elbonian client sits across from Dogbert, who is acting as a consultant. The Elbonian explains that his country's reputation has suffered and describes why. They found leprechauns under the mud and began exporting them, apparently as food.
punchline: Elbonia's bad reputation comes from exporting leprechauns as a food product, and the country was shocked that vegetarians objected.
summary: An Elbonian seeks image-repair help from Dogbert after his mud-soaked nation's bizarre new export business sparks outrage.

file: 2003/2003-09-06_top priority_smoldering mound_rubble_career_didn't like_desk.gif
title: Top Priority Dumped on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, take care of this. It's our top priority.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I'll just let my other top priorities slip until my career is a smoldering mound of rubble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So what is it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know...I just didn't like it on my desk.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a piece of paper and declares it the company's top priority. Dilbert sarcastically points out that tackling it means neglecting his other top priorities and wrecking his career. When he asks what the paper actually is, the Boss admits he has no idea and just wanted it off his desk.
punchline: The so-called top priority is really just clutter the Boss wanted to get rid of, exposing how arbitrarily management labels things as urgent.
summary: A boss offloads an unidentified document onto an employee under the banner of urgency, only to admit he merely wanted it off his desk.

file: 2003/2003-09-26_engineer_moved to marketing_lisa_old apple computer_old wife_engineering.gif
title: Marketing Man's Old Lisa

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: I was an engineer before I moved to marketing.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Now I don't even remember how to turn on my Lisa.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have an old Lisa computer from Apple?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Old wife.

situation: At a meeting, a bald man from marketing says he used to be an engineer but has forgotten how to turn on his Lisa. Dilbert assumes he means the vintage Apple Lisa computer. The man corrects him: Lisa is his old wife.
punchline: Dilbert assumes Lisa is an antique Apple computer, but she is the man's wife, so his joke about forgetting how to turn her on is a crude double entendre.
summary: A former engineer turned marketer jokes about being unable to power up his Lisa, and a confused colleague thinks it's vintage computer hardware.

file: 2003/2003-05-19_career_asking for stiff_remind you_feelings.gif
title: Nagging the Boss Makes Me Feel

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I just realized that my career primarily consists of asking you for stuff...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: ...and wondering how long I should wait before I remind you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you know how that makes me feel?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How what makes you feel?

situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, stands before his desk and reflects that her whole job is requesting things from him and then deciding when to nag him about them. She asks if he knows how that makes her feel. The Boss, who has not been listening, asks what she is even talking about.
punchline: The Boss's blank 'How what makes you feel?' proves he wasn't listening to a word she said, which is exactly why she has to keep reminding him.
summary: A frustrated assistant vents about constantly chasing her boss for things, only to discover he tuned out her complaint entirely.

file: 2003/2003-03-31_ceo placements_magic 8 ball_performed better_dogbert the headhunter.gif
title: Dogbert's CEO Placements Perform Averagely

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Headhunter

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let me tell you how good my CEO placements have been.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: An astonishing fifty percent of them have performed better than the other half!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you're on a budget, I recommend one of our stuffed CEO units with a "Magic 8 Ball" head.

situation: Dogbert, working as an executive headhunter, pitches his CEO placement service to a client seated across the desk. He brags about his success rate, which turns out to be a statistical tautology. He then offers a cheaper alternative: a stuffed CEO doll with a Magic 8 Ball for a head.
punchline: Claiming half of your placements beat the other half is meaningless, implying CEO performance is essentially random and a Magic 8 Ball would do just as well.
summary: A headhunter touts a statistically empty success rate for his executive hires and then suggests a novelty fortune-telling toy as a bargain substitute.

file: 2003/2003-07-04_alice_cell phone_every two minutes_flushable_owner wonders where_technology.gif
title: Alice Flushes Noisy Cell Phone

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Beep-Beep-a-Beep Beep-a-Beep

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Every two minutes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Have you seen my cell phone?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Was it metallic, noisy and flushable?

situation: Alice sits in her cubicle, irritated by a nearby cell phone that beeps every two minutes. In the second panel she storms out of her cubicle and a phone is seen lying on the floor of the next area. Later a coworker asks if she has seen his cell phone, and she replies with a description that reveals she flushed it.
punchline: Alice's deadpan question reveals she got fed up with the constantly beeping phone and disposed of it down the toilet.
summary: After being driven to distraction by a coworker's constantly chirping phone, Alice quietly gets rid of it in the most final way possible.

file: 2003/2003-07-16_business reporter_wall times post gazette_new product line_nick name for ceo.gif
title: Dilbert Impersonates a Business Reporter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, this is Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, I'm a business reporter for the Wall Times Post Gazette.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm doing a story about how dumb... I mean dynamic... your new product line is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he promised not to print the amusing nickname I have for our CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are so dynamic.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and another man's office, over the phone
situation: Dilbert phones a man at another company pretending to be a business reporter from a newspaper, and says he is writing about the man's new product line. He slips and calls the product line dumb before correcting himself to dynamic. Afterward he tells Dogbert that the man promised not to print Dilbert's nickname for the CEO.
punchline: Dilbert tricked a gullible man into promising confidentiality about an insulting nickname for the CEO, and Dogbert sarcastically praises him as dynamic, the same word Dilbert had used to cover his insult.
summary: Posing as a newspaper journalist, Dilbert tricks a man into promising to keep a rude secret about the chief executive.

file: 2003/2003-08-24_boss_touched by new hire_cry_hired_special skill_identifying good people_part instinct_favorite color.gif
title: Boss Hires Obvious Liar, Boasts Judgment

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: When I'm not helping team members, I like to feed the poor or read to blind people.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I don't care about money. All I want is a chance to help humanity reach its fullest potential.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're so wonderful, it's making me cry! You're hired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come meet the team.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Excellent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a special skill for identifying good people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's part instinct, part experience.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And yes, maybe just a little ESP.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Watch this.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: Alice, your favorite color is... mitten?

situation: A job candidate piles on absurdly saintly claims about feeding the poor and caring nothing for money, and the Boss is moved to tears and hires him on the spot. The Boss then brags about his special talent for spotting good people, only for the new hire to be revealed as a fanged green monster who confuses Alice by asking about her favorite color being "mitten."
punchline: The Boss proudly claims superb judgment of character while hiring an obvious fraud who turns out to be an inhuman monster who can't even fake normal human conversation.
summary: A gullible manager swoons over a too-good-to-be-true applicant, then introduces the creature he hired as proof of his hiring genius.

file: 2003/2003-01-12_evil_great idea_ignorant and worthless_manage budgets_poorly conceived_project managers_pummel with fists.gif
title: Employee Punishes Himself Over Idea

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I thought of a great idea.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You could let the project managers manage their own budgets...what?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You're giving me a look. I must try to guess what it means.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We don't do things that way? If it were a good idea you'd already be doing it?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My ideas are poorly conceived?! I can't see the big picture?!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I am ignorant and worthless!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I must pummel myself with my own tiny fists!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They're kinda self-managed now.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Very evil; I purr in your general direction.

situation: An employee pitches the idea of letting project managers control their own budgets, and the boss answers only with a silent look. The employee imagines the boss's objections, takes them as insults, and ends up berating and punching himself. At the end the boss reports to Catbert that the employees are now effectively self-managed, and Catbert approves.
punchline: The boss never says a word and the employee does all the criticizing and punishing himself, which the boss counts as a management success that even earns Catbert's praise.
summary: A worker's suggestion is met with a wordless stare, and he proceeds to insult and beat himself up on the boss's behalf.

file: 2003/2003-06-02_disgruntled employees_open door policy_rush hour_safely dropped_traffic_trap door_eliminate whiners.gif
title: Trap Door Drops Whiners Into Traffic

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The trap door will work with your "open door policy" to eliminate the whiners.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Disgruntled employees will be safely dropped into rush hour traffic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to remember that's there.

setting: Office presentation room, then a city street outside the building
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, presents a diagram of a trap door that works alongside the boss's open door policy to get rid of complaining employees. He claims they will be safely dropped into rush hour traffic. In the last panel the boss lies battered on the pavement in front of a stopped car, having fallen through the trap door himself.
punchline: The boss, who approved the trap door, forgot about it and falls through it himself, and the "safely" dropped victim is clearly injured in the road.
summary: A scheming HR cat unveils a chute that dumps complainers onto a busy street, and the boss promptly becomes its first victim.

file: 2003/2003-03-24_no budget_project_budget_begger_laughed guts up.gif
title: Laughed His Guts Out Literally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no budget for your project; you need to tin-cup it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Be like a beggar and ask each department to give you a bit of their budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, now that you've laughed your guts out, do you feel better?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Erk!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert there is no budget for his project and instructs him to go begging to other departments for spare money. Dilbert doesn't reply, and in the last panel the Boss is sprawled in his chair with his intestines spilled out on the desk, having apparently laughed his guts out.
punchline: Dilbert's silent amusement at the absurd budget advice is taken literally, as the Boss's guts have actually spilled out from laughing, and Dilbert dryly asks if he feels better.
summary: After being told to panhandle other departments for funding, Dilbert's wry reaction ends with his boss's innards splayed across the desk.

file: 2003/2003-08-11_30 years_award for five years_sick day.gif
title: Thirty Years, Five-Year Award

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I'd like to recognize Walter for his five years of work for this company.

transcript.speaker: Walter
transcript.text: Thanks, but I've been here for thirty years... Oh, I get it now.

transcript.speaker: Walter
transcript.text: I feel a sick day coming on.

setting: Office, during an employee recognition presentation
situation: The Boss publicly presents a long-service award to Walter, saying he is honoring five years of work. Walter points out he has actually been at the company for thirty years, then realizes the boss has either forgotten or never valued his real tenure. Disheartened, he walks off announcing he feels a sick day coming on.
punchline: Being thanked for only five of his thirty years shows how little the company values him, so he responds by planning to call in sick.
summary: A veteran employee receives an award that undercounts his tenure by decades and decides his loyalty isn't worth much after all.

file: 2003/2003-01-19_despartment_normal scope_over loaded_flexible_client driven_outside of scope_avoid projects_cheerfully accept assignments.gif
title: Accept Assignments, Never Do Them

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Can your department do this for us?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No problem.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Really? It's outside of your normal scope of work and I know you're overloaded.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're a flexible, client-driven organization!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, how can I avoid projects that are outside of my scope of responsibility?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Cheerfully accept the assignments and then never work on them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It bolsters your claims of being overloaded while leaving you free for work that matters.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Work matters?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, not to us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not even sure what they want.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll start ignoring it immediately.

setting: Office meeting room and hallway/cubicle area
situation: A woman from another department asks The Boss whether his team can take on an out-of-scope project, and he eagerly agrees, boasting of being a flexible, client-driven organization. Dilbert then asks Wally how to avoid out-of-scope work, and Wally advises cheerfully accepting assignments and never working on them. Dilbert later tells The Boss he'll start ignoring the new project right away.
punchline: Wally's trick of accepting every assignment and then ignoring it lets you look overloaded and agreeable while avoiding work, and Dilbert immediately applies it to the very project his boss just accepted.
summary: A manager enthusiastically takes on extra work for his team while Wally teaches Dilbert to sidestep such tasks by agreeing to everything and doing nothing.

file: 2003/2003-12-30_office relocation_studied boss_learned methods_corner you_scream about bright light.gif
title: Studying the Boss's Management Methods

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: I am in charge of the office relocation project, also known as O.R.P.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: I have never managed anything, but I have studied our boss to learn his methods.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Let's see...step one, I corner you. Step two, I talk until you scream about seeing a bright light.

situation: A coworker with a clipboard stands over Dilbert's desk and announces he is running the office relocation project. He admits he has never managed anything but says he learned by studying the boss. His plan is to corner Dilbert and talk at him until Dilbert screams about seeing a bright light.
punchline: The boss's only management method is to corner people and talk at them so relentlessly that they feel like they are dying and see a bright light, which makes imitating him an act of torture.
summary: A newly appointed project lead plans to copy his boss's management style, which turns out to be bludgeoning people with endless talking.

file: 2003/2003-07-23_being male_excellence award_bend metal_steel spike_highest paid_department.gif
title: Steel Spike Award and Pay Gap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to find a way to bend this steel rod into a "U."

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'll take care of it.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I won the prestigious "Steel Spike Award" for engineering excellence.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What??!!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I guess it's validation for being the highest paid in the department...and for being male.

situation: Dilbert says he needs to bend a steel rod into a U, and a smug male engineer offers to handle it. He then brags about winning the Steel Spike Award for engineering excellence. When he adds that it validates his being highest paid and male, Alice furiously bends the rod around his head.
punchline: The engineer's tone-deaf boast about being highest paid and male provokes Alice into solving Dilbert's rod-bending problem by wrapping it around his head.
summary: A boastful colleague gloating about his award and unequal pay gets an angry coworker to bend the rod using his own head.

file: 2003/2003-01-03_reporter_dump garbage inparks_20 years_spreading_secret.gif
title: Secretly Dumping Garbage in Parks

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: A reporter wants to see you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He claims we've been delivering all of our garbage to the local park for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How is that even possible?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The secret is in the spreading.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, tells him a reporter is waiting and explains that the reporter accuses the company of dumping all its garbage in the local park for twenty years. Instead of denying it, the Boss calmly explains how the company has gotten away with it.
punchline: The Boss doesn't deny the scandal; he proudly reveals his dumping technique, treating a serious environmental crime like a clever trade secret.
summary: A boss responds to a reporter's pollution accusation by casually sharing the trick that kept two decades of illegal dumping unnoticed.

file: 2003/2003-05-15_corner cubicle_window control_mad woman_giant magnifiying glass_life support.gif
title: Alice Controls the Window Shades

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice moved into the corner cubicle and claimed control over the window shades!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our life support systems will be in the hands of a mad-woman!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe she'll be kind.

situation: Dilbert tells a nervous coworker that Alice has taken the corner cubicle and the right to control the window shades. They worry that everyone's 'life support systems' are now in a madwoman's hands. In the final panel Alice, with wild hair, grips a giant magnifying glass beside the window, implying she will focus the sun's light on her coworkers.
punchline: Controlling the window shades is treated as life-or-death power, and Alice's giant magnifying glass suggests she will use the sunlight like a death ray to torment her colleagues, proving the coworker's hope for kindness is naive.
summary: Two coworkers fret that the fearsome Alice now rules the sunlight from her new corner cubicle, and she appears ready to prove them right with an enormous magnifier.

file: 2003/2003-10-02_new hire_guy_bothering workers_love golf_rain tomorrow_plans_sad paper body_roll in salt_scoring system.gif
title: Golf Invitation Declined With Sandpaper

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I love golf. Golfing is fun. It's a good day to golf. Do you want to go golfing in the rain tomorrow at 6 a.m.?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, thanks. I have plans to sandpaper my entire body and roll around in salt.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hope no one ever creates a scoring system for that.

situation: An enthusiastic coworker holding a coffee mug stands over Wally's desk and invites him to go golfing in the rain at 6 a.m. the next day. Wally declines by saying he would rather sandpaper his whole body and roll in salt. The coworker then thinks to himself that he hopes nobody invents a scoring system for that activity.
punchline: The coworker is so obsessed with golf that he fears even Wally's self-torture could be turned into a competitive scored game, implying he would invite Wally to play that too.
summary: A pushy golf fanatic gets a painfully vivid rejection from a coworker and responds by worrying it might become a sport.

file: 2003/2003-07-28_new ad campiagn_music from artsits_willing to sell out_dead musicians_not descomposed.gif
title: Ad Campaign Uses Dead Musicians

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Our new ad campaign will use familiar music from artists who are willing to sell out.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Due to budget cuts, we'll limit our search to musicians who are dead but not yet totally decomposed.

transcript.speaker: Director
transcript.text: Makeup!!!

setting: Conference room, then a commercial film set
situation: At a meeting, a marketing employee tells The Boss that the new ad campaign will feature familiar music from artists willing to sell out. Citing budget cuts, he says they will only hire musicians who are dead but not yet fully decomposed. On a film set, a director shouts for makeup while a propped-up corpse in period clothing holds a lute and a cameraman films it.
punchline: Since living artists who sell out are too expensive, the company cheaply films freshly dead musicians, treating the corpses as the ultimate budget-friendly endorsers.
summary: To save money on an advertising push, the company decides to recruit celebrity musicians who have died recently enough to still look presentable on camera.

file: 2003/2003-08-20_scolded by employee_boss late_dumb move_irish line dancing_mail document_late bid.gif
title: Blaming the Irish for Late Bid

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you failed at your primary objective of winning a bid for the Galatikus job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you said you'd deliver the bid on time, but you got seduced by Irish line-dancing lessons and forgot to mail it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't believe you're trying to pin the blame on the Irish.

situation: The Boss reads from a paper and accuses Dilbert of failing to win the Galatikus bid. Dilbert points out that the Boss himself promised to deliver the bid on time but got distracted by Irish line-dancing lessons and never mailed it. The Boss responds by indignantly accusing Dilbert of blaming the Irish.
punchline: The Boss deflects responsibility for his own mistake by misreading Dilbert's accusation as an attack on the Irish, showing his total refusal to accept blame.
summary: After a lost contract, a manager's own forgetfulness is turned into an absurd complaint about someone else unfairly blaming a nationality.

file: 2003/2003-07-25_unnesccesry cahnges_irrelevant document_while and dance_working_be happy too.gif
title: Suggestions, Pointless Edits, Forced Happiness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I made a few suggestions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be happy to make these unnecessary changes to this irrelevant document.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop acting happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I whistle and dance while I work?

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document marked up with his suggestions. Dilbert cheerfully says he will make the unnecessary changes to the irrelevant document. The Boss tells him to stop acting happy, and Dilbert responds by asking if he can whistle and dance while he works.
punchline: Dilbert's cheerful compliance is thinly veiled sarcasm, and when the Boss objects to the tone, Dilbert escalates into even more exaggerated, mocking happiness.
summary: A manager's pointless edits get a suspiciously upbeat response from his employee, who then mocks the boss's complaint by offering to dance.

file: 2003/2003-11-28_edited document_calirty_sent out_amazing_accuracy and relevance_spend career fixing.gif
title: Edited for Clarity, Minus Accuracy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I edited your document for clarity and sent it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. It's amazing how clear it is when you take out all of the accuracy and relevance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I stopped listening after "wow."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll get busy spending the rest of my career fixing this.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has edited Dilbert's document for clarity and already distributed it. Dilbert sarcastically points out that it is only clear because the accuracy and relevance were removed. The Boss admits he stopped listening after Dilbert said "wow," leaving Dilbert to fix the damage.
punchline: The Boss only hears the word "wow" as praise and ignores the sarcastic criticism, so he never realizes he ruined the document and Dilbert faces a career of cleanup.
summary: A manager proudly butchers an employee's document in the name of simplicity, then tunes out the employee's sarcastic complaint.

file: 2003/2003-02-11_cold_addicted_rx drugs_six months_coffeemaker.gif
title: Not Just a Cold

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard you had a cold.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It wasn't a cold.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was addicted to prescription drugs and I grew an exoskeleton. I've been in rehab and surgery for six months.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just to be clear: can I catch any of that by touching the coffeemaker after you?

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a mug says he heard Dilbert had a cold. Dilbert corrects him with an absurd account of drug addiction, growing an exoskeleton, and six months of rehab and surgery. The coworker responds only by asking whether he could catch any of it from the coffeemaker Dilbert touched.
punchline: Faced with an alarming confession, the coworker cares only about whether he might catch it, showing self-centered office germ paranoia and zero sympathy.
summary: A coworker's polite sick-day small talk turns into a bizarre medical confession that he answers with nothing but concern for his own health.

file: 2003/2003-01-17_lost cash_consultectomy_wallet_transfusion_sedate unwilling donor_happy hour.gif
title: Consultectomy Drains Boss's Wallet

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The consultectomy was successful, but you lost a lot of cash.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're giving your wallet a transfusion, but we had to sedate an unwilling donor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoever thought of happy hour at a hoshpital ish a geniush.

situation: Dogbert, dressed as a doctor, tells the Boss in his hospital bed that his 'consultectomy' (the removal of a consultant) was a success but cost a lot of money. He adds that they are giving the Boss's wallet a transfusion, using an unwilling sedated donor, which appears to be a rat hooked up to a machine. The Boss, drunk and cheerful, raises a martini glass and praises happy hour at a hospital.
punchline: The Boss is too drunk to notice that the 'treatment' is draining his money and exploiting a sedated victim, and he happily celebrates hospital happy hour.
summary: A doctor-costumed Dogbert reports on a surgery that removed a consultant and drained the patient's cash, while the tipsy patient toasts the hospital's bar.

file: 2003/2003-06-04_casino for morons_concept_court room_dogbert_gaming commission_ratbert_room full dolts_jury_legal.gif
title: Casino Exclusively for Morons

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Gaming Commission

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My concept is a casino exclusively for morons.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Imagine a room full of oblivious dolts, and I'm taking advantage of them for personal gain.

transcript.speaker: Commissioner
transcript.text: When would that concept begin?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: About a minute ago.

situation: Dogbert and Ratbert sit at a table before the Gaming Commission, pitching a casino aimed only at morons. As they describe the plan, a commissioner asks when the concept would begin, and Dogbert answers that it already has, implying the commissioners themselves are the dolts being exploited.
punchline: Dogbert reveals the panel of commissioners are the oblivious dolts being taken advantage of in the pitch, and the scheme is already under way.
summary: A pitch for a casino that preys on fools turns out to be targeting the very officials who are listening to it.

file: 2003/2003-04-13_hard day_meeting with ceo_billion dollar comapny_free stock_cash fow_revenue_disaster events_tragic evenets_slpping_fear induced meeting.gif
title: Venture Capitalists Grill Dilbert's Business Case

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm taking my business case to some venture capitalists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm hoping that their wisdom and resources will make it a billion-dollar company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you like some free stock?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Bah!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would I do without the support of my loved ones?

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: What would the cash flow look like if...

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: ...revenue was zero, Microsoft and IBM entered the market, your factory burned down and a piano fell on your head?

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: And what about civil unrest, lawsuits, natural disasters and locusts?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Then the little one slapped me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now re-e-el them in.

setting: Dilbert's home, then a venture capital boardroom
situation: Dilbert tells his pets he plans to pitch his business case to venture capitalists, and Dogbert offers him free stock. At the pitch, the investors pile on absurd worst-case scenarios to test his cash flow projections, including disasters and locusts. Dilbert comes away battered and tells Dogbert that Ratbert slapped him, so he wants the investors reeled back in.
punchline: Dilbert's confidence in venture capitalists collapses under their brutal and ridiculous questioning, and his bitter 'reel them in' shows he now sees Dogbert's predatory scam as the sensible alternative.
summary: A hopeful entrepreneur pitching to investors is bombarded with catastrophic what-if questions and returns ready to join his dog's con game.

file: 2003/2003-02-22_i.t function_outsource_save money_corporations_full time employees_reaplce_panic_warning sound.gif
title: Outsourcing, Then Reversing, to Save Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll save money by outsourcing our I.T. function.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we'll save more money by replacing our outsourcing with full-time employees!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When it's time for us to panic, will there be a warning sound, or was that it?

setting: Conference room during a management presentation
situation: The Boss presents a plan at a whiteboard diagram: first outsource the I.T. function to save money, then bring it back in-house with full-time employees to save even more. Wally, Dilbert and Alice sit at the meeting table, and Wally asks sarcastically whether the panic alarm has already sounded.
punchline: The plan is so self-contradictory, claiming savings from both outsourcing and reversing the outsourcing, that Wally sarcastically suggests the presentation itself should have been the panic signal.
summary: A manager claims two opposite I.T. strategies will each save money, leaving his baffled staff wondering whether they should already be alarmed.

file: 2003/2003-07-21_psychics on televison_software testing staff_one medium_punish them.gif
title: Replace Testers With One Medium

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've noticed that dead people know a lot. They're always yapping to psychics on television.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We could kill the entire software-testing staff and replace them with one medium.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you see any problem with that?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If the dead people lie, how would we punish them?

situation: The Boss, sitting at his desk, proposes killing the whole software-testing department and replacing them with a single psychic medium who can consult the dead. He asks Catbert, the evil HR director, whether he sees any problem. Catbert's only concern is how to punish dead people if they lie.
punchline: Catbert, the sadistic HR director, ignores the absurd, murderous plan and worries only that he would be unable to punish deceitful dead people.
summary: A manager wants to swap his entire testing team for one spirit-channeling psychic, and his HR chief's sole objection is that ghosts can't be disciplined.

file: 2003/2003-08-21_spam filter_sexy photos_tiffany sent email_boss_eyes pop.gif
title: Spam Filter Turned Off Chaos

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someone named Tiffany sent me e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yagga wagga!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Someone turned off the spam filter.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert happily notes that someone named Tiffany has emailed him, then opens it and reacts with wild-eyed, hair-raised astonishment at his computer. Alice, standing in the Boss's office, explains that someone turned off the spam filter, while the Boss sits at his desk with his own hair standing on end and a similarly stunned expression.
punchline: Both Dilbert and the Boss have received lurid spam emails once the filter was disabled, and their identical shocked reactions reveal what they were looking at.
summary: A disabled spam filter lets suggestive junk mail flood in, leaving two male coworkers equally dazzled and flustered.

file: 2003/2003-03-03_respond email_reply_vicious cycle_voice mails.gif
title: Ignoring Email to Stop Email

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't respond to my e-mail anymore.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I reply to e-mail, it attracts more e-mail. I'm trying to break the vicious cycle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well...I'll leave you voice-mails.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me know how that works out for you.

situation: Dilbert complains that the Boss no longer answers his e-mails. The Boss explains that replying only generates more e-mail, so he has stopped responding to break the cycle. When Dilbert threatens to leave voicemails instead, the Boss sarcastically invites him to report back on how that goes.
punchline: The Boss's sarcastic 'let me know how that works out for you' implies he will simply ignore voicemails too, and that he has no intention of being reachable by any channel.
summary: A manager dodges his employee's messages by refusing to answer email, then brushes off the threat of voicemail with a sarcastic shrug.

file: 2003/2003-12-19_made up language_inventing language_downsized_no word.gif
title: Boss Invents Language Without Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I don't know the best way to say this but I'll try.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oog- nah wahgoo yagga bliphnow elga nooey fip wah!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's a language I'm inventing in my spare time. It has no word for "you're downsized."

situation: The Boss stands over Alice's desk and says he has bad news but doesn't know how to say it. He then spouts a string of gibberish, which Alice stares at in confusion. He explains it is a language he is inventing in his spare time, and it has no word for "you're downsized." Alice ends up gritting her teeth in anger.
punchline: The Boss, too cowardly to deliver the layoff news directly, shows off a made-up language that conveniently can't express it, effectively dodging the task while making clear that Alice is being fired.
summary: A manager fumbles through nonsense syllables to avoid telling an employee she is being let go, then blames his invented tongue for lacking the right word.

file: 2003/2003-08-17_netwrok security_buggy_complicated_user guide_pure evil_tech support dept_chimp with typewriter_strategy_victims_hair quiver_consultants_paid by hour.gif
title: Consultant Profits From Broken Products

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your network-security product is buggy and complicated.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your user guide is an inspired work of pure evil.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And your tech-support department is an inebriated chimpanzee with a typewriter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One strategy would be to fix all of those problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the other strategy?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sell consulting services to your victims...I mean customers!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm so happy, it's making my hair quiver!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But what do we do when our consultants can't make our products work either?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're paid by the hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quiver!!

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert consulting across the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, insults the Boss's buggy network-security product, its terrible user guide and its dreadful tech support. He offers two strategies: fix the problems, or sell consulting services to the customers who suffer from them. The delighted Boss asks what happens when the company's own consultants can't make the products work either.
punchline: Because consultants are paid by the hour, a product that never works is a permanent revenue stream, so failure becomes profitable for everyone but the customers.
summary: A consultant tells a boss that the cheapest way out of his awful product is to profit from its flaws, and the boss quivers with delight.

file: 2003/2003-09-22_lead odg_view never changes_look at face_imlying_insightful analogy.gif
title: Lead Dog Analogy Insults Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, if you're not the lead dog, the view never changes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not the lead dog, and I have to look at your face all day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you implying?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was admiring your insightful analogy.

situation: The Boss is leading a meeting and offers a motivational saying about the lead dog and the view never changing. Alice responds that she is not the lead dog and has to look at his face all day, which is a clear insult. When he asks what she means, she pretends she was just praising his analogy.
punchline: Alice turns the boss's clichéd motivational saying into a personal insult about his face, then escapes blame by pretending she was complimenting him.
summary: A manager's sled-dog pep talk gets turned into a dig at his appearance, and the employee dodges consequences with feigned admiration.

file: 2003/2003-03-09_eargarette_smoking breaks_downside_cigarette for ear_ear mint_15 min break.gif
title: The Eargarette Smoke Break Invention

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call my invention the "eargarette."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a cigarette for your ear!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It allows non-smokers to take smoking breaks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is there any downside?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've been working for fifteen minutes straight. I need an eargarette break.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ear mint?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Two, please.

setting: Dilbert's office and a conference room
situation: Dilbert shows off his invention, the eargarette, a cigarette that goes in the ear so non-smokers can take smoking breaks. Dogbert asks about the downside, but Dilbert can't hear him because of the device. Later Dilbert takes an eargarette break in a meeting, and coworkers around him start using them too and become hard of hearing.
punchline: The downside of an ear cigarette is that it blocks your hearing, so everyone ends up shouting "What?" and the coworkers beg for ear mints and more eargarettes.
summary: A man invents a smoking substitute worn in the ear, then discovers its side effect when he and his colleagues can no longer hear anything.

file: 2003/2003-02-01_saved money_hired guy_unlucky_many problems_ex boyfreind_sobers up.gif
title: Boss Hires Troubled Man, Calls Unlucky

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We saved money by hiring a guy who's had many personal problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we're sure he was just unlucky; no one would invite that many problems into his life.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, of course your ex-boyfriend can stay with us until the choppers leave and he sobers up.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss explains that the company saved money by hiring a man with many personal problems, and insists he was merely unlucky. A coworker at the table takes a phone call and, in the final panel, agrees that his ex-boyfriend can stay with them until the helicopters leave and he sobers up.
punchline: The Boss claims nobody would invite so many problems into his life, while the coworker's phone call shows that a person can in fact attract constant chaos, including an ex who needs to hide from helicopters and sober up.
summary: A manager brags about a cheap hire with a messy history while a colleague's own phone call reveals how troubled lives really work.

file: 2003/2003-06-21_employee of year_awrd_better luck_next year_jealousy_unattractive.gif
title: Employee of the Year: No One

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The "Employee of the Year" award goes to...no one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks for coming. Better luck next year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not as bad as the time that you won it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Jealousy is unattractive.

setting: Company auditorium during an awards ceremony, then the crowd afterward
situation: The Boss stands at a podium holding a trophy and announces that the Employee of the Year award goes to no one, then thanks the audience for coming. Afterward Dilbert tells Wally that this is not as bad as the time Wally won it, and Wally, holding his coffee mug, replies that jealousy is unattractive.
punchline: Dilbert's insult implies that Wally winning the award was even more embarrassing than no one winning it, and Wally brushes it off by accusing him of jealousy.
summary: After management scraps the top employee honor entirely, one coworker mocks another for a past win and gets a smug retort about envy.

file: 2003/2003-11-17_floating_happy_relaxed_vacation_floating to furious_broken promise.gif
title: From Floating to Furious Instantly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My vacation was so relaxing that I'm still floating.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, Alice, you know how I promised to cover all of your meetings for two weeks? I forgot until right now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: From floating to furious in 27 seconds. It's a personal best.

situation: Alice returns from a vacation so relaxing that she is literally floating above the floor. A coworker casually admits he forgot his promise to cover her meetings for two weeks. Alice crashes down into her chair, hair bristling and teeth clenched, and coldly notes how fast she went from blissful to enraged.
punchline: Alice's vacation calm is destroyed in seconds by a coworker's careless broken promise, and she dryly times her own fury like a sporting record.
summary: A serenely hovering Alice is jolted back to earth in a rage when a colleague casually reveals he never covered her meetings.

file: 2003/2003-02-21_customer references_parking lot_ring.gif
title: Customer Reference Is Salesman's Own Phone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any customer references I could call?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Right here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Beep beep boop beep.

transcript.speaker: Salesman's phone
transcript.text: R-r-ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No answer.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Try again when I'm in the parking lot.

transcript.speaker: Salesman's phone
transcript.text: R-r-ring

setting: Office or meeting room, across a desk
situation: Dilbert asks a vendor's salesman for customer references he can call before buying. The salesman hands over a sheet of paper, but the number on it turns out to be his own cell phone, which rings on his side of the desk. He cheerfully suggests Dilbert try again once he is in the parking lot.
punchline: The 'customer reference' is a fake: the salesman is the one who would answer the phone and pose as a satisfied customer, revealing the vendor has no real references.
summary: A vendor's list of glowing testimonials turns out to lead straight to the salesman's own mobile phone.

file: 2003/2003-11-08_nutty boss_halluciantions_sadistic nut_having problems_unhealthy boss.gif
title: Boss Hallucinates Insults to Yell

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm having problems at home, so I'll be taking it out on you today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll begin by hallucinating that you said something bad. Then I'll yell at you for saying it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am not a sadistic nut!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I go to my cubicle, can you hallucinate that I'm here?

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he is having problems at home and plans to take them out on him. He explains he will hallucinate that Dilbert said something offensive and then yell at him for it. When the Boss shouts that he is not a sadistic nut, Dilbert asks if he can leave and have the Boss imagine him being present instead.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the Boss's abuse requires no real participation from him, so the Boss could just hallucinate the whole encounter, including Dilbert being there, while Dilbert escapes.
summary: A manager openly plans to vent his home troubles on an employee by imagining insults, and the employee suggests he simply imagine the whole meeting without him.
themes: taking out personal problems on others

file: 2003/2003-12-05_fist of death_foot of death_doctor_exam room_dont use_advice_health_carpal syndrome_medical.gif
title: Fist of Death Replaced by Foot

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You've got a bad case of carpal punchel syndrome.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Don't use your "fist of death" for a few weeks.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The "foot of death" is not the same.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It is only slightly menacing.

setting: A doctor's exam room, then a conference room
situation: A doctor tells Alice she has carpal punchel syndrome from overusing her violent fist and orders her to rest it for a few weeks. In the next scene at a meeting, Alice sits at the conference table with her foot propped up as a substitute weapon, while Asok comments on how threatening it is.
punchline: Alice's replacement for her fist of death is a foot, which is far less intimidating, as Asok points out, so her aggressive reputation takes a hit.
summary: A medical ban on punching forces Alice to threaten her coworkers with her foot instead, to underwhelming effect.

file: 2003/2003-07-19_cooperate with hunt_17 suspects_talked to reporter_email archives_phone records_linguistic patterns_punish all of them.gif
title: Punishing Everyone on the Suspect List

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Corporate witch-hunt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've narrowed the list to seventeen suspects who might have talked to that reporter.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now we'll check their e-mail archives, phone records and linguistic patterns until we identify the offender.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And then we can punish all of them just for being on the list.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like the way you stink.

situation: The Boss sits in his chair holding a list of seventeen employees suspected of leaking information to a reporter. Catbert, the evil human resources director, proposes digging through their emails, phone records and writing style to find the culprit. He then suggests punishing everyone on the list regardless of guilt, and the Boss approves.
punchline: The witch-hunt is a pretext to punish innocent employees, and the Boss's compliment 'I like the way you stink' shows he admires Catbert's cruelty.
summary: Management plans an invasive investigation of suspected leakers and then decides to penalize every suspect anyway, whether guilty or not.

file: 2003/2003-12-11_insincere optimism_artificial sense of urgency_delusion_work for challenge_not money_good ideas_sound bad.gif
title: Engineer's Plan: Fake Optimism and Delusion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm developing an insincere optimism to complement my artificial sense of urgency.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope to top it off with a delusion that I work for the challenge and not the money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can you make good ideas sound so bad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an engineer.

situation: At a meeting, Dilbert calmly lists the mental attitudes he is cultivating to cope with his job: fake optimism, a manufactured sense of urgency, and a delusion that he works for the challenge rather than the pay. The Boss, listening, asks how he manages to make good ideas sound so bad. Dilbert answers that it comes with being an engineer.
punchline: Dilbert's candid description of the self-deception needed to be a motivated employee shows that engineers can't help stating the uncomfortable truth, which makes workplace expectations sound ridiculous.
summary: An engineer cheerfully outlines the false attitudes he's building to survive his job, and when his boss objects to how it sounds, he blames his profession.

file: 2003/2003-07-26_subatomic particle_statisfied cutomers_arthur quark_george meaon_signed certificate.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Particle Naming Rights

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For five hundred dollars, I'll name a subatomic particle after you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Some of my satisfied customers include Arthur C. Quark, and George Meson.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It comes with an unsigned certificate!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like 'em clean.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert on the green couch
situation: Dogbert, holding a clipboard, pitches Dilbert on paying five hundred dollars to have a subatomic particle named after him. He cites dubious past customers with physics-pun names and mentions the deal comes with an unsigned certificate. Dilbert, in his bathrobe, responds with a pun about preferring his particles clean.
punchline: Dogbert's scam is thinly disguised by customers with physics-pun names like Quark and Meson, and Dilbert's reply plays on the word 'unsigned' as 'unsigned' sounds like 'unsoiled/clean' in a dry, nonsensical joke about liking things clean.
summary: Dogbert hawks a dubious star-naming-style scheme for subatomic particles, complete with pun-named references and a certificate lacking a signature.

file: 2003/2003-05-01_unimportant project_inspirational quotes_lobby walls_eagle.gif
title: Sarcastic Quote for Lobby Walls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have an unimportant project, so I thought of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Find a bunch of inspirational quotes that we can put on the lobby walls.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "If being an eagle is such a good idea, why are there so few of them?"

situation: The Boss hands Wally a project he openly calls unimportant, asking him to find inspirational quotes for the lobby walls. Wally sits at his computer and, instead of a genuine motivational quote, types out a cynical one that undermines the idea of striving to be an eagle.
punchline: Wally responds to a pointless motivational-poster assignment with a sarcastic, deflating quote that mocks corporate inspiration culture.
summary: Handed a throwaway task of collecting uplifting sayings for the lobby, a cynical employee searches up a quote that skewers the whole premise.

file: 2003/2003-10-17_tunnel shark_dig forever_red button_don't push button.gif
title: Don't Push The Red Button

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call it the "Tunnel Shark." It converts dirt and rock into energy and can dig forever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So whatever you do, don't ignore what I'm saying and push the red button.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Button!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Now what's gotten into you?

setting: Dilbert's presentation at a desk, then a picnic on a grassy hill
situation: Dilbert demonstrates his drilling machine, the Tunnel Shark, to The Boss and warns him not to push the red button. The Boss thinks only about the button, and in the last panel he is shown at a picnic with a woman, apparently having pushed the button and lying shocked on the blanket.
punchline: Dilbert's clumsily worded warning ('don't ignore what I'm saying and push the red button') makes The Boss fixate on the button, so he pushes it and ends up in a ridiculous situation.
summary: A demonstration of a digging machine goes sideways when a muddled warning about a red button becomes an irresistible temptation for the clueless boss.

file: 2003/2003-12-14_boss_engineering manager_graphic artist_graphics guy upset_logo_mocks him_puts down idea_thinks idea_threatned_graphics dept..gif
title: Boss's Rectangle Logo Wounds Artist

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's totally brilliant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must show this to our creative department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I designed a new logo for the company. See what you can do with it.

transcript.speaker: Graphic Artist
transcript.text: Well, well, well, an engineering manager becomes an artist.

transcript.speaker: Graphic Artist
transcript.text: Apparently I wasted my time getting a master's degree in graphic arts and design.

transcript.speaker: Graphic Artist
transcript.text: All I needed was a dull pencil and a scrap of paper.

transcript.speaker: Graphic Artist
transcript.text: Art is not that easy, you arrogant pile of perfectly symmetrical crud!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if the logo is inside a rectangle?

transcript.speaker: Graphic Artist
transcript.text: Sob

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and the graphics department
situation: The Boss sketches a company logo on a sticky note and proudly decides it is brilliant. He takes it to the graphic artist, who sarcastically mocks the idea of a manager doing an artist's job. When the artist finally explodes in anger, the Boss calmly responds by suggesting the logo be put inside a rectangle.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he answers an artist's furious tirade about the skill of design by offering another amateur suggestion, driving the professional to tears.
summary: A manager's amateur logo sketch so offends a trained graphic designer that the designer snaps, only to be met with yet another clueless design tip.

file: 2003/2003-01-01_selective breeding_produce offspring_no biometric impression_no pulse_no fingerprints_no dna.gif
title: Family Bred to Evade Biometrics

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For thousands of generations the males in my family practiced selective breeding.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The goal was to produce offspring that leave no biometric impression: no pulse, no fingerprints, no DNA.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We like to ask "Why not?"

situation: Wally sits at a meeting table with snacks and explains that the men in his family spent thousands of generations selectively breeding offspring who leave no biometric trace, with no pulse, fingerprints or DNA. Alice asks why anyone would do that, while Dilbert listens. Wally answers with a shrug-worthy motto.
punchline: Wally's ancestors devoted millennia to an absurd goal with no purpose, and his 'Why not?' answer shows his family shares his love of effortless pointlessness, hinting he is a living example of someone who barely registers at work.
summary: Wally describes an ancestral breeding program aimed at producing undetectable people, and justifies it with the least meaningful reason imaginable.

file: 2003/2003-10-13_best negotiator_vendor_engineering_training_resist_facts_infinite liability_unidentified gizma.gif
title: Engineer Negotiates Away Infinite Liability

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The vendor is sending their best negotiator.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must use all of your engineering training to resist her tricks and look only at the facts.

transcript.speaker: Vendor Negotiator
transcript.text: And if you agree to infinite liability, you get a .00001% chance of dating me, plus a minute to play with an unidentified gizmo.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the vendor is sending their best negotiator and instructs him to rely on his engineering training and stick to the facts. In the meeting, the female negotiator dangles a tiny chance of a date and a gadget to play with in exchange for Dilbert accepting infinite liability. Dilbert looks flustered and tempted.
punchline: The engineer's supposed immunity to persuasion collapses instantly because a negligible chance of a date and a toy is enough to make him consider a ruinous contract term.
summary: A manager warns his engineer to stay rational against a sly vendor, who then lures him into a terrible deal with a flirtatious long shot and a shiny gadget.

file: 2003/2003-03-18_marketing genius_rebate program_process_impenetrable fortress_unclear instructions_physical impossibilities_hidden 300 digit_serial number.gif
title: Rebate Program Nobody Can Redeem

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing genius

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: We designed a rebate program that won't cost a penny.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: The rebate process is an impenetrable fortress of unclear instructions and physical impossibilities.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: Next we have to find the hidden 300-digit serial number and write it in a box that's half an inch long.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Stinkin' weasels.

setting: Conference room, then a customer's table at home
situation: A marketing executive proudly explains to colleagues around a conference table that their rebate program is designed to cost the company nothing. The reason is that the redemption process is so confusing and impossible that nobody can complete it. The final panel shows a frustrated customer trying to follow the absurd instructions and cursing the company.
punchline: The company advertises a rebate but deliberately makes it impossible to claim, so it never has to pay out, and the angry customer realizes they are being swindled.
summary: A smug marketing team brags that their rebate offer is free because its claim rules are deliberately impossible, while a baffled customer fumes over the paperwork.

file: 2003/2003-07-29_price quote_every expense_alice side agreement_hidden costs_customer punch vendor_freaking weasel.gif
title: Alice's Hidden Costs Side Agreement

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: As you requested, this price quote includes absolutely every expense you'll incur!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If that's true, you won't mind signing the "Alice side agreement."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "In the event of hidden costs, customer will repeatedly punch vendor while yelling 'You freaking weasel!'"

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Pen?

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
