situation: A vendor assures Alice, the customer, that his price quote covers every possible expense. Alice calls his bluff by producing a side agreement stating she may repeatedly punch him if any hidden costs appear. She then holds out a pen, asking him to sign.
punchline: If the vendor truly believes there are no hidden costs, he should happily accept a penalty clause for them, but Alice's violent clause exposes how little anyone trusts such promises.
summary: A customer tests a salesman's claim of total price transparency by demanding he sign a clause letting her beat him up if surprise fees show up.

file: 2003/2003-05-02_collecting quotes_cubilce_freakish waste_inspirational quotes_lobby wall_over elevators.gif
title: Alice's Insult Becomes Inspirational Quote

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I've been asked to collect inspirational quotes for the lobby wall.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Get out of my cubicle, you freakish waste of carbon.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: That'll look good over the elevators.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker with a notepad tells Alice he has been asked to gather inspirational quotes for the lobby wall. Alice responds by furiously telling him to get out of her cubicle and insulting him. He calmly writes it down, deciding it will look good over the elevators.
punchline: The coworker is so oblivious or thick-skinned that he treats Alice's angry insult as an inspirational quote worth displaying in the lobby.
summary: A quote-gathering employee cheerfully records a coworker's vicious insult as if it were corporate wisdom.

file: 2003/2003-06-24_announce record losses_graphics department_inebriated simians_ratbert_drawing_monkey_animals.gif
title: Drunk Monkeys Announce Record Losses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to announce our record losses in a way that doesn't make management look like...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Inebriated simian miscreants?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Graphics department

transcript.speaker: Graphics Department Employee
transcript.text: They want to go in a whole other direction.

setting: Conference room and the graphics department
situation: The Boss tells Dogbert, who is acting as a consultant, that the company must announce record losses without making management look bad. Dogbert finishes his sentence with 'inebriated simian miscreants,' and The Boss agrees. In the graphics department, a worker stands beside a drawing of a drunk monkey and says management wants a different approach.
punchline: Management insists on hiding its blame for the losses, yet the only way it can finish the thought is by describing itself as drunk monkeys, and the 'whole other direction' line shows they will keep drawing the monkeys anyway.
summary: A boss wants to spin terrible financial news so management escapes blame, but a consultant's blunt guess about the image to avoid turns out to be exactly what the graphics team was already drawing.

file: 2003/2003-08-26_million lines of code_irrelevent data_key your car_no choice.gif
title: Translating a Salesman's Empty Pitch

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our new product has half a million lines of code!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Translation: There's nothing good about this product, so you hope I'm impressed by irrelevant data.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Now available in ecru!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You leave me no choice but to key your car on the way out.

setting: Office meeting room or desk during a sales pitch
situation: A salesman pitches his new product to Alice, boasting about how many lines of code it contains. Alice translates his pitch as a sign that the product has no real merits. When he then touts that it's available in ecru, she decides to vandalize his car on his way out.
punchline: The salesman's pitch is so irrelevant and desperate, touting code volume and a color option, that Alice responds with a threat to key his car.
summary: A product pitch built on meaningless boasts pushes a skeptical customer to vow revenge on the seller's car.

file: 2003/2003-11-19_competitive strategies seminar_house keeping_energency_stay seated_no mens room.gif
title: Seminar Host Puts Himself First

transcript.speaker: Seminar Leader
transcript.text: Welcome to the Competitive Strategies Seminar.

transcript.speaker: Seminar Leader
transcript.text: First, some housekeeping. In the event of an emergency, stay seated so I'll have a clear path to the exit.

transcript.speaker: Seminar Leader
transcript.text: And... there is no men's room in the building as far as you know.

setting: Conference room during a business seminar
situation: A speaker opens a Competitive Strategies Seminar with housekeeping announcements to a seated audience, which includes Dilbert. He tells everyone to stay seated in an emergency so he can escape first, then adds that there is no men's room as far as they know, hoarding the facilities for himself.
punchline: The seminar leader is literally practising cutthroat competition on his own audience, putting his own escape and bathroom access ahead of everyone else's.
summary: A seminar presenter demonstrates ruthless competition by rigging the safety rules and bathroom access in his own favor.

file: 2003/2003-10-19_budget for research and development_confidential_witty_appreciation_laugh_teeth fall out.gif
title: Fake Laugh Knocks Out Teeth

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Ted, what's the budget for research and development?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: It's confidential. I could tell you, but then I'd have to kill you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I've never heard that one. It's very witty.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Allow me to show my appreciation with the following fake laugh.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Those are my real teeth. I need them back.

situation: Tina asks Ted about the research and development budget, and he deflects with a tired 'I'd have to kill you' joke while laughing at himself. Tina sarcastically claims she has never heard it and delivers an exaggerated fake laugh so loud that Ted's teeth fly out. She then demands them back, saying they are her real teeth.
punchline: Tina's sarcastic, exaggerated fake laugh is so forceful that it knocks out teeth, and she absurdly claims the teeth are hers, underscoring her contempt for Ted's stale joke.
summary: A coworker mocks a colleague's clichéd joke by unleashing a theatrical fake laugh so violent that dental work goes flying.

file: 2003/2003-04-02_enjoy opportunity_new paranoid employee_not invied_plotting_peri noid_perimeno.gif
title: Paranoid Peri Suspects Meeting Exclusion Plot

transcript.speaker: Peri
transcript.text: We'll have the data by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do you know that?

transcript.speaker: Peri
transcript.text: You must be getting invited to meetings and then saying, "Don't invite Peri."

transcript.speaker: Peri
transcript.text: Would it be wrong to enjoy this opportunity?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Plotting!! Right there!!!

situation: Peri, a paranoid coworker whose nameplate reads 'Peri Noid', sits in a meeting and announces a deadline. A female coworker asks how she knows, and Peri accuses her of secretly telling people not to invite Peri to meetings. When the coworker reacts with irritation, Peri asks if it would be wrong to enjoy the chance to be proven right, and the coworker points and accuses her of plotting.
punchline: Peri's paranoia is so extreme that she treats a normal question as proof of a conspiracy, and then declares the coworker's reaction as evidence of plotting, making her delusion unfalsifiable.
summary: A coworker with a pun-laden name and a suspicious mind accuses a colleague of conspiring to keep her out of meetings, then gleefully interprets the reaction as confirmation.

file: 2003/2003-01-06_self evaluation_performance review_core values_honesty_integrity_wally_dishonest.gif
title: Rate Your Honesty, Wally's Dishonest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need your self-evaluation so I can write your performance review.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember to rate yourself on our core values of honesty and integrity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally claims he did no work this year. But he's dishonest, so you can't be sure.

situation: The Boss asks Wally, who is holding a coffee mug, to hand in a self-evaluation for his performance review and reminds him to rate himself on honesty and integrity. Wally says nothing, and the Boss then comments that Wally claims to have done no work all year, but because Wally is dishonest the Boss can't be sure it's true.
punchline: Wally's honest admission that he did no work is dismissed by the Boss as untrustworthy because Wally is supposedly dishonest, so the Boss can't even trust a confession of laziness.
summary: A manager requests a self-review emphasizing honesty, then refuses to believe the slacker's candid admission of doing nothing.

file: 2003/2003-10-31_rick_mustaully exclusive_transofrm_package ultra light_absorb impact_brick wall.gif
title: Rick Becomes a Brick Wall

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Rick. Allow me to explain why your specifications are mutually exclusive.

transcript.speaker: Rick
transcript.text: Must transform.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we make the package ultra light, there won't be enough material to absorb impact when...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think I'm getting through.

situation: Dilbert tries to explain to Rick, a coworker holding a coffee mug, that his product specifications contradict each other: an ultra-light package cannot also absorb impact. Rick thinks 'must transform' and gradually turns into a brick wall. Dilbert concludes he isn't getting through.
punchline: Rick's stubborn refusal to listen is shown literally as him turning into a brick wall, so Dilbert's explanation can't get through.
summary: A coworker who won't hear that his demands conflict physically morphs into a wall of bricks while an engineer explains the problem.

file: 2003/2003-09-04_make exceptions_created on seeing machines_dead dinosaurs_animal prodcuts_naked_electricity from oil.gif
title: Vegan Walks Away Naked

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mike the Vegan

transcript.speaker: Mike the Vegan
transcript.text: I use no animal products whatsoever!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your clothes were created on sewing machines that used electricity from coal and oil, and those come from dead dinosaurs.

transcript.speaker: Mike the Vegan
transcript.text: I need to start making exceptions.

situation: Mike the Vegan brags to Dilbert that he uses no animal products at all. Dilbert points out that his clothes were made with machines powered by electricity from coal and oil, which come from dead dinosaurs. Mike, having taken the logic to heart, is then shown walking away completely naked.
punchline: Mike takes Dilbert's argument so literally that he strips off all his clothes, and his only conclusion is that he needs to make exceptions to his own rule.
summary: A self-righteous vegan discovers that even his shirt is tainted by prehistoric creatures and responds by abandoning his clothing entirely.

file: 2003/2003-04-22_down to 40 cups_won't survive_lucky_coffe rehab.gif
title: Coffee Rehab Cuts Wally to Forty

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, I'm sending you to a coffee rehab program.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They'll get you down to forty cups a day.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not double digits!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You monster!!! I won't survive!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you're lucky.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, announces he is sending Wally to a coffee rehab program. Wally panics, and it turns out the program's goal is merely to reduce his intake to forty cups a day, which he still finds unbearable. A large man grabs Wally by the shoulders to take him away, and Catbert coldly says he may not survive if he's lucky.
punchline: Even the cure for Wally's coffee addiction still allows forty cups a day, yet he considers that an unsurvivable hardship, and Catbert's 'if you're lucky' implies the ordeal is meant to be cruel.
summary: Catbert condemns the notoriously coffee-dependent Wally to a rehab program whose idea of success is still a staggering daily caffeine habit.

file: 2003/2003-01-30_excellent visibility_secret_created mindless replica_totally real.gif
title: Mindless Replica Attends Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your visibility has been excellent lately. What's your secret?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created a mindless replica to attend meetings. He has no personality whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! You look totally real.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's replica
transcript.text: Hee hee! Burn, dude.

situation: The Boss compliments Dilbert on his recent visibility and asks for his secret. Dilbert explains that he built a mindless duplicate of himself to go to meetings in his place. The Boss admires how real the replica looks, and the replica laughs and says 'Burn, dude', a remark that seems to be aimed at the Boss.
punchline: The Boss is so unobservant that he mistakes the mindless replica for a real person, and the replica's insult goes right over his head, which implies that being visible in meetings matters more than having a real personality or contributing anything.
summary: A manager praises an employee's high profile at meetings, never noticing that the one being praised is a brainless duplicate who has been attending in his place.

file: 2003/2003-08-18_multiple personalities_fired cowboy_little girl_twins_aftrenoon_mime.gif
title: Firing Every Personality Separately

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to fire a guy who has multiple personalities.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm exhausted. I fired the cowboy, the little girl, and the astronaut this morning. I'll do the twins later this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm tired, but it's a good tired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I do the mime?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss he is firing an employee with multiple personalities and is doing it one personality at a time. He lists the cowboy, little girl, and astronaut he has already fired and the twins still to come. The Boss, seeing how satisfying it is, asks if he can fire the mime.
punchline: Catbert treats each personality as a separate employee to be fired individually, and the Boss eagerly wants a turn at the cruelty, picking the mime.
summary: An HR cat gleefully dismisses a troubled worker one alter ego at a time, and his boss asks to join in on the fun.

file: 2003/2003-04-17_mood swings_deficit_piece of dirt_family_defect_defected worker.gif
title: Irene's Mysterious Defect Revealed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Irene. I don't yet know what her defect is.

transcript.speaker: Irene
transcript.text: Stop being rude to me, you piece of dirt!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm thinking: mood swings.

transcript.speaker: Irene
transcript.text: We're like family now.

situation: The Boss introduces a new employee, Irene, to Dilbert and admits he hasn't yet figured out her defect. She immediately screams an insult at Dilbert, then hugs him and declares they are family. The Boss concludes her flaw must be mood swings.
punchline: The Boss treats employees as products with hidden defects, and Irene's abrupt flip from abuse to affection reveals the defect in real time.
summary: A manager presents a new hire whose flaw he hasn't identified yet, and her sudden switch from hostility to hugging gives him his answer.

file: 2003/2003-12-09_retired_do anything_all day long_banging head_earn money_social infrastructure_warm_tingly_sensation_guilty.gif
title: Dogbert Gloats About Retirement Leisure

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's nice to be retired. I'll do a-a-anything I want to do all day long.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I guess you'll be banging your head against a wall today, trying to earn money for the social infrastructure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever feel guilty?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it a warm, tingly sensation that makes you wag?

situation: Dogbert lounges on Dilbert's bed announcing how nice retirement is while Dilbert gets dressed for work. Dogbert mocks Dilbert for spending his day working to fund society's infrastructure. When Dilbert asks if he ever feels guilty, Dogbert misreads guilt as a pleasant feeling.
punchline: Dogbert is so devoid of conscience that he can't recognize guilt, mistaking it for a pleasant sensation that makes him wag his tail.
summary: A smug retired Dogbert needles his working owner and then reveals he has no idea what guilt even feels like.

file: 2003/2003-11-01_too much work_give too much work_blame others_angry_its all you!.gif
title: Alice Blames Boss for Workload

transcript.text: Alice, your problem is that you take on too much work.

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your second problem is that you blame others, and your third problem is that you're always angry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's all you!!

Alice points out that he is the one assigning the work, and he responds by adding that she blames others and is always angry. Alice explodes in frustration, proving his point while still being right.
punchline: The Boss labels Alice as someone who blames others and is always angry right after she correctly blames him, and her furious outburst seems to confirm his criticism.
summary: A manager faults his overloaded employee for her workload and then criticizes her for reacting angrily to being blamed unfairly.

file: 2003/2003-05-14_corner cubicle_most pretigious_entre row_control window_harness sun_no screen glare.gif
title: Corner Cubicle Power Grab

transcript.speaker: Carol

transcript.text: Buwaha!! From there I will control the window shades and harness the sun!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Carol stands by Dilbert's cubicle and announces she is taking the newly vacant corner cubicle. She gleefully declares it the most prestigious spot in the row and boasts that she'll control the window shades and harness the sun like a supervillain. Dilbert calmly responds with a modest request to avoid screen glare.
punchline: Carol treats a minor office perk like world domination, while Dilbert's deadpan reply shows he only cares about the mundane practical concern of glare on his monitor.
summary: A coworker gloats with villainous glee about claiming the best cubicle and its window shades, and her colleague responds with a humble request about his computer screen.

file: 2003/2003-06-22_performance review_denial_anger_bargaining_depression_acceptance_trash talking_lunch_objectives_glowing email_7 stages_psychology.gif
title: Seven Stages of Performance Review

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Seven stages of a performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Denial

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What the...? These aren't even my objectives!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Anger

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who said these things about me?!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bargaining

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What if I make someone write a glowing e-mail about me?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Depression

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Morale slipping away...hair...so...limp.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Acceptance

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Whatever. There's no budget for raises anyway.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Trash-talking

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...Wool-covered pile of ignorant monkey spit.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Lunch

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's desk
situation: The Boss delivers a performance review to Alice, who works through a parody of the stages of grief: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. She then adds two stages of her own, insulting the boss and going to lunch. The review itself is framed as an emotional process to be gotten through.
punchline: After the formal stages of grief, the real-world stages of a performance review are venting about the boss and moving on to thinking about lunch, showing how little the review matters to her.
summary: An employee goes through a comic checklist of emotional reactions to a bad review, ending with name-calling and a craving for falafel.

file: 2003/2003-08-31_reamin annoynomous_blank card_just like family_my card_business card.gif
title: Anonymous Coworker With Blank Business Card

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this is...

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'd rather not say.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I prefer to remain anonymous, so you won't feel comfortable asking me for anything later.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Here's my card. It's blank.

transcript.text: The phrase that you're least likely to hear today is, "We're just like family."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you worried that he'll turn over the card and see your name?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I've been handing them out for years.

situation: A new employee named Matt introduces himself on his first day, and Dilbert introduces himself, then a bald coworker refuses to give his name. The coworker explains he wants to stay anonymous so nobody will ask him for favors, and hands Matt a blank business card. It turns out the blank card he handed over was actually Dilbert's, which he has been using for years.
punchline: The anonymous coworker has been handing out Dilbert's business cards for years, hiding his own identity while pinning any requests on Dilbert.
summary: A secretive colleague dodges future work requests by staying nameless and passing off someone else's card as his own.

The Boss takes it and walks off, starting to think about whether Dilbert thinks he is an idiot, but gets distracted by a sign advertising discounted Irish line-dancing lessons.
punchline: Just as the Boss is about to grasp the importance of delivering the bid, he is sidetracked by a trivial discount sign, implying the crucial bid will be late and the company's future is at the mercy of his distractibility.
summary: A engineer entrusts his boss with an all-important, time-sensitive proposal, only for the boss to be lured away by a dance-class promotion.

file: 2003/2003-06-29_late worker_coffee and bagel_starts late_woman_worked 6am_paid same_smarter_casual brillaince.gif
title: Late Arrival Beats Early Bird

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: By the time you get your coffee and get your bagel, it'll be ten o'clock!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I started at six! I've already worked for four hours, and I'll probably stay late!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Over the course of a lifetime, I'll work twice as much as you!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But...we'll be paid the same...and we'll both die anyway.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So...I guess what you're saying is that you're smarter than I am.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I curse the casual brilliance of your life strategy!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My bagel will be extra tasty today.

situation: Alice, who has been at work since six in the morning, scolds Wally for strolling in at nine-thirty and taking time for coffee and a bagel. Wally calmly points out that they get paid the same and will both die eventually. Alice realizes his laziness is actually the smarter life strategy and angrily curses him for it.
punchline: Alice's lecture about her superior work ethic backfires when Wally's logic that effort earns no extra pay convinces even her that the slacker is the smart one.
summary: A hard-working early arriver berates a late-arriving coworker, only to be outmaneuvered by his unbothered logic about equal pay and mortality.

file: 2003/2003-11-03_conference calls from mens room_idiotssyncrasies_conference calls_finished newspaper.gif
title: Wally's Bathroom Conference Call Excuse

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ok, perhaps I have a few idiosyncrasies, but it's only because I care so much about the work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one invited you to those conference calls.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What if I've already finished the newspaper?

situation: The Boss confronts Wally, who is holding his coffee mug, about complaints that he takes conference calls from the men's room. Wally claims it's because he cares so much about the work. The Boss points out Wally wasn't even invited to those calls, and Wally responds by asking what if he has already finished the newspaper.
punchline: Wally reveals he joins conference calls he wasn't invited to only because he has run out of other things to do in the bathroom, exposing that his dedication claim is just a cover for killing time.
summary: A boss scolds an uninvited, coffee-clutching employee for eavesdropping on meetings from the restroom, and the employee's lame defense gives away his real motive.

file: 2003/2003-02-09_customers current_future needs_new design_need to upgrade_flaws in design_flaws_inetrface_confounding_crippling electric shocks_guy with mullet_marketing_business.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Flaws would work.

transcript.text: We need flaws.

transcript.speaker: Marketing woman
transcript.text: Flaws, flaws, flaws.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please... no...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make it freeze every hour.

transcript.speaker: Marketing man
transcript.text: The interface needs to be more confounding.

transcript.speaker: Marketing woman
transcript.text: And...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

Dilbert is reduced to pleading and finally collapses on the floor.
punchline: Marketing insists on deliberately making the product worse so customers will keep buying upgrades, and their ideas escalate to absurd and harmful extremes.
summary: A flawless product design is rejected by marketing and management, who pile on intentional defects to force customers into repeat purchases.

file: 2003/2003-09-27_network design_local trees_social skills.gif

situation: A marketing employee who used to be an engineer offers Dilbert advice on his network design. His suggestions are absurd, including replacing a Cisco device with a homemade catapult. Dilbert asks whether it has been a while since he did engineering, and the marketer responds with an insult.
punchline: The marketer claims to have gained good social skills while insulting Dilbert in the same breath, proving his skills are no better than his technical advice.
summary: A former engineer turned marketer gives ridiculous networking advice, then insults Dilbert while bragging about his improved people skills.

file: 2003/2003-09-13_heart and sould_high speed data_talent pool_in charge_mentor_panicking.gif

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wouldn't rule out panicking.

setting: Boss's office, then a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Wally tells the boss he has devoted himself to the risky data-by-sewer project, but then recommends handing it to Asok under the banner of developing the talent pool, with himself as mentor. When Asok excitedly asks what to do first, Wally's only advice is to consider panicking.
punchline: Wally dumps a doomed project on the eager young intern under the guise of mentorship, and his useless 'guidance' is to suggest panicking.
summary: Wally dodges a hopeless project by pushing it onto Asok and calling it career development, then offers him no help beyond a nudge toward hysteria.

file: 2003/2003-04-04_defective coworker_trade in_co workers with defects_parts hair in middle_defects yet discovered.gif
title: Trading In Defective Co-Workers

transcript.text: What's wrong with this one?

transcript.text: He parts his hair in the middle; that's just wrong.

setting: A co-worker exchange lot that resembles a car dealership
situation: Dilbert visits a lot where a yellow-capped attendant explains that defective co-workers can't be repaired, only swapped for others. Dilbert inspects a nervous man in a display alcove and asks what's wrong with him, and the attendant gives a trivial, absurd flaw.
punchline: The only 'defect' offered for the co-worker is how he parts his hair, which mocks how arbitrary and petty complaints about colleagues are, while the attendant's earlier point implies every co-worker has hidden flaws.
summary: A dealer-style attendant sells replacement colleagues like used cars, admitting every one has flaws and justifying a trade-in with a ridiculous trivial fault.

file: 2003/2003-11-16_wally_downsized candidate_alice glad_boss thanks wally_ride to church_on good side.gif
title: Alice Thanks Wally's Terrible Performance

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzzz

situation: Alice gloats to Wally that his awful performance makes him the first candidate for downsizing, which protects her own job. Then the Boss arrives and thanks Wally for driving his family to church and bringing bagels, revealing that Wally has secured the Boss's favor. Alice is horrified at the prospect of Wally being safe, and the Boss awkwardly calls her a heathen.
punchline: Wally, the supposedly worst performer, has actually guarded his job by chauffeuring the Boss's family to church and bribing him with bagels, undermining Alice's smug assumption that he's a doomed buffer.
summary: Alice mocks Wally as her layoff shield, only to learn he has quietly won the boss over with church rides and pastries.

file: 2003/2003-01-29_visibuddy_mindless replica_increases visibility_golf_nice guy_invention_fake clone_robot_sports.gif

summary: An engineer builds a brainless double of himself to sit in meetings and finds that bland platitudes win over the boss.

file: 2003/2003-11-30_manager of executive compensation_plan to steal_meeting_back slapping_pormises_raises_ponys_vacations_huge raise_business.gif

transcript.text: Bradley is totally objective.

situation: The Boss introduces Bradley, the new manager of executive compensation, who is supposed to recommend executive pay objectively. punchline: The supposedly objective compensation manager and the executive he evaluates openly reward each other, and when Dilbert objects, they treat his outrage as a nuisance to be bought off with a trivial perk.
summary: A pay-setting official and the executive he is meant to judge shower each other with gifts and raises while the one honest employee in the room rages.

file: 2003/2003-02-02_budget_engineers_came prepared_audio clips_recording of voice.gif

summary: Armed with recordings of her past concessions, an engineer corners a furious coworker, who responds by destroying the proof in an ape-like tantrum.

file: 2003/2003-01-04_investigative reporter_garbage dumps_wasteful car_tires_park_boss_wasteful.gif

file: 2003/2003-11-02_focusing on bandwidth_organic growth_table an issue_sudebar_managing expectations_ducks in a row_no project.gif

punchline: Wally has produced a convincing, buzzword-laden status report for a project that doesn't exist, and he's baffled because the effort left him exhausted.

summary: A coworker seeks help with a database, but Wally won't share his know-how because being useful would only generate more tasks he'd have to dodge.

file: 2003/2003-02-03_bad hand writing_harmful medication_marketing_mild rash_prescription_doctor_exam room_medical_business.gif

file: 2003/2003-06-05_evil hr dircetor_layoffs_improve moral_making tough deciosn_feel more optimistic_your fired.gif

file: 2003/2003-01-25_decompose_digits_million dollars_planned obsolescene_upgarde_upgrade now_version_newest software.gif

file: 2003/2003-06-27_record loss_press release_ceo stepped down_100 million_tenure_shareholders_bought stock.gif

punchline: The CEO openly mocks the shareholders who lost money, pointing out that the only profitable investment was in himself, which satirizes executive pay that is untethered from company performance.
summary: A press release reveals that a failing company's departing chief executive pocketed more than the firm ever made and then taunted his investors about it.

file: 2003/2003-05-04_smarter not harder_important looking document_pretend to be angry_avoid people_more problems_shirt toothpaste color_smells minty.gif
title: Wally's Lessons in Looking Busy

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, can you teach me to work smarter, not harder?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grab an important-looking document and follow me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Walk briskly and pretend to be angry about what you're reading.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Grrrr...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, Asok, would you help me...?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Never mind.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grrr

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Grrr

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As a rule, people try to avoid anyone who has more problems than they do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Lesson two: Make sure your shirt and your toothpaste are the same color.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This baby is covered with toothpaste stains, but you'd never know it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And how often do you need to launder a shirt that smells minty?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Never!

situation: Asok asks Wally to teach him how to work smarter, not harder. Wally has him carry an important-looking document and walk briskly while pretending to be angry so that coworkers will avoid them. Wally then shares a second lesson: wear a shirt the same color as your toothpaste so stains never show and you never have to wash it.
punchline: Wally's idea of working smarter is fooling coworkers into leaving you alone and never doing laundry, which is really just a way of avoiding effort and hygiene.
summary: Wally mentors Asok in the art of dodging work by looking perpetually furious and by hiding toothpaste stains on a shirt that never gets washed.

file: 2003/2003-03-20_cost cutting_job for a day_dream of grave_less motivating.gif
title: CEO Does Your Job Prize

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our department won the cost-cutting contest, so our CEO will do your job for a day.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I feel like a failure...darkness fills my days...I dream of the grave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is less motivating than I'd hoped.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'll never be loved again!!

situation: The Boss announces to Alice that her department won a cost-cutting contest and the prize is that the CEO will do her job for a day. The CEO sits at her desk and despairs, speaking of failure, darkness and dreaming of the grave. The Boss admits the stunt is less motivating than he hoped while the CEO wails that he will never be loved again.
punchline: The CEO's brief experience of an ordinary employee's job is so miserable that it leaves him despairing, showing the prize is hardly a reward and that the job is soul-crushing.
summary: A cost-cutting prize sends the chief executive into a gloomy spiral when he briefly takes over a worker's desk.

file: 2003/2003-12-15_watching tv_news anchors_report_tv cameras_shows_evil or stupid_heart disease_stupid_banter_stinks.gif
title: News Anchors Banter About Stupid Coworkers

transcript.speaker: TV news anchor
transcript.text: Researchers have proven that working with evil or stupid people causes heart disease.

transcript.speaker: Male news anchor
transcript.text: Ha ha! I wonder if the amount of stupidiousness makes a difference.

transcript.speaker: Female news anchor
transcript.text: Your witty banter stinks today.

setting: Dilbert's living room watching a TV news broadcast
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit in an armchair watching the evening news. The anchors report on research linking evil or stupid coworkers to heart disease, and the male anchor jokes about whether the degree of stupidity matters, using a made-up word. His female co-anchor bluntly tells him his banter is bad.
punchline: The male anchor's feeble joke, which even includes the made-up word 'stupidiousness', proves he is stupid himself, so his co-anchor insults him and, ironically, illustrates the study about stupid people being bad for your heart.
summary: A pair of television newscasters demonstrate the very problem they are reporting on when one makes a clumsy joke and the other shoots it down.

file: 2003/2003-11-21_status reprrts_costs of projects_business plan_budget_throw on pile.gif
title: Status Reports Go on the Pile

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Lately I am overcome with doubt that you read my status reports.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, the biggest value of a status report is that it makes you consider all the costs of your project.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Actually, that is the biggest value of a business plan or a budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever. Throw it on the pile.

situation: Asok stands in front of the Boss's desk holding a status report and says he doubts the Boss actually reads them. The Boss claims the value of a status report is that it forces the writer to consider project costs. Asok points out that this is really the purpose of a business plan or budget, and the Boss dismisses him and tells him to add the report to the pile on the desk.
punchline: The Boss's justification for status reports is exposed as a made-up excuse for never reading them, and when caught he simply dismisses the point and sends the report to the pile.
summary: A junior employee suspects his manager ignores his reports, and the manager's flimsy defense collapses into a brush-off.

file: 2003/2003-03-10_life insurance_exclusions_self inflicted wounds_re existing illness_criminal acts_war_quilting bees.gif
title: Dilbert Reads Insurance Fine Print

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you like to buy some life insurance?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exclusions: self-inflicted wounds, pre-existing illness, criminal acts, war, dangerous sports, smoking...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Much later that day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and pistol duels resulting from quilting bees.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No one reads it, freak!

situation: Dogbert, acting as an insurance salesman, offers Dilbert life insurance and hands him the policy. Dilbert reads through the exclusions clause by clause, and is still reading hours later. Dogbert is exasperated that Dilbert actually reads the fine print.
punchline: Salespeople rely on customers never reading the fine print, so Dogbert insults Dilbert for doing the one thing no buyer is supposed to do.
summary: A pitchman is irritated when his customer meticulously studies the lengthy list of policy exclusions that nobody normally bothers to read.

file: 2003/2003-03-06_loser magazine_featuring you_cover photo_breakroom_napping_show offs.gif
title: Loser Magazine Cover Feature Declined

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: A man from "Loser Magazine" wants to see you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He said something about featuring you on the cover.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Send him over.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I tried, but he keeps going into the break room and napping.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hate show-offs.

situation: Carol tells Wally that a man from 'Loser Magazine' wants to feature him on the cover and he agrees to meet him. She then explains the visitor keeps wandering into the break room to nap instead. Wally, annoyed, calls the visitor a show-off.
punchline: Wally is so lazy that he resents the magazine's representative for napping on the job, seeing it as showing off rather than recognizing that he himself is the loser being celebrated.
summary: A reporter seeking a lazy employee for a magazine cover turns out to be napping in the break room, which irritates the very slacker he came to honor.

file: 2003/2003-06-15_clammy offcie_all clammy_hands are clammy_underpants.gif
title: Boss's Clammy Office Mystery

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not just my desk; it's the chair, too!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, come here!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything in my office feels clammy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I first noticed when I touched my phone...then my mouse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All clammy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What could it mean?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It could mean your hands are clammy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must never speak of this.

transcript.speaker: Man in Meeting
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed that everything you sit on feels like underpants?

setting: The Boss's office, then a conference room meeting
situation: The Boss summons Dilbert to complain that everything in his office feels clammy, from his desk and chair to his phone and mouse. Dilbert points out the obvious explanation: the Boss's own hands are clammy. The Boss, embarrassed, orders him never to mention it, then is seen in a meeting where a coworker raises the same odd observation about everything feeling like underpants.
punchline: The Boss blames his office for a problem caused by his own clammy hands, and Dilbert's simple diagnosis is so mortifying that the Boss demands secrecy.
summary: A manager is baffled by a damp-feeling office until his employee suggests the dampness is coming from his own palms.

file: 2003/2003-05-26_summarize for ceo_obliterate persuasiveness_being wordy.gif
title: Summarizing for the CEO Costs Billions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you summarize this on one page for our CEO?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but it will obliterate the persuasiveness of the document and cost us billions in lost opportunity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see your point, but being wordy is bad, too.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document and asks for a one-page summary for the CEO. Dilbert warns that condensing it will destroy its persuasiveness and cost billions in lost opportunity. The Boss concedes the point but then dismisses it by saying that wordiness is also a problem.
punchline: The Boss claims to understand Dilbert's warning but ignores it, showing he cares more about brevity for the CEO than about the document's substance or the money at stake.
summary: A manager demands a condensed version of a long report for the top executive and brushes aside his employee's warning about the financial damage of cutting it down.

file: 2003/2003-05-12_write rebuttal_technical recommendation_reject_rebuttal_mock yourself_got to bed.gif
title: Rebutting Your Own Recommendation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write a rebuttal to this technical recommendation so I can reject it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't write a rebuttal to my own recommendation!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Then I had to write myself up for insubordination.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Mock yourself and go to bed.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a technical recommendation and orders him to write a rebuttal so the boss can reject it. Dilbert objects that the recommendation is his own. At home, Dilbert tells Dogbert that he then had to write himself up for insubordination, and Dogbert tells him to mock himself and go to bed.
punchline: The boss's absurd demand forces Dilbert to argue against his own work, and his refusal gets him punished, so he ends up disciplining himself, which Dogbert answers with deadpan sarcasm.
summary: A manager wants his employee to argue against the employee's own proposal to justify turning it down, and the objection earns the employee a reprimand.

file: 2003/2003-04-01_critical_engineer_handshake_head with lies_new team player_parinoid_soft and clammy hand_undead_engineering.gif
title: Paranoid Coworker Suspects Dilbert Is Undead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet your new team member, Peri Noid.

transcript.speaker: Peri Noid
transcript.text: Why haven't you invited me to a meeting? Who's filling your head with lies?

transcript.speaker: Peri Noid
transcript.text: Your hand is soft and clammy! Are you the undead?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Engineer.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a new team member named Peri Noid. She immediately accuses Dilbert of excluding her from meetings and of feeding her lies. When they shake hands, she declares his hand soft and clammy and asks if he is undead, and Dilbert answers that he is an engineer.
punchline: Dilbert's one-word reply implies that being an engineer fully explains having a pale, soft, clammy hand, since engineers rarely leave their desks or see sunlight.
summary: A suspicious new colleague whose name is a pun on paranoia mistakes a sweaty handshake for a sign of the living dead.

file: 2003/2003-04-05_new guy_middles part_forbid_near work space_not good people_1970's called.gif
title: New Guy Insults Carol's Hairstyle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, this is our new guy, Harry Middlepart.

transcript.speaker: Harry Middlepart
transcript.text: I don't approve of your hair-style. I forbid you to be near my workspace.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's not good people.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The seventies called. They want their hair back!!

situation: Dilbert introduces the new coworker, Harry Middlepart, to Carol, the boss's assistant. Harry immediately criticizes her hairstyle and forbids her from coming near his workspace. Dilbert warns Harry that she is not good people, and Carol retaliates by phoning in a joke that the seventies want their hair back.
punchline: Harry insults Carol's hairstyle and picks a fight with someone who can retaliate, and Carol answers by making a dated-hair joke about him on the phone.
summary: A new hire picks on a coworker's looks and workspace boundaries within seconds of meeting her, and she pays him back with a quick jab about his old-fashioned haircut.

file: 2003/2003-07-17_engineers_said to reporter_technology is purtrid_compensate_ignore complaints_witch hunt.gif
title: Catbert Prefers Witch-Hunt Over Fixing

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Look what one of our engineers said to a reporter!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "Our technology is putrid, but we compensate by ignoring complaints."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You know what would be more fun than fixing those problems?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Witch-hunt!!!

setting: Office, next to a filing cabinet or copier
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, and the Boss read a newspaper in which an engineer has publicly admitted the company's technology is terrible and complaints are ignored. Instead of addressing the actual problems, they gleefully decide that hunting down the engineer who spoke to the press would be more fun.
punchline: Management reacts to a damaging but accurate public admission by punishing the messenger rather than fixing the product.
summary: Faced with a news story exposing their shoddy technology, the company's leaders eagerly choose to hunt for the leaker instead of solving anything.

file: 2003/2003-05-07_exporting leprechaun meat_cameras_elbonians_no excuse.gif
title: Leprechaun Meat PR Campaign

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: P.R. for Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The media give you a bad rap for exporting leprechaun meat.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our ad campaign will feature a leprechaun explaining that they enjoy being eaten.

transcript.speaker: Leprechaun
transcript.text: Elbonians are our best friends. Now excuse me while I tenderize myself.

setting: Conference room, then a TV commercial set
situation: Dogbert, acting as a PR consultant, meets with Elbonian leaders who are criticized for exporting leprechaun meat. He proposes an ad campaign in which a leprechaun claims to enjoy being eaten. In the final panel, the leprechaun stands in a frying pan on camera and prepares to tenderize himself with a mallet.
punchline: The ad campaign meant to defend the meat trade has the leprechaun cheerfully volunteering to prepare himself for cooking, which is absurd and darkly horrifying.
summary: A consultant pitches a commercial in which the victim of a questionable food export cheerfully assures viewers he loves being dinner.

file: 2003/2003-12-22_career counseling_mad about downsized_involves punching_kicking_resume_alice_seeking job.gif
title: Alice's Revenge-Themed Job Search

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Career counseling

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently you're still mad about being downsized.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to your resume, you're seeking a job that involves "punching a short, stocky guy with pointy hair."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that the only job you'd consider?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I also like kicking.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a career counselor, reviews Alice's resume across his desk. She was recently downsized and her listed job objective is to punch a short, stocky man with pointy hair, an obvious reference to the Boss. When Dogbert asks if that's the only job she'd consider, she adds that she also likes kicking.
punchline: Alice's resume lists violence against her former boss as her career goal, and she cheerfully offers kicking as an alternative, showing how bitter she remains about being laid off.
summary: A downsized employee tells her career counselor that the work she wants is assaulting her old boss, with a bit of kicking on the side.

file: 2003/2003-02-04_drug_happy_mood altering_pharmacy_pick up_skin rash_unhappy_pharmacist.gif
title: Pharmacist Prescribes Happiness Instead of Cure

transcript.speaker: Pharmacist
transcript.text: I can't read your doctor's handwriting.

transcript.speaker: Pharmacist
transcript.text: I'll give you this mood-altering drug to make you happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a skin rash!

transcript.speaker: Pharmacist
transcript.text: And it's making you unhappy, right?

situation: Dilbert brings a prescription to a pharmacist, who admits he cannot read the doctor's handwriting. Instead of figuring out the correct medicine, he hands over a random mood-altering drug to make Dilbert happy. Dilbert protests that he actually has a skin rash, and the pharmacist simply assumes the rash is what's making him unhappy.
punchline: The pharmacist, unable to decipher the prescription, substitutes a mood-altering drug and rationalizes it as a treatment for the unhappiness caused by the rash, ignoring the rash itself.
summary: A pharmacist who can't decode a prescription improvises by dispensing a happy pill, treating the patient's mood rather than his actual ailment.

file: 2003/2003-08-06_description_projected course_impossible_uncertainty principle_understand project_know cost.gif
title: Project Uncertainty Principle Defense

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: I need a description of your project and its projected cost.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's impossible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Project Uncertainty Principle says that if you understand a project, you won't know its cost, and vice versa.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: You just made that up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't make it wrong.

situation: A woman with a notepad asks Dilbert for a description of his project and its projected cost. Dilbert claims this is impossible and invokes a so-called Project Uncertainty Principle, modeled on Heisenberg's. When she points out he invented it, he calmly says that doesn't make it wrong.
punchline: Dilbert fabricates a pseudo-scientific principle to dodge cost estimation, and when caught, notes that being made up doesn't disprove it.
summary: Asked to estimate what his project will cost, Dilbert dodges with an invented law of physics-style uncertainty and shrugs off the accusation that he fabricated it.

file: 2003/2003-03-25_feng shui_pet psychic_new career_furniture psychic_wastebasket loves desk.gif
title: Dogbert Becomes Furniture Psychic

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They believe in feng shui. They believe in the pet psychic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This suggests an excellent new career for me.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Wife
transcript.text: The furniture psychic is here. He says my wastebasket is in love with my desk.

setting: A kitchen table in Dilbert's home, then the Boss's office
situation: Dogbert and Dilbert sit at a table drinking coffee while Dogbert observes that people believe in feng shui and pet psychics. He decides this points to a lucrative new career for himself. In the final panel, a woman in a nightgown tells the Boss that the furniture psychic has arrived and says her wastebasket is in love with her desk.
punchline: Dogbert exploits gullible people's belief in pseudoscience by posing as a furniture psychic, and the Boss's household has already fallen for his absurd con.
summary: Spotting a market among people who trust mystical fads, Dogbert invents a ridiculous psychic profession and promptly finds a customer.

file: 2003/2003-10-04_different decsions_iq 240_intuition and experence_chinese astrology.gif
title: Boss Decides by Chinese Astrology

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that every decision you make is different from what I would have done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My IQ is 240. Your IQ aspires to the three-digit range. I assume that your intuition and experience are guiding you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please be that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Chinese astrology!

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that all of the boss's decisions differ from what Dilbert would have chosen. The boss, who is seated at his desk, boasts an IQ of 240 and insults Dilbert's intelligence, assuming Dilbert's decisions come from intuition and experience. When Dilbert hopefully asks what guides the boss's own choices, the boss reveals he uses Chinese astrology.
punchline: The boss's supposedly superior judgment is actually based on Chinese astrology, which makes his bragging about a 240 IQ absurd.
summary: A manager brags about his genius-level intellect, then admits his bad decisions come from consulting horoscopes.

file: 2003/2003-12-07_intern_cheap boss_full size cubicle_half size_cubicle_treats poorly_no budget_garbage can_misunderstand.gif
title: Intern Denied Empty Full-Size Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: May I move to one of the empty cubicles?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Those are full-size cubicles; interns get half-size cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Yes...ordinarily, but there are hundreds of vacant cubicles because of downsizing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not following you.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: They're empty! They will never be occupied. I want to use one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't have the budget to turn a full-size cubicle into a half-size cubicle just for you.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! That's not what I... Never mind! Forget it!

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Furthermore, I do not believe this is a half-size cubicle.

setting: The Boss's office, then a cubicle
situation: An intern asks the boss if he can move into one of the many empty cubicles left by downsizing. The boss insists interns only get half-size cubicles and refuses to spend money converting a full-size one. The exasperated intern gives up, and the final panel shows him upside down in a trash can, imagining that this is his half-size cubicle.
punchline: The boss's absurdly rigid cost-cutting logic leaves the intern so defeated that he ends up wedged in a garbage can, doubting even that counts as a half-size cubicle.
summary: A junior employee's sensible request for free empty space is defeated by a manager's rigid budget logic, leaving him stuffed in a trash bin.

file: 2003/2003-11-20_take training_mismanagement skills_awed_send wally.gif
title: Awed by Boss's Mismanagement Artistry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I desperately need to take this training.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't spare you. Send Wally and have him tell you what he learned.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm awed by the sheer artistry of your mismanagement skills.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: Dilbert hands his boss a training request form, saying he desperately needs the course. The boss refuses because Dilbert can't be spared and suggests sending Wally, the least productive employee, to pass on what he learns. Dilbert sarcastically compliments the boss's mismanagement, and the boss takes it as genuine praise.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic praise of the boss's mismanagement is taken as a sincere compliment, since the boss is too oblivious to recognize the insult.
summary: A worker's request for training is turned down in favor of sending a slacker colleague, and the manager mistakes the worker's sarcasm for genuine admiration.

file: 2003/2003-12-04_accidentally eat_apple core_care values_customer service_respect_stem is loyalty_teamwork_apple product.gif
title: Apple Core Values Presentation Mishap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This apple will remind us of our core values: respect, customer service, and teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The apple's core is the part you throw away.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not always. Sometimes I accidentally eat it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe the stem can represent our loyalty to the company.

situation: The Boss presents a slide of an apple to illustrate the company's 'core values' of respect, customer service, and teamwork. Dilbert points out that an apple's core is the part people throw away. The Boss brushes this off and then tries to turn the apple's stem into a symbol of employee loyalty.
punchline: The Boss's apple metaphor undermines itself, since the core is discarded, and his attempt to patch it with the stem shows the company's real priority is employee loyalty rather than the values it claims.
summary: A manager's fruit-based analogy for company values falls apart when an employee notes that the core is what gets tossed out.

file: 2003/2003-07-31_criticize things_dont understnd_kyoto treaty_flat tax_unfair_stem cells.gif
title: Dogbert Mocks Uninformed Political Opinions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to spend more time criticizing things I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I say we should flat-tax the Kyoto treaty all the way back to the Security Council!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that be unfair to stem cells?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bah!

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on the couch while Dogbert announces he will criticize things he doesn't understand. He then spouts a nonsensical political statement mashing together flat taxes, the Kyoto treaty and the Security Council. Dilbert replies with an equally nonsensical objection about stem cells, and Dogbert dismisses it.
punchline: Dilbert joins in with an equally meaningless objection, showing that confident-sounding opinions about topics nobody understands are interchangeable gibberish.
summary: A dog and his owner swap jumbled political buzzwords on the sofa, parodying people who pontificate about issues they know nothing about.

file: 2003/2003-01-13_cash_conflicts if interest_corporate skin_huge failures_no red flags_potential client_track record.gif
title: Consultick Warns Client, Client Ignores

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Hello, potential client. I'm a consultick.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'll burrow into your corporate skin, suck your cash and never leave.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: My firm has a track record of huge consulting failures and conflicts of interest!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No red flags.

situation: A horned consultant in a red jacket introduces himself as a 'consultick' (a consultant-tick) to a prospective client sitting at his desk. He openly admits he will burrow into the company, drain its money and never leave, and that his firm has a history of failures and conflicts of interest. The Boss, thinking to himself, sees no warning signs.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious or eager to hire consultants that he ignores blatantly honest warnings and thinks there are 'no red flags'.
summary: A consultant cheerfully confesses he is a parasite with a record of failure, yet the gullible client perceives nothing worrying.

file: 2003/2003-10-21_guest cartoonist_rob the dinosuar_bob_million degrees_costume_you idiot_no pay_every has cotsume.gif
title: Guest Cartoonist Dinosaur Costume Shoot

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Who's today's guest cartoonist?*

transcript.speaker: Rob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: Hi! Rob the Dinosaur here! Today I want to-

transcript.speaker: Director
transcript.text: Cut!!! Your name is Bob!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Sir, it's like a million degrees in here. Can't we take a two minute break?

transcript.speaker: Director
transcript.text: No! You'll do it until you get it right, you idiot! You have displeased me. No pay for you!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I hate Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ssh! He'll hear you!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Answer: Go to dilbert.com

setting: A film or photo shoot set with a director's chair, and a backstage area with costumed animal characters
situation: A man in a hot green dinosaur costume introduces himself as Rob the Dinosaur as a guest cartoonist, but the director yells cut and corrects him that his name is Bob. When Bob begs for a short break because of the heat, the director refuses, insults him, and denies him pay. In the last panel, other costumed characters whisper that they hate Dilbert.
punchline: The guest cartoonist gag is a mock-promotion for the website, with the costumed actor abused by a tyrannical director, while the other costumed characters (in animal costumes) fear being overheard badmouthing Dilbert.
summary: A sweltering man in a dinosaur suit is berated and stiffed by a petty director while fellow costumed performers nervously gripe about their employer.

file: 2003/2003-06-01_revenue projections_email_reading email_song_multi task_stupid nbinder_slow down_comprehend_reading goes quickly.gif
title: Single-Task Bob Sings Instead

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Bob, can I have your revenue projections?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: No. I'm reading my e-mail. I can't do two things at once.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: But I offer you this song instead.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Ooh-waa-waa! I'm Single-Task Bob. I'm Single-Task Bob

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I can't multitask. I only do one job

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Just give me the stupid binder that's on your desk!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Sure. And I guess my e-mail can just read itself, right?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Reading goes quickly when you don't slow down to comprehend.

situation: Carol asks coworker Bob for his revenue projections, but Bob refuses because he is reading e-mail and claims he can only do one thing at a time. He then sings a song about being Single-Task Bob, which infuriates Carol into demanding the binder on his desk. She sarcastically mocks his excuse, and Bob admits he reads e-mail quickly because he skips actually understanding it.
punchline: Bob's claim that he can't multitask is a flimsy excuse, and his e-mail reading is so superficial that he isn't really comprehending any of it anyway.
summary: A coworker who refuses a simple request by claiming he can only do one thing at a time is revealed to be skimming his e-mail without understanding it.

file: 2003/2003-12-02_merging with evil compnay_downsize_how valuable.gif
title: Boss Learns of Evil Merger

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: What?!! According to the paper, we're merging with an evil company that plans to downsize us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did they run my quote about how valuable you are?

situation: During a meeting, a bald coworker reads a newspaper and angrily reports that the company is merging with an evil firm that intends to downsize them. Dilbert, Alice, and the others glare furious at the news. The Boss, seated across the table, calmly asks whether the paper printed his quote praising how valuable they are.
punchline: The Boss is only concerned about whether his flattering quote got printed, ignoring that the employees are about to be laid off, which implies his praise is hollow PR.
summary: Staff fume over a newspaper report of a layoff-minded merger while their manager only wonders if his compliment about them made the article.

file: 2003/2003-04-24_coffee rehadb_rip beard_death_state name_coffee addicting withdrawl_sleeping_mean_nasty_cutting_violent_falls asleep_medical.gif
title: Coffee Rehab Meeting Turns Violent

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Coffee rehab

transcript.speaker: Group leader
transcript.text: State your name and how long you've been without coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am going to rip off your little beard and beat you to death with it.

transcript.speaker: Group leader
transcript.text: (thinking) Don't panic... wait... wait...

transcript.speaker: Group leader
transcript.text: And then I'll... um... zzzzzzz zzzzz zzz.

situation: A bearded group leader at a podium asks the attendees to state their name and how long they have been without coffee. Dilbert, sitting among sleeping and drowsy attendees, angrily threatens to rip off the leader's beard and beat him to death with it. The leader tries to stay calm and think of a response but drifts off to sleep himself.
punchline: Coffee withdrawal makes everyone in the support group either homicidally irritable or asleep, including the leader who is supposed to be running the meeting.
summary: At a caffeine-quitters' support group, one deprived attendee issues a violent threat while the rest doze, and even the facilitator nods off mid-thought.

file: 2003/2003-03-14_just in time_inventory_strategy_deepest sympathy_sharp stabbing pain_promises.gif
title: Just-in-Time Customer Dependency Pain

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: My company is moving to a "just in time" inventory strategy. You'll deliver when we need it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So...your success depends on my company doing what it promises? You have my deepest sympathy.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I feel a sharp, stabbing pain in my chest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And so it begins.

situation: A customer tells Dilbert, who works for a supplier, that his company is adopting just-in-time inventory and will rely on Dilbert's company to deliver exactly when needed. Dilbert responds with mock sympathy, since his company is unreliable. The customer immediately feels chest pain at the realization.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic sympathy reveals that depending on his company's promises is a terrible idea, and the customer's instant chest pain suggests he already regrets the strategy.
summary: A buyer proudly announces a plan that makes him dependent on a supplier, and the supplier's deadpan pity gives him a heart-clutching preview of the trouble ahead.

file: 2003/2003-08-14_billion dollar product line_designed and launched_meets expectations_high expectations_worng.gif
title: Billion Dollar Success, Merely Meets Expectations

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, this year you single-handedly designed and launched a billion dollar line of new products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For that accomplishment, I give you the highly coveted "meets expectations" designation!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, if having high expectations of you is wrong, then I don't want to be right.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss conducts Alice's annual review and notes that she single-handedly designed and launched a billion dollar product line. He then gives her only a "meets expectations" rating. When Alice reacts with visible anger, he defends himself by saying his high expectations of her are justified.
punchline: The Boss justifies giving an average rating for extraordinary results by claiming his sky-high expectations are a compliment, which is a self-serving excuse for withholding recognition.
summary: A manager hands a star employee a mediocre rating despite her huge achievement and then spins his stinginess as faith in her abilities.

file: 2003/2003-10-08_profitability_year 3_key revenue_comet strike oil_crashes through wall_abstractions_presentation.gif
title: Business Plan Relies on Armored Car Crash

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As requested, I wrote the business plan to show profitability by year three.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The key revenue assumption is that an armored car crashes through that wall and spills its contents.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And don't stand where the comet is assumed to strike oil.

setting: Conference room during a business plan presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a business plan to a meeting audience, pointing at a chart showing an upward trend. He explains that the plan only shows profitability because it assumes absurd windfalls: an armored car crashing through the wall and spilling its cash, and a comet striking oil. The audience in the foreground watches him.
punchline: Because management demanded a plan showing profitability by year three, Dilbert has to build it on ridiculous, impossible assumptions, mocking how business plans are reverse-engineered to reach a desired result.
summary: Told to produce a profitable plan, Dilbert builds the numbers on freak accidents like a cash-spilling truck crash and a comet that hits an oil field.

file: 2003/2003-09-05_stalled career_psychological pressure_reach stars_hopeless_burn your hand.gif
title: Wally's Hopeless Advice on Stalled Careers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, how do I handle the psychological pressure of a stalled career?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Remember that when you reach for the stars, they're too far away, so it's hopeless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But sometimes you can reach a star...can't you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That would burn your hand clean off.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally, who is sitting at his desk with a coffee mug, how to cope with the stress of a stalled career. Wally replies that reaching for the stars is hopeless because they are too far away. When Dilbert points out that a star can sometimes be reached, Wally says it would burn his hand off.
punchline: Wally's cynical advice leaves no room for ambition: stars are either unreachable or deadly, so there is no good outcome to striving.
summary: A worker seeking comfort about his going-nowhere career gets a bleak, no-win metaphor from his lazy coworker.

file: 2003/2003-01-10_extreme programming_ruin my life_user story_features.gif
title: User Story: Give Me Features

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Extreme Programming

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't give you all of these features in the first version.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And each feature needs to have what we call a "user story."

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, here's a story: You give me all of my features or I'll ruin your life.

situation: Dilbert, working under an Extreme Programming approach, tells a client he cannot deliver every requested feature in the first version, and explains that each feature needs a 'user story'. The client, holding a long list of demands, responds by offering her own 'story' that is really a threat.
punchline: The customer deliberately misreads 'user story' as a narrative and uses it to deliver a threat, showing that client demands trump agile process.
summary: A developer's request for narrative justification of each feature is answered with a menacing ultimatum from a demanding client.

file: 2003/2003-09-02_tech solution_simple_cost fortune_internal approvals_vast herds_management dolts.gif
title: Vast Herds of Management Dolts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The technical solution is simple and inexpensive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it would cost a fortune to get internal approvals because vast herds of management dolts would get involved.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I should just do it, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you call me a vast herd?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a technical fix is cheap and easy but that getting internal approvals would be hugely expensive because so many managers would have to weigh in. He asks whether he should simply implement it without approval. The Boss ignores the actual question and takes offense at being lumped in with the 'vast herds'.
punchline: The Boss fixates on whether he was personally insulted instead of addressing the absurd approval overhead, which proves Dilbert's point about management dolts.
summary: An engineer suggests skipping a costly approval process for an easy fix, and his manager responds only by worrying that he was called part of the herd.

file: 2003/2003-09-01_times are tough_optimism_find good in bad_wild pigs_pigs are cute.gif
title: Pigs Are Cute Optimism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I know that times are tough. But you need to show more optimism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to find the one good thing about any bad situation.

transcript.speaker: Man at meeting
transcript.text: Our entire sales force has been eaten by wild pigs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Pigs are cute!

situation: The Boss lectures Alice about being more optimistic and tells her to find the one good thing in any bad situation. A colleague then announces that the entire sales force was eaten by wild pigs, and Alice complies with the advice by saying pigs are cute.
punchline: Alice follows the boss's advice to the letter with a deadpan, absurdly trivial silver lining, mocking forced positivity in the face of a disaster.
summary: Told to look on the bright side, Alice responds to news of a grisly catastrophe with the most useless possible compliment.

file: 2003/2003-11-24_evil director_cut costs_bottom of ocena_crushed by pressure_breathing issue_whiner_labeled a whiner.gif
title: Relocated to the Ocean Floor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert, Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: In order to cut costs, some of you will be relocated to the bottom of the ocean.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Wouldn't we be crushed by the pressure?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Every job has some pressure.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And then there's the breathing issue.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I label you a whiner.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a meeting of employees that some of them will be relocated to the bottom of the ocean to save money. When an employee raises sensible objections about crushing pressure and being unable to breathe, Catbert dismisses the first with a pun and then labels the employee a whiner.
punchline: Catbert answers life-threatening objections to an absurd cost-cutting plan by dismissing them with a pressure pun and branding the employee a complainer.
summary: An HR cat proposes sending staff to the seafloor to save money and punishes anyone who points out the obvious dangers.

file: 2003/2003-05-10_drive ny management_sprayed cubicle_irrational orders_waddled away_wadlle_funny word_empathy.gif
title: Drive-By Management Victim Lacks Empathy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a victim of drive-by management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He sprayed my cubicle with irrational orders and waddled away.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Heh-heh. Waddle is a funny word.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel your empathy slipping away.

setting: Dilbert's office, with Ratbert sitting on a blue couch
situation: Dilbert, wearing a sling on his arm, tells Ratbert he has been a victim of drive-by management, explaining that his boss dropped irrational orders on him and waddled off. Ratbert, who is supposed to be sympathetic, giggles instead about how funny the word 'waddle' is.
punchline: Dilbert's sympathetic listener gets distracted by a silly word in the middle of his complaint, showing that even a sympathetic ear can't stay focused on a serious workplace grievance.
