summary: A sling-wearing engineer complains about a manager who dumps orders and flees, only to have his listener snicker at the wording instead of offering comfort.

file: 2003/2003-03-02_abuse_audio menu system_freezing_love problem_low level technician_same questions_too much optimism_waited in que_tech support.gif
title: Dogbert's Abusive Tech Support Hotline

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's tech support. How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Finally!! It took me an hour to penetrate your inscrutable audio menu system!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Then I waited in queue for forty minutes!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: My problem is that my computer keeps freezing...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not so fast.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need to know your name, address, phone number, operating system, e-mail address, serial numbers, software versions and video drivers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I'll put you in queue for the low-level technician who can only tell you to reboot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He'll ask you the same questions for reasons that will baffle you.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: But eventually you'll solve my problem, right?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure, if your problem is too much optimism.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk, phone conversation
situation: A customer calls Dogbert's tech support after an hour in an audio menu maze and forty minutes in a queue. Dogbert demands a long list of personal and technical details, then explains the customer will be passed to a low-level technician who only says to reboot and asks the same questions again. The customer hopes the problem will eventually be solved.
punchline: Dogbert admits the support process can never fix the computer, only the caller's overly optimistic belief that it will.
summary: A frustrated caller learns that reaching help means endless menus, repeated questions and useless advice, with nothing actually getting fixed.

file: 2003/2003-01-27_bailing on project_ensure survival_loser pill_rejected by wally_pill_therapy_therapist_psychology.gif
title: Rejected by Wally, Needs Loser Pill

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm bailing out of your project; it has the scent of failure.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I will attach myself to a more successful host to ensure my survival.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a pill for someone who gets rejected by Wally?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: A loser pill?

setting: Office hallway, then a therapist's office
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Dilbert he is abandoning Dilbert's project because it smells of failure and he will latch onto a more successful project to survive. Dilbert then lies on a therapist's couch and asks for a pill for people rejected by Wally.
punchline: Being dumped by Wally, the laziest and least ambitious employee, is so humiliating that the therapist concludes Dilbert needs a pill for losers.
summary: A coworker famous for doing nothing ditches a colleague's doomed project, leaving the colleague seeking medication from a therapist, who bluntly labels the cure.

file: 2003/2003-02-25_blank cd_demo_empty case_forgetting blank cd_new product_software_travel_travelled four hours_unit_once we write_engineering.gif
title: Product Demo Of Empty Case

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an appointment to see a demo of your new product.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: And the unit will be in a case like this, but completely different, and it will have software, once we write it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You let me travel four hours to see an empty case?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Are you forgetting the blank CD?

setting: Vendor's office reception area and meeting room
situation: Dilbert arrives for a scheduled demo of a vendor's new product. The salesman shows him an empty case and explains that the real unit will look different and that the software hasn't been written yet. When Dilbert complains about travelling four hours to see nothing, the salesman points out the blank CD as if it counts for something.
punchline: The vendor's 'demo' consists of an empty case and a blank CD, and he thinks the blank disc makes it more substantial.
summary: A visiting customer discovers the supposed product demo is just an empty box for software that does not exist yet.

file: 2003/2003-11-18_destroy refrigeration_crushed ice_annoying noise_cubilces_crunch.gif
title: Crushed Ice Cubicle Rage

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: This might be the greatest innovation in annoying cubicle noises.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Chewing crushed ice.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crunch crunch crunch

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must...destroy all refrigeration facilities...on Earth.

situation: Phil sits in his cubicle proudly crunching crushed ice from a cup, convinced he has found the ultimate annoying cubicle noise. In the neighboring cubicle, Alice listens to the constant crunching and becomes so enraged that her hair bristles and she grits her teeth, plotting to wipe out every freezer on the planet.
punchline: Phil deliberately chews ice to annoy coworkers, and it works so well that Alice is driven to fantasize about eliminating all refrigeration just to stop the noise.
summary: A cheerfully irritating coworker munches ice in his cubicle until his neighbor is pushed into a murderous, freezer-hating fury.

file: 2003/2003-03-19_ceo_secretary for a day_deeply offended_trivial_train.gif
title: CEO Secretary Prize Offends Secretary

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The department that cuts costs the most will get our CEO as its secretary for a day.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm deeply offended by the implication that my job is so trivial that it can be used as a prize.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you can train him to phone your kids and yell at them.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Not funny!!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces a cost-cutting contest whose prize is having the CEO serve as the winning department's secretary for a day. Carol, his secretary, says she is offended that her job is treated as so trivial it can be a prize. The Boss responds with a tone-deaf joke about having the CEO phone her kids and yell at them, which she says is not funny.
punchline: The Boss tries to smooth over his insult to his secretary with an even more insulting joke, showing he has no idea why she is upset.
summary: A manager's contest prize belittles his secretary's work, and his attempt at humor only makes things worse.

file: 2003/2003-03-11_meeting_scheduled_secretary_moron_doesn't respect_stuck in traffic_business.gif
title: Late Visitor Insults the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, where's my ten o'clock?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He said he'd be late because you're a moron and he doesn't respect you.

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Did you tell him I was stuck in traffic?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's not always about you.

situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol where his ten o'clock appointment is. Carol bluntly relays that the man is late because he thinks the Boss is a moron and doesn't respect him. When the visitor finally arrives and asks if she passed along that he was stuck in traffic, Carol tells him it's not always about him.
punchline: Carol delivers the visitor's insult to the Boss's face without a flinch, then deadpans that the Boss's feelings aren't the center of the universe when the visitor complains, deflating everyone's ego equally.
summary: A deadpan assistant relays a tardy visitor's honest opinion of her boss and then brushes off the visitor's excuse too.

file: 2003/2003-01-02_dimwitted twins_free long distance_low cost video phones.gif
title: Selling Videophones to Dim Twins

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My plan is to sell low-cost videophones to dim-witted identical twins.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll even throw in free long-distance calling because that's the kind of guy I am.

transcript.speaker: Bald man
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! What are you doing at my girlfriend's house???

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then a bald man's home
situation: Dogbert lounges on the couch next to Dilbert and explains his business plan of selling cheap videophones to dim-witted identical twins, sweetening the deal with free long-distance calling. In the last panel, a bald man looks into a hand mirror on a videophone and panics, thinking his twin is at his girlfriend's house.
punchline: The twin is so dim-witted that he mistakes his own reflection on the videophone for his identical twin, proving Dogbert's scheme preys on exactly the right customers.
summary: Dogbert pitches a scam product to gullible lookalike siblings, and a baffled customer instantly proves the plan will work by misreading a mirror image.

file: 2003/2003-12-20_human resources_evil director_severance package_spittle_laugh_purr_bad package_business.gif
title: Catbert's Spittle Severance Package

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Laid-off Employee
transcript.text: What kind of severance package do I get?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can't decide if I should laugh or purr, but there's definitely spittle in your future.

transcript.speaker: Laid-off Employee
transcript.text: This is a bad package.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purrr-ha-ha ha-purrr-ha ha-purrr!!!

situation: A fired employee asks Catbert, the evil HR director, what severance package she will receive. Catbert can't decide whether to laugh or purr and promises spittle in her future. He then cackles and purrs so hard that he sprays her with saliva, and she realizes she has gotten a bad package.
punchline: Catbert's severance package literally consists of being spat on, a gross and sadistic parody of the usual meagre payout given to laid-off workers.
summary: A dismissed worker learns her parting gift from the sadistic HR cat is a face full of saliva.

file: 2003/2003-08-15_approve plan_software commitee_soar like eagles_millions of dollars_sidetracked_eagles_software_engineering.gif
title: Soaring Eagles Skip Software Approval

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can either wait three months for the software committee to approve our plan...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we can soar like eagles, and act without approval, saving millions of dollars!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't be sidetracked by the analogy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Since when do eagles use software?

situation: Dilbert pitches his boss two options: wait three months for the software committee to approve a plan, or bypass approval and save millions of dollars. He dresses up the second option with an eagle metaphor and asks the boss not to get sidetracked by it. The boss immediately fixates on the metaphor and asks when eagles ever use software.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to inspire the boss with a grand analogy backfires because the boss ignores the substantive proposal and fixates on the silly metaphor, proving Dilbert's fear of him being sidetracked right.
summary: An engineer tries to persuade his boss to skip a slow approval process with a soaring bird metaphor, only for the boss to latch onto the metaphor instead of the money-saving point.

file: 2003/2003-07-27_surplussed ted_absorb function_2 jobs one salary_absorb his funtion_osmosis_symbiosis_syneregy_key learning_tragic series_monkey brained.gif
title: Absorbing a Laid-Off Coworker's Function

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I surplussed Ted. You'll need to absorb his function.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Absorb his function?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you telling me to do two jobs for one salary?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'm telling you to absorb his function... in an absorptive fashion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...Using osmosis, symbiosis, and synergy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you change reality by inventing new names for ordinary things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I sure hope so. Otherwise my entire career has been a... a...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tragic series of monkey-brained mistakes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Key learning.

situation: The Boss announces he has laid off Ted and tells Dilbert to take over Ted's duties. When Dilbert points out this means two jobs for one salary, the Boss rebrands it as 'absorbing' the function through osmosis, symbiosis and synergy. Dilbert asks if renaming things changes reality, and the Boss hopes so, since otherwise his career has been a string of mistakes, which he relabels as 'key learning'.
punchline: The Boss relies on buzzword relabeling to disguise obvious problems, and when Dilbert names his career a series of mistakes, the Boss simply renames it 'key learning', proving his own point.
summary: A manager dumps a fired coworker's workload on an employee and tries to dress it up with fancy jargon, then does the same to his own failures.

file: 2003/2003-07-20_functions to outsorce_dont do well_management_sales_quality control_core competenece_brown table startegy_business.gif
title: Outsourcing Everything Except the Brown Table

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As requested, I put together a list of functions we should outsource.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I limited my list to things we don't do well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Management, sales, marketing, quality control, engineering, finance, human resources, and customer support.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That leaves us with our core competence...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...sitting around a brown table.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And, of course, our ability to speak honestly without fear of retribution.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will never get another raise as long as I'm alive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, that puts a lot of pressure on the brown table strategy.

setting: Conference room during a management presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a list of company functions to outsource, limiting it to things the company does poorly. The list covers nearly every department, leaving only sitting around a brown table as the core competence. When Dilbert adds that employees can speak honestly without fear of retribution, the Boss immediately threatens his future raises.
punchline: The Boss instantly punishes Dilbert for his honest criticism, proving the claim of speaking without retribution false and leaving the company's last supposed strength in doubt.
summary: Dilbert proposes shipping out every function the firm does badly, and when his frankness earns an instant threat from the Boss, the only remaining strategy looks shaky.

file: 2003/2003-04-03_reapir_defective co workers_paramoid_invited to meetings_fix her_trade in_liar_moron_whistler.gif
title: Repair Shop for Defective Co-Workers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Repair defective co-workers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's paranoid about not being invited to meetings. Can you fix her?

transcript.speaker: Repairman
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I trade her in?

transcript.speaker: Repairman
transcript.text: Would you like a liar, a moron, or a whistler?

setting: A storefront shop that repairs defective co-workers
situation: Dilbert drags a co-worker into a repair shop whose window sign advertises fixing defective co-workers. He asks the repairman to cure her paranoia about not being invited to meetings, and the repairman says it can't be done. When Dilbert asks to trade her in, the repairman offers only replacement models that are equally flawed.
punchline: Every replacement co-worker on offer is just as defective, implying that all co-workers come with serious flaws, so swapping one for another gains nothing.
summary: A man tries to get a paranoid colleague fixed at a repair shop, only to learn the replacements available are all worse in different ways.

file: 2003/2003-04-09_body double_despots_most successful_double_take hit_personal dress code_dress intern.gif
title: Boss Gets a Body Double

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need a body double. They're popular with your most successful despots.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If someone tries to ambush you into making a decision, the double will take the hit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to think of this as your own personal dress code.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss to get a body double like successful despots have, so the double can absorb any ambush by people demanding decisions. The Boss then brings in a junior employee and tells him to treat the job of standing in for him as his own personal dress code.
punchline: The Boss hires an employee as a body double and disguises the dangerous, humiliating job as merely a dress code requirement, forcing the underling to dress like him and take the heat.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a decoy stand-in for a manager dodging decisions, and the manager promptly drafts a subordinate and calls it a wardrobe policy.

file: 2003/2003-01-26_boss_dilbert_dont idel well_freaks out_gets phone call_lost connection_meeting_sit still challenge_mind body connection_business.gif
title: Engineers Don't Idle Well

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, come here for a minute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to talk to you about...

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Ring ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's giving me the "wait" signal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have nothing to look at, nothing to fiddle with, nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll try thinking about how my mind controls my muscles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... I'm getting too conscious of my muscles and it's freaking me out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I've lost my mind-body connection!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The problem with engineers is that they don't idle well.

situation: The Boss calls Dilbert over, then answers a phone call and signals him to wait. With nothing to do, Dilbert tries to occupy his mind by thinking about how his mind controls his muscles, becomes overly conscious of them, and ends up flailing on the floor. The Boss, with his feet up and still on the phone, shrugs it off as a typical engineer problem.
punchline: The Boss blames engineers for not idling well, ignoring that he made Dilbert stand around waiting while he chatted on the phone.
summary: Left standing idle while his boss takes a phone call, Dilbert overthinks his own body until he collapses in panic.

file: 2003/2003-01-11_extreme programming._code writing_team_tw programmers_one computer_productive arrangement_whistle both nostrils_saved on harmonicas_business.gif
title: Pair Programming With a Nostril Whistler

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Extreme programming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The two of you will be a code-writing team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Studies prove that two programmers on one computer is the most productive arrangement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sometimes I can whistle through both nostrils. I've saved a fortune in harmonicas.

situation: Under the banner of extreme programming, the Boss pairs Wally and Dilbert and tells them to share a single computer, citing studies that this is the most productive arrangement. Dilbert is stuck at the keyboard with an annoyed expression while Wally sits beside him with a coffee mug and cheerfully announces his odd whistling talent.
punchline: Being forced to share a computer with Wally means Dilbert has to endure his pointless chatter and nostril whistling, which makes the supposedly proven productivity boost of pair programming look absurd.
summary: Two engineers are squeezed onto one computer by management, and the lazy partner fills the time by bragging about an irritating bodily talent.

file: 2003/2003-03-05_chronic lateness_repertoire_classic excuses_traffic_loserville_jinx.gif
title: Wally Plans Chronic Lateness Excuses

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to add chronic lateness to my repertoire.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll start with the classic excuses: car problems, traffic, and misplaced items. Then I'll branch out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're the mayor of Loserville.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't jinx it.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, announces to Dilbert that he is adding chronic lateness to his repertoire of slacking behaviors. He explains he will begin with standard excuses like car trouble, traffic, and misplaced items before inventing new ones. Dilbert calls him the mayor of Loserville, and Wally asks him not to jinx it.
punchline: Wally treats being a loser as a point of pride and fears that Dilbert's insult will somehow ruin his carefully planned career of laziness.
summary: A scheming coworker lays out his strategy for showing up late, then reacts to an insult as if it were bad luck for his plan.

file: 2003/2003-01-31_cat show_clothing_date_good listener_mindless replica_uninteresting stories.gif
title: Dilbert's Clone Gets Asked Out

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Would it be okay if I asked your mindless replica for a date?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm full of uninteresting stories and I need a guy who's a good listener.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Now I'll describe the clothing of each person at the cat show.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thunk!

setting: Office area, then a restaurant table
situation: A woman with a black bob haircut asks Dilbert if she can date his mindless replica, who stands beside him. She explains she tells dull stories and wants a good listener. On the date, she starts describing the clothing of everyone at a cat show, and the replica drives a fork into his own forehead to escape the boredom.
punchline: The woman's stories are so tedious that the supposedly mindless replica would rather stab himself in the head with a fork than keep listening.
summary: A talkative woman picks the vacant-minded double of Dilbert as her ideal date, only to bore him so badly that he resorts to self-harm at dinner.

file: 2003/2003-02-27_toxic tom_new coworker_potatoe_too many questions.gif
title: Toxic Tom Insults Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet your new co-worker, Toxic Tom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He complained about his last job all through his interview. But he'll be happy here.

transcript.speaker: Toxic Tom
transcript.text: He says he thinks you're stupid because you ask too many questions.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to his new co-worker, a smelly, hunched, lumpy brown creature named Toxic Tom. The Boss cheerfully says Tom complained throughout his interview but will be happy here. Tom then mutters an insult at Dilbert, saying he thinks Dilbert is stupid for asking too many questions.
punchline: The Boss hired a chronically negative complainer and assumes he'll suddenly be happy, while Tom immediately demonstrates his toxicity by insulting Dilbert.
summary: A manager introduces a perpetually grumbling new hire to a colleague, confident he will be content, only for the newcomer to promptly belittle his new neighbor.

file: 2003/2003-12-13_feet off desk_random mangement_stock rise_so random_commands.gif
title: Random Management Nudges the Stock Price

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take your feet off the desk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this an example of random management or do you think it will make our stock rise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's up .02%. Heh-heh-heh, not so random after all.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's cubicle and orders him to take his feet off the desk. Dilbert asks whether this is random management or something meant to lift the stock price. Back at his own desk, the Boss checks the stock and gleefully notes it has risen slightly.
punchline: The Boss treats a pointless, arbitrary order as a strategy because the stock ticked up a trivial 0.02%, mistaking coincidence for effective management.
summary: After barking a petty order at an employee, a manager smugly credits it for a tiny uptick in the share price.

file: 2003/2003-08-10_charging hours to project_one meeting_one hour_extensive preparation_evaluated_57 hours_sat quiet_charging.gif
title: Wally Bills Fifty-Eight Hours Per Meeting

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, why have you been charging all of your hours to my project?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I invited you to one meeting. It lasted one hour.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you think I would go to a meeting without extensive preparation?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay... that's another hour.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How many more do you need explained?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: After the meeting, I sat quietly and evaluated what everyone said. That took fifty-seven hours.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ha! You're still an hour short. Explain THAT!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you mind if I sit quietly and think about that question for a while?

situation: Alice confronts Wally about billing all of his hours to her project even though he attended only one one-hour meeting. Wally justifies the charges as preparation time and fifty-seven hours of sitting quietly to evaluate the meeting, and when Alice points out he is still an hour short, he asks for time to sit and think about it.
punchline: Wally turns the last missing hour into another excuse to bill more time by sitting quietly to 'think', showing he will pad his hours no matter what.
summary: A lazy engineer defends charging a full work period to a colleague's project by claiming endless preparation and reflection time, then uses her final challenge to justify yet more idle time.

file: 2003/2003-10-28_employee of week_hose off_company hose_landing pad_helicopter_bird droppings.gif
title: Employee of the Week: Hosing Bird Droppings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, you've been named "Employee of the Week"!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The title gives you access to the executive helicopter landing pad on the roof.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by "access" I mean you hose off the bird droppings every morning.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I get to use the company hose!!!

situation: The Boss tells Asok he has been named Employee of the Week and explains the prize is access to the executive helicopter landing pad. He then reveals that 'access' really means Asok must hose bird droppings off the pad every morning. Asok, still enthusiastic, is thrilled to be allowed to use the company hose.
punchline: The so-called reward is actually an extra chore, and naive, eager Asok is delighted by it anyway, showing how little recognition programs really give employees.
summary: A manager disguises a nasty cleaning duty as a prestigious award, and the overly eager young intern happily accepts it.

file: 2003/2003-02-17_take call_excuse me_inconsiderate guts_crushing head_imagine.gif
title: Excuse Me While I Hate You

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: Excuse me while I take this call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I hate your inconsiderate guts.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: No, nothing important.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I imagine crushing your head.

situation: A coworker interrupts a meeting with Dilbert to take a phone call. Dilbert politely agrees, then uses the same 'excuse me while I...' phrasing to announce that he hates the man's inconsiderate guts and is imagining crushing his head.
punchline: Dilbert mimics the coworker's polite 'excuse me while I...' phrasing to openly voice his hostile thoughts while being ignored.
summary: When a rude colleague stops a meeting to chat on the phone, Dilbert fills the wait by politely announcing his violent resentment.

file: 2003/2003-04-16_excellent all year_rating poor_paper trail_fire you_surge of motivation_feedback.gif
title: Excellent Work, Poor Rating

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, your work has been excellent all year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm rating you "poor" so I'll have a paper trail in case I ever need to fire you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll probably feel a little surge of motivation because you got feedback.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss meets with Asok for an annual performance review and praises his excellent work all year. He then reveals he is giving Asok a "poor" rating anyway, just to create documentation in case he ever wants to fire him. Asok is left in tears while the Boss claims the feedback will motivate him.
punchline: The Boss gives a deliberately false bad review to build a firing paper trail and absurdly insists the unjust, demoralizing feedback will motivate Asok.
summary: A manager tells his best performer he is being rated poorly purely to stockpile evidence for a possible future dismissal, then pretends the news will inspire him.

file: 2003/2003-11-15_produce breakthrough_meeting_coach me_higher perfromance_no hope for progress_business.gif
title: Fantasizing About Meeting Breakthroughs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project has no progress and no hope for progress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I scheduled a meeting so I can fantasize that it will produce a breakthrough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend that we have a meeting next week so you can fantasize that you'll coach me to higher levels of performance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds good.

setting: Office meeting room and the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert stands at a whiteboard and announces that his project is going nowhere. He then tells the Boss he has scheduled a meeting just to fantasize that it will yield a breakthrough. He proposes a follow-up meeting so the Boss can fantasize about coaching him to better performance, and the Boss happily agrees.
punchline: Both Dilbert and the Boss use meetings as a way to indulge comforting fantasies of progress and leadership, with no expectation that anything real will result.
summary: A stalled project leads an engineer to schedule pointless meetings that let both him and his boss pretend that something productive is happening.

file: 2003/2003-05-13_ruler of heck_devils advocate_do devil work_not certified_sarcastic_good time_move on.gif
title: Phil Can't Do Real Devil Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've hired Phil, the Ruler of Heck, to act as devil's advocate.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm not certified to do devil work. The best I can do is roll my eyes and be sarcastic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... moving on...

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Oh yeah, this is a good time to move on.

situation: The Boss, whose hair is styled into devil horns, announces he has hired Phil, the Ruler of Heck, to play devil's advocate in a meeting. Phil, dressed in a red devil costume, explains he is not certified for actual devil work and can only roll his eyes and be sarcastic. When the Boss tries to move on, Phil sarcastically agrees it is a good time to do so.
punchline: The literal-minded hiring of Phil as a devil's advocate results in a mild-mannered sarcastic heckler rather than a genuine critic, and his sarcasm is the only pushback the Boss gets.
summary: A manager brings in a devil-costumed colleague to challenge ideas in a meeting, but the recruit can only offer eye-rolling and sarcasm.

file: 2003/2003-05-21_power to become invisible_sit home_get paid_wally_boss_hiding.gif
title: Wally's Plan to Become Invisible

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Long term, I hope to convince our boss that I have the power to become invisible.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I can just sit home and get paid. Oh, it will be sweet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally? Is that you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Right in front of you.

setting: Office break room table and the Boss's office
situation: Wally eats a banana at a table with a coworker and explains his long-term scheme to convince the Boss he can turn invisible so he can stay home and still collect a paycheck. In the last panel, the Boss sits in his big chair looking confused while Wally crouches in plain sight right in front of him, hiding his face behind his hand.
punchline: Wally's invisibility act is so transparently ridiculous that he is clearly visible, yet the gullible Boss is already starting to wonder if he can be seen at all.
summary: A lazy employee hatches a scheme to get paid for staying home by faking invisibility, and the first trial run has his baffled manager looking right past him.

file: 2003/2003-05-05_new thoughts_head heavier_compensate_meeting_no goals_be on stamp_future golas_business.gif
title: Heavy Head, Stamp-Sized Ambitions

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think my head is getting heavier from all the new thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I plan to compensate by propping it up with my arm during meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some people think you have no goals.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Long term, I hope to be on a stamp.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Wally and Dilbert stand in the break room with coffee mugs. Wally claims his head is getting heavier from new thoughts and says he will prop it up with his arm during meetings. When Dilbert mentions that people think Wally has no goals, Wally says he hopes to be on a stamp someday.
punchline: Wally's idea of a long-term career goal is to be commemorated on a postage stamp, which is a grandiose-sounding ambition that still requires no actual effort, fitting his lazy, do-nothing persona.
summary: Wally jokes that his brain is overloaded and that he'll lean on his own arm at meetings, then answers accusations of aimlessness with an absurdly lofty yet effortless dream.

file: 2003/2003-07-08_a bad day_a worse day_a much worse day_ne job online_trying to fill_unqaulified.gif
title: Job Hunting Reveals Own Position

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A bad day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's time to look for a new job online.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A worse day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, that's my job they're trying to fill.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A much worse day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I'm unqualified.

situation: Dilbert, having a bad day, decides to search online job listings for a new position. He discovers that his own job is being advertised, meaning the company is looking to replace him. He then reads the requirements and realizes he doesn't meet the qualifications for the role he currently holds.
punchline: Dilbert's day keeps getting worse as he learns he is being replaced and that he isn't even qualified for his own job.
summary: A man browsing job ads to escape a lousy day finds his own position listed and then realizes he couldn't even get hired for it.

file: 2003/2003-06-16_international sales call_dress_one level above customer_cherub_lighting bolt_vatican_overdress.gif
title: Dressing Above the Pope's Level

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to go on an international sales call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How should I dress?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Salespeople should dress one level above the customer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's better - the cherub or the lightning bolt?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take both. You can't overdress at the Vatican.

situation: The Boss sends Dilbert on an international sales call and advises him to dress one level above the customer. Dilbert, whose customer turns out to be the Vatican, asks Dogbert for fashion advice while holding a winged cherub and a lightning bolt as accessories. Dogbert tells him to take both.
punchline: If the customer is the Pope, dressing one level above him is impossible, so Dogbert advises going absurdly over the top with divine accessories.
summary: Told to outdress his client, Dilbert seeks wardrobe tips for a sales call to the Vatican and is advised to bring heavenly props.

file: 2003/2003-04-27_customer diservice program_tech supprt_stretched telephone_cleansed online support_useful articles_support groups_train customers.gif
title: Training Customers to Do Everything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've expanded our customer disservice program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...doubled our unhelpful technical support advice.

transcript.speaker: Tech support worker
transcript.text: Uh... reboot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...stretched our telephone hold times to lethal durations...

transcript.speaker: Caller on hold
transcript.text: So... hungry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...and cleansed our online support database of all useful articles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal is to force customers to form support groups.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Over time, with luck, we'll train customers to do our manufacturing and shipping, too.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: May I train a customer to do my job?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So... what do I do?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're doing it.

setting: Conference room and office, with inset panels of a call center and a caller on hold
situation: The Boss proudly presents a series of measures that make customer service worse: useless tech advice, lethal hold times, and a support database stripped of useful articles. He says the goal is to push customers into running their own support groups and eventually doing manufacturing and shipping. A coworker asks to train a customer to do his job, and moments later the customer is sitting at his desk, already doing it.
punchline: The company's strategy of offloading work onto customers is so successful that a customer ends up doing an employee's job for free, and the employee is happily sipping coffee.
summary: A manager brags about wrecking customer support so clients must do the work themselves, and an employee promptly hands his own job to a customer.

file: 2003/2003-03-04_statue_front entrance_unlucky guy_karl_feed birds_serving example.gif
title: The Statue Was Once Karl

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our facilities management says the new statue by the front entrance isn't a statue.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's an unlucky guy named Karl who had been warned many times not to feed the birds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then it talks about statistical clustering... blah, blah, blah... and serving as an example.

situation: The Boss reads from a memo to colleagues seated at the conference table. He reveals that the new statue outside the front entrance is actually an employee named Karl who was turned into one for repeatedly feeding the birds. He then skips ahead through the dull statistical content to the part about Karl serving as an example.
punchline: The company punishes a rule-breaking employee by literally turning him into a statue as a warning to others, while the boss casually reads it out like routine paperwork.
summary: A manager calmly reads a memo explaining that the lobby statue is really a worker who was petrified for ignoring bird-feeding warnings.

file: 2003/2003-08-29_magic management_doubted powers_single employee_hard at work.gif
title: Necklace Warns Employees Boss Approaching

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tinkle tinkle tinkle

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Boss approaching.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks for the magic management necklace! I have to admit that I doubted its powers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But since I've been wearing it, I haven't seen a single employee who wasn't hard at work.

situation: An employee at his computer hears a tinkling sound and thinks 'boss approaching,' then quickly clicks to look busy. The Boss thanks him for a 'magic management necklace' he's been wearing and praises its power, claiming that since he started wearing it he's never seen a slacking employee.
punchline: The necklace's bell announces the boss's arrival, so employees always have time to look busy, and the oblivious boss credits magic instead of his own noisy jewelry.
summary: A jingling necklace gives the boss's approach away to his staff, who instantly look productive, leaving him convinced the trinket has supernatural powers.

file: 2003/2003-12-06_dating_party_phone number_information_email_voicemail_home phone_offcie_work email_personal website_too much info_skeleton_relationships.gif
title: Too Many Ways to Contact

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I've never done this before, but may I have your phone number?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Home phone... cell phone... work phone... home e-mail... work e-mail... other home e-mail... personal web site.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and if that fax machine is out of paper, try the one down the hall, but leave me a voice mail if you do.

setting: A cocktail party or social mixer
situation: At a party, a woman nervously asks Dilbert for his phone number. Dilbert rattles off a long list of phone numbers, email addresses and a website, writing them down for her. By the end he is still adding fax instructions, and the woman has been reduced to a desiccated skeleton-like husk slumped in her chair.
punchline: Dilbert gives so many contact methods and instructions that the woman dies of boredom or old age before he finishes, showing how impossibly complicated he makes a simple request.
summary: A simple request for a phone number turns into an endless recitation of contact options that wears the listener down to a withered corpse.

file: 2003/2003-10-26_boosting prformance_vacation days_use all_recahrged_issed days_copeantetive advantage_retirement_return_15 year vacation_20 years in minutes.gif
title: Fifteen-Year Vacation Before Retirement

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have an idea for boosting my performance.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You wisely coached us to use all of our vacation days every year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Because we come back recharged!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our renewed motivation is more than enough to compensate for the missed days.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My plan is to leverage that competitive advantage.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll take a fifteen year vacation and return ten minutes before retirement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'll be so recharged that I'll pounce and do twenty years of work in minutes!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Unless it's near a holiday, in which case, do you mind if I leave early?

situation: Wally tells The Boss he has a plan to boost his performance, building on the Boss's advice to use all vacation days so employees come back recharged. He proposes taking a fifteen-year vacation and returning just before retirement to do twenty years of work in minutes. The Boss listens silently while Wally ends by asking to leave early if it's near a holiday.
punchline: Wally twists the 'vacation makes you more productive' logic to absurd extremes, justifying doing almost no work at all, then undercuts even his own pounce plan by asking to leave early.
summary: Wally stretches management's claim that time off boosts productivity into a plan to skip most of his career and then cram it all in at the very end.

file: 2003/2003-10-22_hapy_spacious offcie_ocean view_workplace_personalized environemnt_brad pitt.gif
title: Virtual Headset Replaces Real Office

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Who's today's guest cartoonist?*

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm so happy in my new spacious office with an ocean view.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Finally I have the workplace I've always dreamed of.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Employee
transcript.text: The personalized environment headset works, sir.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brad Pitt! Shouldn't you put a shirt on?

setting: Office cubicle, with Dilbert's imagined spacious ocean-view office
situation: Dilbert appears to sit happily in a spacious office with an ocean view, gleefully imagining his dream workplace with suns, hearts, rainbows and music notes. The final panel reveals he is actually in a cramped cubicle wearing a virtual-reality headset. A coworker confirms the headset works, while the Boss, also wearing a headset and seeing something else entirely, thinks Dilbert is Brad Pitt and tells him to put a shirt on.
punchline: Instead of giving employees real offices, the company hands out VR headsets that let them imagine a nicer workplace while they remain stuck in cubicles.
summary: A worker's idyllic seaside office turns out to be a headset illusion masking the dreary cubicle where he actually sits.

file: 2003/2003-06-30_eating tongue_flaming squirrels_project_sanity check_meeting_sanity for project_business.gif
title: Flaming Squirrels Fail Sanity Check

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I called this meeting to do a sanity check on my project.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Flaming squirrels are eating my tongue!!!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?

situation: Asok calls a meeting with his boss and Alice to do a sanity check on his project. He then suddenly shouts that flaming squirrels are eating his tongue. When his colleagues stare at him, he reacts with an innocent 'What?'
punchline: Asok's wild outburst shows he is clearly not sane, which ironically answers his own request for a sanity check, and he doesn't even realize it.
summary: A man asks colleagues to verify his project is rational, then immediately blurts out a bizarre hallucination and acts baffled by their stares.
